h1_text: Zero Click Searches: What They Are and How to Win Anyway
lede: What zero click searches are, how common they are in three studies, whether they hurt SEO, how to be the source of the answer, how to measure value without clicks and a worked example.
copy_text: Home Blog Search Engine Optimization Zero Click Searches: What They Are and How… Guide Search Engine Optimization Zero Click Searches: What They Are and How to Win Anyway What zero click searches are, how common they are in three studies, whether they hurt SEO, how to be the source of the answer, how to measure value without clicks and a worked example. Jamil Ahmed Published 26 Jan 2025 Updated 16 Nov 2026 15 Chapters 12 Min read A to Z Glossary 01 What is a zero click search? 1 min 02 How common are zero click searches? 2 min 03 Do zero click searches hurt SEO? 1 min 04 What is zero click SEO and zero click content? 1 min 05 How do you win anyway? 2 min 06 Does structured data help you win zero click answers? 1 min 07 Where do zero click answers come from? 1 min 08 Which searches are hit hardest? 1 min 09 How do you measure value without clicks? 1 min 10 When does zero click visibility hurt? 1 min 11 Is zero click bad for users? 1 min 12 Worked example: a software review site 1 min 13 What are the common mistakes? 1 min 14 Our interest in this topic 1 min 15 Final thoughts 1 min Chapter 01 of 15 0% read Chapters 0% 01 What is a zero click search? 02 How common are zero click searches? 03 Do zero click searches hurt SEO? 04 What is zero click SEO and zero click content? 05 How do you win anyway? 06 Does structured data help you win zero click answers? 07 Where do zero click answers come from? 08 Which searches are hit hardest? 09 How do you measure value without clicks? 10 When does zero click visibility hurt? 11 Is zero click bad for users? 12 Worked example: a software review site 13 What are the common mistakes? 14 Our interest in this topic 15 Final thoughts About 12 min in total Short answer A zero click search is a search that ends without a click on any result. Roughly 58.5% of US Google searches ended that way in SparkToro's 2024 study, and AI summaries make it more likely. You cannot avoid them. Be the source of the answer, give people a reason to visit, aim at searches where a visit pays, build your name across the web and measure impressions, mentions and leads. 01 A zero click search ends without a click on any result. It may mean the person was satisfied, frustrated or changed the query. 02 SparkToro and Datos (2024): 58.5% of US and 59.7% of EU Google searches had zero clicks. The panel has limits and likely undercounts. 03 Pew (2025): people clicked a regular result in 8% of visits with an AI summary and 15% without, and 1% inside the summary. Google disputes the method. 04 Bain (Dec 2024, 1,117 consumers): about 80% rely on zero click results in at least 40% of searches. Bain estimates organic traffic falls 15% to 25%. 05 You cannot avoid zero click searches. Be the source, give people a reason to visit, and target searches where a visit pays. 06 Measure impressions, Google's Generative AI performance report, branded search, mentions and leads, not clicks alone. 07 Decide page by page what an appearance and a visit are worth. A zero click search is a search that ends without the person clicking any result. Some are answered on the results page, such as a weather check, a store opening time, a definition or an AI summary. Others end because the person changes the query or gives up. You cannot avoid zero click searches, and no one can stop Google from answering questions on its own page. What you can do is be the source those answers use, be named in them, and earn the clicks that still happen. This guide explains what zero click searches are, how common they are, what the data says about clicks and AI summaries, and how to win anyway. It covers the content that tends to be used in answers, how to measure value without clicks, when zero click visibility hurts and a worked example. We cite only studies we could read at the publisher, and we state the limits of each. This page replaces an older post on the same address. 01 Chapter 1 · 1 min What is a zero click search? A zero click search is a search on which the person never clicks a result. SparkToro, whose 2024 study is the best-known count, defines it as a search that ends without clicking on any of the results presented. That includes searches where the person was satisfied, searches where they were frustrated, and searches where they changed the query and tried again. So “zero click” does not always mean the page gave a full answer. The answer can come from several places on the page: a featured snippet, a knowledge panel, a weather or sports box, a map pack, “People also ask”, a calculator or, increasingly, an AI summary such as Google’s AI Overviews. People also get answers from AI tools such as ChatGPT, where there is no results page at all. End of chapter 1 Next: How common are zero click searches? → 02 Chapter 2 · 2 min How common are zero click searches? Three studies give a picture. They use different methods, so do not add them together. SparkToro and Datos (2024). Using clickstream data from Datos, a Semrush company, for September 2022 to May 2024, SparkToro found that 58.5% of US Google searches and 59.7% of EU searches ended with zero clicks. About 37% of searches ended the session, and about 22% led to a new query. SparkToro’s own headline is that, of every 1,000 US Google searches, 374 clicks go to the open web. Limits: the panel has little coverage of iPhones and iPads, mobile data starts in January 2024, ad blockers may distort paid search counts, and SparkToro says it is likely undercounting zero click behavior because it misses voice answers and the Google app. Pew Research Center (2025). Pew tracked the browsing of 900 US adults in March 2025, covering 68,879 Google searches, of which 12,593 produced an AI summary. People clicked a regular result link in 8% of visits to pages with an AI summary and 15% of visits to pages without one, and clicked a link inside the summary in 1% of visits. Around two-thirds of all searches ended in either more browsing on Google or leaving without a click. Google disputes Pew’s method and says it does not see significant drops in aggregate web traffic. Bain and Dynata (2024). Bain surveyed 1,117 consumers in December 2024 and reported that about 80% rely on zero click results in at least 40% of their searches, and estimated that this reduces organic web traffic by 15% to 25%. It also said about 60% of searches on traditional engines now end without a visit to another site. This is a survey with an estimate attached, and the traffic figure is Bain’s own estimate. The direction is clear in all three: many searches end on the results page, and AI summaries make that more likely. The exact size depends on the method, the country and the type of search. Informational searches are affected most. End of chapter 2 Next: Do zero click searches hurt SEO? → Reinforce Lab service · AI Search Optimization Want to be the source of the answer? Reinforce Lab starts with a free diagnostic of your Google and AI search visibility and a 90-day plan. See AI search optimization → Or get a free diagnostic first 03 Chapter 3 · 1 min Do zero click searches hurt SEO? They change what SEO is worth, but they do not end it. If your business depends on clicks for simple questions, such as “what is X” or “opening hours”, you will see less traffic from those queries. If your business depends on buyers who compare, decide and contact you, those searches still produce clicks, and the answers you appear in can add awareness before the click. Bain’s view is that SEO alone will not be enough, and that brands should keep refining it while testing how to be visible in AI summaries and AI tools. So the useful questions are these. Which of your pages target queries that Google answers on its own page? Does a click on those pages make you money? And could being named in the answer help you in ways you can measure? End of chapter 3 Next: What is zero click SEO and zero click content? → 04 Chapter 4 · 1 min What is zero click SEO and zero click content? Zero click SEO means optimizing so you still gain value when the searcher does not click. Your brand is shown, your answer is quoted and people remember you. Zero click content is content built to give its value on the spot, such as a clear answer in a snippet, a useful social post or a short video, with a next step for readers who want more. You measure both by impressions, brand searches and later leads, not clicks alone. End of chapter 4 Next: How do you win anyway? → 05 Chapter 5 · 2 min How do you win anyway? 1. Be the source of the answer For queries that show a featured snippet or an AI summary, write the answer in the first sentence or two under a clear heading, then add detail. Use the question as the heading when it reads naturally, keep paragraphs short and add lists and tables where they help. Our guide to how to rank in AI Overviews explains what Google says about eligibility: a page must be indexed and eligible to show with a snippet. 2. Give people a reason to click An answer box shows a fact. A click is worth it when the page offers more: a worked example, a template, a calculator, original data, a comparison or a way to take the next step. Write the first lines so that they answer, and the rest so that it earns the visit. Do not hide the answer to force a click, because it harms trust and may lose the snippet. 3. Target searches where clicks still happen Buying and comparison searches, such as “best X for Y”, “X vs Y” and “X pricing”, tend to produce more clicks than simple fact questions. Pew found that clicks to regular results fall when an AI summary appears. We expect buying and comparison searches to hold up better than simple facts, but we found no study that measures this, so check your own Search Console data. Build your keyword plan around searches where a visit creates value, and treat simple fact queries as awareness. 4. Be named, not only linked People who see your brand in an answer may search for you later, visit directly or ask a colleague. Build the signals that lead to a mention: consistent facts about your business across your site and profiles, honest reviews, and mentions on the sites that answers cite. Our guides to checking if AI tools mention your brand and generative engine optimization cover this work. 5. Use your own listings For local businesses, many zero click answers are map packs and business profiles. Keep your Google Business Profile complete and accurate, answer questions on it, add photos and respond to reviews. Calls and direction requests count as results even though no one visits your website. 6. Own the channels you control Give searchers a way to stay in touch: an email list, a useful tool or a community. If a click is rarer, each visit is worth more to you when you capture the relationship. End of chapter 5 Next: Does structured data help you win zero click answers? → 06 Chapter 6 · 1 min Does structured data help you win zero click answers? It can help with clarity, but it is not a switch. Google says that structured data is not required for its generative AI search features and that no special schema.org markup is needed, although it is a good idea to keep using it because it helps with eligibility for rich results. Use markup that matches the page, such as Article, Organization and Product, and validate it. Then focus on the things that decide whether you are used as a source: a clear answer under a clear heading, an indexable page that can show with a snippet, accurate and current facts, and signs of real expertise. Search intent matters too. If the searcher wants a quick fact, an answer box may fully satisfy them. If they want to choose, compare or act, a page that helps them do so still has value. End of chapter 6 Next: Where do zero click answers come from? → 07 Chapter 7 · 1 min Where do zero click answers come from? Answer type What it is What you can influence Featured snippet A short answer taken from a page, shown above the results Write a clear answer under a matching heading, and keep the page indexable AI summary A written answer with links, such as Google’s AI Overviews and AI Mode Be eligible and useful, answer first, support claims with sources Knowledge panel A fact box about a person, place or company Clear facts, consistent profiles, independent coverage. Panels are generated automatically. People also ask Expandable questions with short answers Answer related questions inside your page Map pack and business profile Local listings with hours, calls and directions A complete, accurate Google Business Profile and honest reviews Direct answer boxes Weather, sports, conversions, definitions and calculators Very little. These come from data partners or Google tools. This list shows why one plan does not fit every query. For some answers you can compete. For others you cannot, and it is wiser to move your effort to searches where a visit still pays. End of chapter 7 Next: Which searches are hit hardest? → 08 Chapter 8 · 1 min Which searches are hit hardest? Informational searches that have a short, stable answer are hit hardest. Examples are definitions, facts, conversions, times and simple how-to steps. Searches that need a choice, a comparison, a price or a person, such as “best accountant for a small restaurant”, still send people to pages, because an AI summary cannot make the decision for them. Studies agree on the direction, but we found no study that splits the effect by industry, so use your own Search Console data. Filter by query type, such as questions versus “best” and “vs” terms, and see which groups lost clicks while holding impressions. Those are the pages where an answer box or summary is taking your visit. For these pages, decide between three options. You can keep the page and strengthen it with something worth a visit. You can merge it into a stronger guide. Or you can leave it as is, because the page still wins awareness and costs nothing to keep. Do not delete pages in a hurry. Changes to live URLs on a business site need a plan for redirects and a check of what the page earns. End of chapter 8 Next: How do you measure value without clicks? → 09 Chapter 9 · 1 min How do you measure value without clicks? Clicks and sessions no longer tell the whole story. Track these as well: Impressions and click-through rate in Search Console, by page and query. A page can gain impressions while clicks fall, which may mean you appear in answers. Google’s Generative AI performance report in Search Console, which shows impressions in AI Overviews and AI Mode. Branded search and direct traffic, which may rise when people see your name in answers. Mentions and citations across a fixed prompt list in AI tools. SparkToro found less than a 1 in 100 chance that the same prompt returns the same list of brands twice, so run each prompt several times. Business results: leads, calls, direction requests and sales, tracked by source, with a “how did you hear about us” question. Be careful with causes. If clicks fall and impressions rise, an AI summary may be the reason, but seasons, rankings and competitors also change results. Check the queries before you decide. End of chapter 9 Next: When does zero click visibility hurt? → 10 Chapter 10 · 1 min When does zero click visibility hurt? Zero click visibility is a poor goal when your content only gives away something you sell by the click, such as a simple fact that your site monetizes with ads, or when you lack any way to benefit from awareness. It is a good goal when buyers who see your name later contact you, when you sell something that the answer cannot give, or when your brand is trying to be known in a market. Decide by page. For each important page, ask what a visit is worth, what an appearance in an answer is worth, and which one you can measure. A short checklist helps for each important page. What question does the page answer? Does Google answer it on the results page? What does a visit earn you today? What would an appearance in the answer earn you? If a visit earns little and an appearance earns nothing you can measure, the page is a candidate for a merge. If a visit earns a lead, protect it and add the reasons to click that the answer box cannot give. End of chapter 10 Next: Is zero click bad for users? → 11 Chapter 11 · 1 min Is zero click bad for users? Often it is good. A quick answer saves time when the question is simple, such as a time zone or a unit conversion. It can be bad when the answer is wrong, thin or lacks context, or when it hides the original source. Google’s AI features show links, and OpenAI says ChatGPT search results and citations can be incomplete, outdated or incorrect. Readers should open a source when accuracy matters, and publishers should make their sources clear and their facts current. End of chapter 11 Next: Worked example: a software review site → 12 Chapter 12 · 1 min Worked example: a software review site This is an illustration, not a client result. Imagine a site that explains accounting software to small businesses. Its definition pages, such as “what is accrual accounting”, lost clicks over the past year, while impressions stayed flat. Its comparison pages still bring leads. The team lists 40 pages and sorts them by what a visit is worth. For 12 definition pages, it keeps a clear answer at the top, adds a worked example and a template, and links to the related comparison. It stops writing new pages for simple facts. For 10 comparison pages, it updates tables, dates and sources. It claims its profiles on two software review sites, since AI answers cite them. It tests 15 buyer questions three times each in three AI tools, and records whether the site is named and cited. After 90 days it compares impressions, clicks, newsletter signups and demo requests for each group with the starting numbers, and the prompt results with the baseline. If definition pages still lose clicks but bring signups through the template, it keeps them. If not, it merges them into stronger guides. End of chapter 12 Next: What are the common mistakes? → 13 Chapter 13 · 1 min What are the common mistakes? Trying to avoid zero click searches. You cannot control what Google shows. Aim to be in the answer and earn the next step. Hiding the answer to force a click. It reduces trust and the chance of being quoted. Judging success by clicks alone. Track impressions, mentions, branded search and leads. Making many thin pages for simple facts. Google calls pages made to manipulate results scaled content abuse. Ignoring your own profiles. For local and service searches, listings often are the answer. Treating studies as exact. Each has limits, and numbers differ by method. End of chapter 13 Next: Our interest in this topic → 14 Chapter 14 · 1 min Our interest in this topic Reinforce Lab sells search and AI search services. Nothing here is paid placement. Jamil Ahmed, who wrote this guide, is a Semrush Ambassador, and Reinforce Lab uses affiliate links for some tools. SparkToro’s study used data from Datos, which is owned by Semrush. Read our FTC and affiliate disclosure . You can read about our AI search optimization service or get your free diagnostic . End of chapter 14 Next: Final thoughts → 15 Chapter 15 · 1 min Final thoughts Zero click searches are part of search now, and AI summaries add to them. Do not fight them. Answer first so you can be the source, give people a reason to visit, aim at searches where a visit pays, build your name across the web and measure results beyond clicks. Decide page by page what an appearance and a visit are worth. Back matter Glossary A to Z A AI Overview A short AI-written summary at the top of some Google results, with links. B Branded search A search that includes your company or product name. C Clickstream data Records of the pages people visit and the clicks they make, collected from a panel. F Featured snippet An answer box that Google shows at the top of some results. I Impression One showing of your page in search results, whether or not it is clicked. Z Zero click search A search that ends without a click on any result. Questions FAQs What is a zero click search? A search that ends without the person clicking any result. It includes searches answered on the page, searches where the person gave up and searches where they changed the query. SparkToro defines it as ending without clicking any presented result. How common are zero click searches? SparkToro and Datos found 58.5% of US and 59.7% of EU Google searches had zero clicks between September 2022 and May 2024. Pew and Bain report similar direction with different methods. Numbers vary by method, country and query type. Do zero click searches hurt SEO? They reduce clicks on simple questions and change what SEO is worth. Buying and comparison searches still produce visits, and being named in an answer can add awareness. Check which of your pages depend on clicks from simple queries. Are zero click searches bad for users? Often not: a quick answer saves time for simple questions. They are a problem when the answer is wrong, thin or hides its source. OpenAI says ChatGPT search results and citations can be incomplete, outdated or incorrect, so open a source when accuracy matters. How do AI Overviews affect clicks? Pew tracked 900 US adults in March 2025: people clicked a regular result in 8% of visits with an AI summary and 15% without, and clicked a link inside the summary in 1% of visits. Google disputes the study's method. How do you optimize for zero click searches? Put a clear answer in the first sentence under a question heading, keep facts current and sourced, make pages indexable and snippet-eligible, add something worth a visit, and build mentions on other sites. No one can guarantee a snippet or AI citation. Is there value in zero click searches? Yes. Being named in an answer can raise branded search and direct visits, and local answers such as map packs bring calls and direction requests. Measure impressions, branded search, mentions and leads, not clicks alone. How do you measure zero click performance? Track impressions and click-through rate in Search Console, Google's Generative AI performance report, branded search, mentions and citations across a fixed prompt list, and leads or calls by source with a how-did-you-hear question. When should you not chase zero click visibility? When a page only gives away something you earn from per click and you cannot benefit from awareness. It is worth chasing when buyers who see your name later contact you, or when you need to be known in a market. Can you avoid zero click searches? No. You cannot control what Google shows. Aim to be the source of the answer, give people a reason to visit and target searches where a visit creates value. What is zero click SEO? It is optimizing so that you gain value even when searchers do not click, through brand exposure, quoted answers and later brand searches. What is zero click content? Content built to give its value without a click, such as a clear answer, a useful post or a short video, with an easy next step for those who want more. title: Local SEO Audit: 12-Step Checklist | Reinforce Lab
meta: A 12-step local SEO audit you can do yourself: Google Business Profile, citations, reviews, website, links and AI search, with a checklist and worked example.
h1_text: Local SEO Audit: A 12-Step Checklist You Can Do Yourself
lede: A 12-step local SEO audit covering Google Business Profile, citations, reviews, website, links, competitors, tracking and AI search, with a checklist, worked example and report template.
copy_text: Home Blog Local SEO Local SEO Audit: A 12-Step Checklist You Can… How-To Local SEO Local SEO Audit: A 12-Step Checklist You Can Do Yourself A 12-step local SEO audit covering Google Business Profile, citations, reviews, website, links, competitors, tracking and AI search, with a checklist, worked example and report template. Jamil Ahmed Published 20 Jan 2025 Updated 13 Nov 2026 Steps 01 What is a local SEO audit? 02 Why should you run a local SEO audit? 03 What does a local SEO audit include? 04 How does Google decide who appears in local results? 05 Service-area businesses and more than one location 06 How to read your reviews like an auditor 07 How to write a local title and description 08 What local schema markup looks like 09 How voice and mobile searches change the audit 10 Before you start: what you need 11 Step 1: Check your Google Business Profile 12 Step 2: Check your NAP and citations 13 Step 3: Audit your reviews 14 Step 4: Check your local keywords 15 Step 5: Audit your website for local SEO 16 Step 6: Check your map and local pack position 17 Step 7: Check your local links 18 Step 8: Check your competitors 19 Step 9: Check your tracking 20 Step 10: Check technical basics 21 Step 11: Check AI search visibility 22 Step 12: Write your fix list 23 A worked example: a plumbing company 24 Local SEO audit tools 25 What goes in a local SEO audit report? 26 How long does a local SEO audit take? 27 Common local SEO audit mistakes 28 A quick local SEO audit checklist 29 Final thoughts 0 of 29 done Short answer A local SEO audit checks how well your business appears in local results, Google Maps and AI answers. Check your Google Business Profile, citations, reviews, local keywords, website, local pack position, links, competitors, tracking, technical basics and AI search, then write a prioritized fix list and repeat it each year. 01 Run a full local SEO audit once a year and a short check each quarter. 02 Start with your Google Business Profile. For many local businesses it matters as much as the website. 03 Keep your name, address and phone number identical on every listing. 04 Reviews affect ranking and choice: ask every customer, reply to all, and never buy or write them. 05 Compare yourself with the three rivals that appear most often, and fill the gaps. 06 Sort fixes by impact and effort, then check again after 30 days. 07 Google says local results rest on relevance, distance and prominence, so each audit area feeds one of them. A local SEO audit is a check of how well your business shows up when people search for something near them. It looks at your Google Business Profile, your website, your listings, your reviews and your links, and it ends with a list of fixes in order of importance. This guide gives you a 12-step local SEO audit you can do yourself, with a checklist, a worked example, a report template and the tools you need. It works for shops, clinics, restaurants, trades, agencies and any business that serves customers in a set area. 1 Step 1 of 29 What is a local SEO audit? A local SEO audit is a structured review of the things that decide whether your business appears in Google’s local results, Google Maps and AI answers for searches such as “plumber near me” or “accountant in Leeds.” It answers four questions: Can searchers find you, and is the information about you correct? Do you look trustworthy compared with nearby rivals? Does your website match what local searchers want? What should you fix first? Mark step 1 done 2 Step 2 of 29 Why should you run a local SEO audit? Wrong details lose customers. A wrong phone number or old opening hours sends people to a rival. Local results change. New rivals, new reviews and new Google features change who appears. It shows quick wins. Most audits find simple fixes that take hours, not weeks. It guides your budget. You see which fix is worth your time first. It sets a baseline. You can measure progress against it. Run a full audit once a year and a short check every quarter. Mark step 2 done 3 Step 3 of 29 What does a local SEO audit include? Area What you check Google Business Profile Name, address, phone, category, hours, services, photos, posts and questions Citations and listings Whether your details are correct and the same across directories Reviews Number, rating, recent activity and how you reply Website Local pages, titles, content, speed, mobile layout and schema Links Local and relevant sites that link to you Rankings and visibility Where you appear for local searches, on the map and in normal results Competitors What the top businesses do that you do not Tracking Whether you can see calls, direction requests and form fills Mark step 3 done 4 Step 4 of 29 How does Google decide who appears in local results? Google says local results are based mainly on three things: relevance, distance and prominence. Knowing them helps you read your audit. Relevance is how well your profile matches what the person searched for. A complete profile with the right categories and clear services helps Google see that you fit the search. Distance is how far your business is from the searcher, or from the place named in the search. You cannot change where you are, but you can make sure your address and service area are right. Prominence is how well known your business is. It comes from reviews, links, mentions and how often people search for you by name. Google also says that good SEO practice helps your website’s role in local ranking. This is why the audit covers so many areas. The profile feeds relevance. The address feeds distance. Reviews, links and citations feed prominence. A gap in one of them can hold back the others. Mark step 4 done 5 Step 5 of 29 Service-area businesses and more than one location Some businesses go to the customer, such as plumbers, cleaners and mobile mechanics. These are called service-area businesses. They can hide their street address on their profile and list the areas they serve instead. The audit for them has two extra checks. First, confirm that the service areas match the places where you really work and do not list more than you can cover. Second, make sure your website has a page for each main area, with real detail about that area, such as typical jobs, local landmarks and customer comments. If you have several locations, audit each one. Every site should have its own profile, its own page and its own reviews. Keep one row per location in your spreadsheet with its profile status, review count, rating, local page and monthly calls. This makes it easy to see which site needs the most work, and it stops one good location from hiding a weak one. Mark step 5 done 6 Step 6 of 29 How to read your reviews like an auditor When you read reviews for the audit, do not stop at the star rating. Look at the words customers use. If several reviews say “fast reply” or “clean and tidy,” those are things you can put on your website and use as proof. If several mention long waits or unclear prices, those are problems to fix in the business, and no amount of SEO will cover them up. Also look at how rivals reply. A calm, short reply that names the problem and offers to fix it shows future customers how you treat people. Copy that approach. Avoid long arguments, and never share private details about a customer in a public reply. Aim for a steady flow of new reviews rather than a burst, since a burst can look odd and a steady flow shows an active business. Mark step 6 done 7 Step 7 of 29 How to write a local title and description The page title is one of the clearest signals of what a page is about, and it is the first thing a searcher sees. For local pages, put the service first, then the place, then your name. Keep it near 60 characters so it is not cut off in the results. For example, a weak title is “Home | Smith and Sons.” A better one is “Emergency Plumber in Leeds | Smith and Sons.” The second tells both people and search engines what the page is for and where. The meta description is the short text under the title. Use it to say what you offer, where and why to call, in a sentence or two. A good one reads like a helpful answer, not a list of keywords. Mark step 7 done 8 Step 8 of 29 What local schema markup looks like Schema markup is code that you add to a page to describe it to search engines. For a local business, it states the business type, name, address, phone number, opening hours, the areas you serve and links to your profiles. It does not change what visitors see. It helps search engines read the page correctly. Many SEO plugins for WordPress and other platforms can add it for you. In the audit, check that the details in the markup match your profile and your page exactly, since a mismatch sends mixed signals. Mark step 8 done 9 Step 9 of 29 How voice and mobile searches change the audit Many local searches are made on a phone, often while walking or driving, and some are spoken to an assistant. People use full questions such as “Where can I find a plumber open now?” Your audit should test for this. Check that your hours are correct and easy to find, that your phone number is clickable, that your pages answer common questions in plain words and that your address is easy to copy into a map. Short answers near the top of a page and a short FAQ section help here, since they match how people ask. Mark step 9 done 10 Step 10 of 29 Before you start: what you need Your exact business name, address and phone number (NAP) as you want it shown Access to your Google Business Profile, website and Google Search Console A spreadsheet for notes, with one tab for each area A list of five to ten searches a customer would use, such as “[service] in [town]” Your three closest local rivals Use a private browser window when you search, so your history changes the results less. Also check from a phone, because local searches are often made on one. Mark step 10 done 11 Step 11 of 29 Step 1: Check your Google Business Profile This is the most important step for most local businesses. Open your profile and check every field. Field What good looks like Business name Your real name, with no added keywords Primary category The one that best describes your main service Other categories A few that are true for your business Address and service area Correct, and the service area matches where you really work Phone and website Correct, working, with a link to the right page Hours Current, including holiday hours Services or products Listed with short, plain descriptions Photos Recent, real photos of the place, team and work Posts and updates Recent Questions and answers Common questions answered Fix what is wrong as you go. Check also that no duplicate profile exists for the same business, since duplicates split reviews and confuse customers. Mark step 11 done 12 Step 12 of 29 Step 2: Check your NAP and citations A citation is any online mention of your business name, address and phone number, such as a directory listing. Search engines compare these to confirm your details. Search your business name and phone number in Google and note every listing that appears. Check the main ones: Google, Bing Places, Apple Maps, Facebook, Yelp where it applies, and the top directories for your trade or country. Write the details you find in a table and mark any that differ. Fix wrong details, and remove or merge duplicates. Small differences count. “Street” and “St.” or a different suite number can look like a different business. Use one format and repeat it exactly. Mark step 12 done 13 Step 13 of 29 Step 3: Audit your reviews Reviews affect both ranking and whether a customer picks you. Count and rating. Compare your number of reviews and your average with the three rivals. Recent activity. A page of old reviews looks stale. Look for reviews in the last three months. Replies. Check whether you reply to reviews, good and bad, in a calm and short way. Themes. Read the reviews for patterns: what customers praise and what they complain about. Your process. Do you ask every customer for a review? A direct link by text or email makes it easy. Do not buy reviews or write your own. Review platforms can remove them, and some countries treat fake reviews as unfair practice. Mark step 13 done 14 Step 14 of 29 Step 4: Check your local keywords Local keywords combine a service with a place, such as “emergency plumber Leeds” or “family lawyer near me.” Do this: List your main services and the places you serve. Use a keyword tool to check volume for each combination. Search the top ones in Google and note who appears in the map results and in the normal results. Note which searches your business already appears for in Search Console. Match each important keyword to one page on your site. If you have no page for a service or place that matters, add it to your fix list. Mark step 14 done 15 Step 15 of 29 Step 5: Audit your website for local SEO Open your site on a phone and on a computer. Check these things. Pages A page for each main service A page for each location, with its own address, hours, map and details A contact page with your NAP, a map and a form Titles and headings Each page title names the service and the place, and is under about 60 characters Each page has one main heading and clear subheadings Content Real local detail: areas you serve, local examples, parking, landmarks and local reviews No copied pages with only the town name swapped Speed and mobile Pages load fast on a phone Click-to-call number and clear buttons Schema markup Local business data with your name, address, phone, hours and area served Mark step 15 done 16 Step 16 of 29 Step 6: Check your map and local pack position The local pack is the box of three businesses with a map at the top of many local results. Check where you appear. Search each key local phrase from a phone, in a private window. Note whether you appear in the pack, in Maps or only in the normal results. Note who appears instead and what is different about them: reviews, distance, categories, photos or website. Results change with the searcher’s location. A business a few streets closer to the searcher may rank higher. That is normal. Look at the pattern across several searches, not one. Mark step 16 done 17 Step 17 of 29 Step 7: Check your local links Links from relevant local sites help you rank. Check who links to you and who links to your rivals. Look for local news, chambers of commerce, trade bodies, schools, charities and local blogs Note links your rivals have that you lack Note any links from poor or unrelated sites Plan honest ways to earn links: sponsor a local event, join your trade body, offer an expert tip to a local paper or partner with a nearby business. Do not buy links. Google’s spam policies treat buying links to affect rankings as link spam. Mark step 17 done 18 Step 18 of 29 Step 8: Check your competitors Compare yourself with the three businesses that appear most often for your key searches. Use a table. Check You Rival A Rival B Rival C Number of reviews Average rating Number of photos Categories used Service pages on the website Location pages Recent posts or updates Fill it in. The gaps tell you what to do first. Mark step 18 done 19 Step 19 of 29 Step 9: Check your tracking If you cannot measure results, you cannot tell what works. Is Google Search Console connected and verified? Is Google Analytics set up with events for calls, form submissions and clicks on directions? Do you use a call tracking number or ask customers how they found you? Do you review the Business Profile performance report, which shows calls, direction requests and website clicks? Mark step 19 done 20 Step 20 of 29 Step 10: Check technical basics Indexing. Your key pages should appear in Google. Search for your page title in quotes to check. HTTPS. The whole site should load securely. Broken links and pages. Fix or redirect them. Duplicate content. Merge near-copies. Accessibility. Readable text, good contrast, labelled forms. Mark step 20 done 21 Step 21 of 29 Step 11: Check AI search visibility More people ask AI tools for local options. Test it yourself. Ask ChatGPT, Google’s AI answers and another AI tool the questions a customer would ask, such as “best family dentist in [town].” Note whether your business appears, what is said about it and whether the details are correct. Note the sources the tools use, such as review sites or directories. If details are wrong, fix them at the source: your profile, your site and your listings. There is no way to force an AI tool to name you, but accurate facts, good reviews and clear pages help. Mark step 21 done 22 Step 22 of 29 Step 12: Write your fix list Put every issue in a table with three columns: the problem, the impact and the effort. Then sort. Priority Type Examples 1 High impact, low effort Wrong phone number, missing category, no review request process 2 High impact, higher effort New service pages, location pages, review growth plan 3 Lower impact, low effort Add photos, answer questions on your profile, fix small listing errors 4 Longer term Link building, content program, reporting setup Work from the top. Re-check after 30 days. Mark step 22 done 23 Step 23 of 29 A worked example: a plumbing company This example is illustrative. A plumbing company with one office covers three towns. It runs the 12 steps and finds this. Area Finding Fix Profile Primary category is “Contractor” Change to “Plumber” and add “Water heater installer” as another Citations Two directories show an old phone number Correct both and merge one duplicate Reviews Fewer reviews than two rivals, no replies Send a review link after each job and reply to all reviews Website One page for all services, no town pages Create separate pages for the three main services and one for each town Links No local links Join the trade body and sponsor a local youth team with a link Tracking No call tracking Set up call events and ask new customers how they found the company The owner fixes the first three rows in one week. The new service and town pages take a month. After 90 days, the company repeats the audit and compares calls and direction requests with the first month. Mark step 23 done 24 Step 24 of 29 Local SEO audit tools Tool type Examples Use Google tools Google Business Profile, Search Console, Analytics Free, accurate data on your own performance Local SEO suites BrightLocal, Semrush, Moz Local, Whitespark and similar Citation checks, rank tracking by location and review monitoring Site crawlers Screaming Frog, Sitebulb and similar Find technical problems across your pages Speed tests PageSpeed Insights Check mobile loading You can do a good first audit with free tools only. Paid tools save time when you manage many locations or clients. Mark step 24 done 25 Step 25 of 29 What goes in a local SEO audit report? If you share the audit with a boss, a client or a team, keep the report short and clear. Summary. Three or four sentences: the main findings and the top actions. Scorecard. A simple rating for each area, for example good, needs work, urgent. Findings. One short section per area with screenshots. Competitor comparison. The table from step 8. Action plan. The prioritized fix list, with owners and dates. Next review date. Usually in 30 to 90 days. Mark step 25 done 26 Step 26 of 29 How long does a local SEO audit take? A small business with one location can finish a first pass in a day. Several locations, or a large site, can take a week or more. The fixes take longer than the audit. Google says changes can take hours to months to show, so give them time and check progress in 30, 60 and 90 days. Mark step 26 done 27 Step 27 of 29 Common local SEO audit mistakes Looking only at the website. For local searches, the Business Profile often matters more. Checking from one place. Results vary by location and device. Ignoring reviews. They shape both ranking and choice. Fixing nothing. An audit is only useful if you act on it. Fixing everything at once. Work in priority order and measure. Skipping the follow-up. Repeat the checks every quarter. Mark step 27 done 28 Step 28 of 29 A quick local SEO audit checklist Profile complete, correct category, hours and services NAP identical across listings, no duplicates Steady reviews and replies to all of them A page for each main service and each location Titles with service and place, local schema, fast mobile pages A few honest local links Calls, directions and form fills tracked Checked in Google, Maps and AI tools A prioritized fix list and a date for the next audit Mark step 28 done 29 Step 29 of 29 Final thoughts A local SEO audit shows where customers lose you and where they can find you. Do the 12 steps, fix the high-impact items first and check again in a month. Repeat the audit each year, and keep a short quarterly check in your calendar. Mark step 29 done Done: all steps complete Your progress 0 of 29 steps done Back matter Glossary A to Z N NAP Name, address and phone number. They should match everywhere online. C Citation Any online mention of your business name, address and phone number, such as a directory listing. L Local pack The box of three local businesses with a map that appears at the top of many local searches. G Google Business Profile Your free listing in Google Search and Maps. S Schema markup Code that tells search engines what a page is about, such as a local business and its address. Questions FAQs What is a local SEO audit? A local SEO audit is a structured review of how well your business appears in local search, Google Maps and AI answers. It checks your Google Business Profile, listings, reviews, website, links and tracking, and ends with a prioritized list of fixes. How do I do a local SEO audit? Check your Google Business Profile, citations, reviews, local keywords, website pages, local pack position, links, competitors, tracking, technical basics and AI search results. Then write a fix list sorted by impact and effort. How long does a local SEO audit take? A small business with one location can finish a first pass in a day. Several locations or a large site can take a week or more. The fixes usually take longer than the audit. How often should I run a local SEO audit? Run a full audit once a year and a short check every quarter. Check sooner after a move, a rebrand, a new location or a drop in calls. What tools do I need for a local SEO audit? You can do a good first audit with free tools: Google Business Profile, Search Console, Analytics and PageSpeed Insights. Paid tools such as BrightLocal, Semrush or Moz Local save time with many locations. What is NAP and why does it matter? NAP is your business name, address and phone number. Search engines compare it across the web to confirm your business is real, so it should be identical everywhere. How do I improve my local SEO after an audit? Fix the high-impact, low-effort items first, such as wrong details, categories and a review request process. Then build service and location pages, grow reviews and earn honest local links, and check again after 30 days. Do reviews affect local SEO? Yes. Reviews are part of how Google judges how well known and trusted a business is, and they strongly affect whether a customer picks you. Ask every customer, reply to every review and never buy or write your own. Is a local SEO audit different from a regular SEO audit? Yes. A regular audit focuses on the website. A local audit adds your Google Business Profile, citations, reviews, local pack position and local links, which often matter more for searches tied to a place. Can AI tools show my local business? Yes, they can draw on your site, profile, reviews and listings. Check what they say about you, fix wrong details at the source and keep your facts consistent. No method guarantees a mention. copy_text: Home Blog Search Engine Optimization How to Optimize LinkedIn Profile For SEO 2025 How-To Search Engine Optimization How to Optimize LinkedIn Profile For SEO 2025 R Reinforce Lab team Published 23 Feb 2025 Updated 13 Apr 2025 Steps 01 How to Optimize LinkedIn Profile For SEO 02 But why LinkedIn SEO optimization is crucial? 03 Relevant Prospects is All You Want 04 How to Optimize LinkedIn Profile For SEO 05 Don’t forget to follow these three steps to quickly grow and expand your business. 06 Additional Methods to Rank Your LinkedIn Profile 07 Wrapping Up 0 of 7 done Anyone can create a LinkedIn account. Nowadays, LinkedIn SEO optimization can help businesses reach a wider audience and connect with potential customers. And you don’t want to miss such opportunities at all. Mark step 1 done 2 Step 2 of 7 But why LinkedIn SEO optimization is crucial? Before anything else, let’s discuss why even LinkedIn can be so valuable in short. The company page on LinkedIn extends your business idea to the whole industry. But it also comes with some additional features that we can use for business deals and purposes. Unfortunately, if your LinkedIn profile isn’t optimized for SEO, your profile is nothing more than trash. But don’t worry! You have the way to go forward. First, companies should ensure that their profile is complete and include keywords that people might use to find them. You can perform keyword research using the online tools available (e.g., Semrush, Ahref, etc.) to extract the best relevant keywords efficiently. The SEO for the LinkedIn Company page is vital. Additionally, businesses can join groups and participate in discussions to update their brain with the latest information and improve opportunities. Entrepreneurs build an SEO-optimized LinkedIn account for both perspectives, whether business or personal networking. meta: Do you know how to use keywords or how to use long tail keywords in Content? If you are looking for the answer, you are in the right place.
h1_text: How to use keywords in Content
lede: Do you know how to use keywords or how to use long-tail keywords in Content? If you are looking for the answer, you are in the right place.
copy_text: Home Blog Search Engine Optimization How to use keywords in Content How-To Search Engine Optimization How to use keywords in Content R Reinforce Lab team Published 3 Feb 2025 Updated 15 Apr 2025 Steps 01 What is a keyword? 02 What is keyword research? 03 What is keyword Stuffing? 04 What is keyword difficulty? 05 How to use keywords in Content? 06 Keywords in Title Tag: 07 Keywords in the introduction: 08 Keywords in the meta description: 09 Keywords in the body: 10 Keywords in the conclusion: 11 Wrapping Up 0 of 11 done Do you know how to use keywords or how to use long-tail keywords in Content? If you are looking for the answer, you are in the right place. Using the keywords properly is a significant part of SEO and content writing. When you want to rank your content for a specific keyword, there is no alternative to using keywords properly. There are certain methods of keyword use that we will share with you. But we will discuss how placing keywords in the content can be your trump card. There are some secret tips that will help you to rank faster than ever, and it’s completely suggested practice. Let’s jump into a complete guide to keyword placement- where to use keywords for SEO. Before that, we will start with some basic concepts. 1 Step 1 of 11 What is a keyword? A keyword can be any word that people search on the internet. This is a basic definition, but we are not going to explain only with the traditional definition; let’s start with an example. You may search: Nugget recipe And here is the answer in the SERP. This “nugget recipe” is a keyword, and the ranked blogs are about how to make nuggets. Now think again; you may also search for it as “how to make nuggets”. And here is the result. Though all results are not the same, you will get similar info on the SERP page. Now, what about writing it differently? Well, we can search for “nugget making process”. Here is the result: As you can see, whatever you search is a keyword, and though the search intent is the same, the variation of words can change the SERP result. You can ask, how many types of keywords are available? Well, you can decide in many ways. like, based on the character count- we decide them as Short-tail keywords Long-tail keywords We have already shown the example, nugget recipe is a short-tail keyword, and how to make nugget is a long-tail one. When you want to learn about how to use keywords in Content, you should know how to use both long-tail and short-tail keywords in Content and short-tail. We can create a type of keyword in another way based on the search intent. They are: Informative Keywords Navigational keywords Commercial Keywords Transitional Keywords Here is a detail; check it out! Mark step 1 done 2 Step 2 of 11 What is keyword research? This is another basic concept and one of the most popular words in SEO – Keyword research. Keyword research is a key factor of SEO, no doubt. If you ask what keyword research is, the easiest way to explain it is finding out how people search a particular topic. Let me give you an example. Suppose you have a website on the beauty and skin care niche. You want to sell skincare and makeup products. Now, how can keyword research help? You will find out how people are searching on the internet about makeup products and skin care. Use the keywords in your content, optimize it, and it will appear in the search results. That’s how it works, well not in this much simple way, there are complications. You can read this blog about: If you use short-tail, highly competitive keywords, then you may have to use the keywords more often. You cannot avoid it even if you want to. There is a standard number, 2 Percent, but it doesn’t always work. So when you are targeting a keyword, short tail and high difficulty, you can use the focus keyword about 10 times in 1000 words. Again, this is not a static number that you must follow. This is for your convenience so that you can make an assumption. Hope you have understood how to do keyword research. Mark step 2 done 3 Step 3 of 11 What is keyword Stuffing? Keyword using and keyword Stuffing are closely related to each other. When you use your keywords in your content, it helps the search engine to understand the topic. But what if you use the keywords too much? Well, this is called keyword stuffing, which is completely harmful for SEO. But how do you get rid of keyword Stuffing? It sounds easy, because you may think “I will not use them too much”. Well, that’s not how it can always be solved. Because sometimes, you need to use the keywords because of the context. You have to use them to make the topic understandable. Now the question is, how to solve the issue? There are some steps you may follow to get rid of the keyword Stuffing issue: Make a plan for how many times you are going to use the keywords. Find out the synonyms of the keywords. If you have to use the keywords more than the expected number, use them. Remember, keyword Stuffing is harmful to SEO. A few years ago, we saw people using it as a trick, and it worked. Google ranked the content with keyword Stuffing. But with the updates of the Search engine, the sites got penalized, and it is going on. So, if you do not want to face any trouble, do not do keyword Stuffing. We have a detailed article about keyword Stuffing; read it for more information. What is Keyword stuffing? Mark step 3 done 4 Step 4 of 11 What is keyword difficulty? Keyword difficulty is one of the common words as well, we can see it everywhere about keyword research. In a basic sense, how difficult it is to rank a keyword is called keyword difficulty. To learn more about it, read our blog about : What is keyword difficulty? Mark step 4 done 5 Step 5 of 11 How to use keywords in Content? You have to use keyword phrases following some basic rules while creating content: You cannot do keyword Stuffing You have to use them accordingly Use the less difficult keywords to rank faster These are basic rules that you must follow. But you need to know where and how to use the keywords in a blog post, right? Mark step 5 done 6 Step 6 of 11 Keywords in Title Tag : Using your primary keyword is recommended and helpful for SEO. So, when your content appears in a search query, it helps the reader to understand what your blog is about. It also helps to appear in voice searches. Mark step 6 done 7 Step 7 of 11 Keywords in the introduction : Using keywords in the introductory paragraph or head term is the best practice of search engine optimization. You have to use the main keywords or focus keyword at least once in the first 100 words. We suggest using the keywords right in the first line, However, you can use it later also, but must be in the first 100 words. Using keywords inthe  introduction is significant because: It helps the reader to understand what you are writing about. Search engine crawlers can understand your context easily. It amplifies your ranking factor. Mark step 7 done 8 Step 8 of 11 Keywords in the meta description: Meta description is an important part, this is what a user sees first when they search for something. So you have to use the keywords in the meta description part. As the meta description is only 160 characters, you can use keywords only once. Mark step 8 done 9 Step 9 of 11 Keywords in the body: We always get questions: How to use keywords in the body? How many times should we use the focus keyword in the body? Well, the answer is not static; there is no magic number. Because: If you use short-tail, highly competitive keywords, then you may have to use the keywords more often. There is a standard number, 2 Percent, but it doesn’t always work. So when you are targeting a keyword, short tail and high difficulty, you can use the focus keyword about 10 times in 1000 words. Again, this is not a static number that you must follow. When you are targeting a long tail and less competitive keywords, you can use the keyword 2 or 3 times in the body; that is enough and will not make any stuffing. You can use paid & free tools to count the number of keywords. Mark step 9 done 10 Step 10 of 11 Keywords in the conclusion : For the conclusion, endnote, or wrapping up whatever you say, use the keyword once in the last 100 words. It means a lot and is a very helpful tactic for SEO. And if you are targeting a short-tail keyword, you can use it more than once. However, your total keyword usage should be maintained with the word count. Number of Words and Keyword Use: Last but not least, keyword use varies with the number of words of the content. If your blog is 2000 words, then you may use the focus keyword 6/7 times. But will it be the same in the case of the 1000-word Content? Of course not! It will differ.  It will be less. Using Secondary Keywords or LSI: There can be many keywords that you are not focusing on, but as they are related to the topic, you will cover them also. Let’s give an example: Your focus keyword is: Best Mobile phone under 100 dollars. Here, you can cover different topics related to the main context. Your secondary keyword or LSI keyword can be: -Mobile phone price -Cheap Mobile phone -Smart phone price When you want to learn about how to use keywords in content writing, here comes the question: how many LSI keywords you use? There are different opinions about it. But we got good results using them 1 or 2 times in the content. Each keyword in one content, it helps to rank in different keywords. Keywords in Anchor Text: You can also use your keywords in the anchor text of your internal and external links. But do not use the main keyword; try to use the LSI keywords in the anchor text. If you use the focus keyword, it may accelerate the bounce rate and lower the user experience as well as lose your target audience. Semantically Related Keywords: There may be some short-tail keywords that are related to your context. Enriching your content by using them can help a lot to make it easier to rank. Maintain it on all pages of your site. You can find them out easily with the SEMRush Tool. But manually finding out is a little bit complicated. We will post a blog about it soon! Read more about it here: What are semantically related words? Mark step 10 done 11 Step 11 of 11 Wrapping Up Hope you have a good idea about how to use keywords in Content and how many times you should use. Do not do keyword Stuffing, and use them properly. If you write good-quality content, then you can appear in Google search results easily. Good-quality content always includes keyword optimization because it is an integral part of SEO.
