13 What happens if your robots.txt is missing or broken? 14 Is robots.txt a law or a lock? 15 Should you block images with robots.txt? 16 How do you fix robots.txt problems? 17 What are the most common robots.txt mistakes? 18 Robots.txt best practices 19 Robots.txt and your sitemap 20 Robots.txt checklist before you publish 21 Robots.txt and AI crawlers 22 Robots.txt or a meta robots tag: which one? 23 Wrapping up About 16 min in total Short answer A robots.txt file is a plain text file at the root of your website that tells search engine and AI crawlers which pages and files they may crawl. It manages crawling, not indexing: to keep a page out of Google, use a noindex tag or a password instead. 01 Robots.txt controls which parts of your site crawlers may open. It lives at the root, such as example.com/robots.txt. 02 It does not keep a page out of Google. A blocked page can still be indexed if other sites link to it. 03 Google supports four fields: User-agent, Disallow, Allow and Sitemap. It ignores crawl-delay. 04 Each subdomain needs its own file, and Google reads only the first 500 kibibytes. 05 AI crawlers such as OAI-SearchBot and GPTBot follow robots.txt too, so decide on purpose whether to allow them. 06 Test the file in a private browser window and in the robots.txt report in Search Console after every change. A robots.txt file is a small text file that tells search engines which parts of your website they may crawl. It sits at the root of your site, for example https://example.com/robots.txt . Every well-behaved crawler reads it before it looks at anything else. This robots.txt guide explains what the file does, what it cannot do, how to write one, and how to check it. Every rule here comes from Google’s own documentation, which is linked at the end. 01 Chapter 1 · 1 min What is a robots.txt file? A robots.txt file is a plain text file with rules for web crawlers. A crawler is the program a search engine uses to read web pages. Search engine crawlers are also called bots or spiders. Googlebot is Google’s crawler. Bingbot is Bing’s. Each rule says which crawler it is for and which paths that crawler may or may not open. Rules are also called directives. Google says the file is used mainly to manage crawler traffic, so your server is not overloaded with requests. The rules follow a standard called the Robots Exclusion Protocol. If a site has no robots.txt file, crawlers assume they may crawl everything. End of chapter 1 Next: How does a robots.txt file work? → 02 Chapter 2 · 1 min How does a robots.txt file work? Here is what happens when a search engine visits your site: The crawler first asks for https://yourdomain.com/robots.txt . If the file loads, the crawler reads it and finds the group of rules that names it. If no group names it, it uses the group for * . For each address it wants to visit, it checks the rules. If a Disallow rule matches, it skips that address. It then crawls the addresses that are allowed, and uses your Sitemap line to find more. The rules are a request, not a lock. Google and other respected web crawlers follow them. Some crawlers do not. That is why robots.txt files are good for managing crawling and poor for keeping things secret. End of chapter 2 Next: Why is robots.txt important for SEO? → 03 Chapter 3 · 1 min Why is robots.txt important for SEO? Search engines do not have unlimited time for your site. SEO people call that time your crawl budget. Robots.txt helps crawlers spend it on the pages that matter. It keeps crawlers out of pages with no search value. Think of admin screens, cart pages and internal search results. The same goes for pages that are near copies of each other (duplicate content), such as filtered product lists. It protects your server. On a large site, crawlers can make many requests. Rules reduce that load. It can keep media files out of Google. Google says you can use it to stop images, video and audio files from showing in search results. It points crawlers to your sitemap. One line tells them where the list of your important pages is. A good SEO robots.txt file is short and careful. A mistake here can also do real harm. One wrong line can block your entire site from being crawled. That is why this file deserves care. End of chapter 3 Next: How does robots.txt help with crawl budget? → 04 Chapter 4 · 1 min How does robots.txt help with crawl budget? Google cannot crawl every page on the web. It gives each site a limited amount of crawling time and effort. SEO people call this your crawl budget. Google says it depends on two things: how much crawling your server can handle, and how much Google wants to crawl your content. Google also says crawl budget matters mainly for two kinds of sites: very large sites (about 1 million pages or more) and medium or large sites (about 10,000 pages or more) whose content changes every day. If you run a small business site, you probably do not need to worry about it. For sites where it does matter, Google gives clear advice about robots.txt: Block pages you never want crawled. Good examples are endless internal search results and differently sorted copies of the same page. Blocking them stops Google spending time on them. Do not use noindex for this. Google still has to fetch the page to see the tag, so the crawling time is wasted. Do not use robots.txt to move crawl budget around for a short time. Google will not shift the saved effort to other pages unless it is already hitting your site’s limit. Return a 404 or 410 for pages you removed for good. A blocked address stays in the crawl queue much longer than an error page. End of chapter 4 Next: What can robots.txt not do? → 05 Chapter 5 · 1 min What can robots.txt not do? This is the part most guides get wrong, so read it twice. Robots.txt does not keep a page out of Google. It stops crawling. It does not stop indexing. Google says a blocked page can still appear in search results if other pages link to it. The result will show the address with no description. To keep a page out of search results, Google tells you to use one of these instead: a noindex tag or header on the page a password on the page removing the page Do not combine a noindex tag with a block in robots.txt. If the crawler cannot open the page, it never sees the noindex tag. Robots.txt is not security. The file is public. Anyone can read it. Google also notes that some crawlers do not obey it. Private files need a password, not a line in a text file. End of chapter 5 Next: What does a robots.txt file look like? → Reinforce Lab service · Technical SEO Not sure what your robots.txt is blocking? Reinforce Lab finds what stops search engines and AI crawlers from reading your pages, fixes it, and re-crawls to prove it. See technical SEO services → Or get a free diagnostic first 06 Chapter 6 · 1 min What does a robots.txt file look like? Here is a simple file with two groups of rules and a sitemap line. User-agent: Googlebot
Disallow: /nogooglebot/

User-agent: *
Allow: /

Sitemap: https://www.example.com/sitemap.xml In plain words: Googlebot may not crawl any address that starts with /nogooglebot/ . Every other crawler may crawl the whole site. The sitemap is at the address shown. Google supports four fields in this file. They are often called robots.txt directives. The Disallow directive blocks a path, and the Allow directive opens one. Together with the user agent and sitemap lines, that is the whole language: Field What it does Example User-agent Names the crawler the rules are for. A star means all crawlers. User-agent: * Disallow A path the crawler must not open. Disallow: /cart/ Allow A path the crawler may open, even inside a blocked folder. Allow: /cart/help/ Sitemap The full address of your sitemap. Sitemap: https://example.com/sitemap.xml Google does not support the crawl-delay directive, which some other search engine bots read. Lines it does not understand are ignored. End of chapter 6 Next: How do you create a robots.txt file? → 07 Chapter 7 · 2 min How do you create a robots.txt file? Google describes four steps: create the file, add rules, upload it, and test it. 1. Create a file named robots.txt Use a plain text editor such as Notepad or TextEdit. Do not use a word processor. Word processors can add hidden characters and curly quotes that break the rules. Save the file as robots.txt in UTF-8 format. The name must be exactly that, in lower case. A site can have only one. 2. Choose the user agent Every group of rules starts with a User-agent line. It says who the rules are for. One crawler: User-agent: Googlebot Several crawlers: put each name on its own line above the same rules. All crawlers: User-agent: * A crawler follows only one group: the one that names it most exactly. If there is a group for Googlebot and a group for * , Googlebot follows its own group and ignores the other. The order of the groups in the file does not matter. 3. Add your rules Under the user agent, add one rule per line. Each path starts with a slash. A folder ends with a slash too. User-agent: *
Disallow: /wp-admin/
Allow: /wp-admin/admin-ajax.php
Disallow: /?s= Three things to remember: Paths are case-sensitive. /File.pdf and /file.pdf are different. A star is a wildcard. It stands for any text in a path. A line that starts with # is a comment. Use comments to say why a rule exists. 4. Upload the file to the root of your site The file must sit in the root directory, the top level of your site, such as https://www.example.com/robots.txt . Crawlers do not look for it in a folder. The file only covers the exact site it is on. Rules on https://example.com do not apply to https://shop.example.com . Each subdomain needs its own file. On some website builders, such as Wix or Blogger, you may not be able to edit the file yourself. Google says to use the platform’s own search settings in that case. On WordPress, SEO plugins such as Yoast SEO let you edit it from the dashboard. 5. Test it and keep it up to date First, open the file in a private browser window. If you can see your rules, crawlers can too. Then open the robots.txt report in Google Search Console. Google lists it as the way to find and fix problems in a file that is already live. Check the file again after every site change, launch or migration. Google usually keeps a copy for up to 24 hours, so a change may take a day to be picked up. End of chapter 7 Next: How does Google choose between rules that clash? → 08 Chapter 8 · 1 min How does Google choose between rules that clash? Sooner or later you will write two rules that both match one address. Google has a clear method. It uses the most specific rule, which is the one with the longest path. If two rules conflict, it uses the least restrictive one, which means the one that allows crawling. These examples come from Google’s own documentation: Address Your rules Rule that applies Why /page Allow: /p and Disallow: / Allow: /p It is more specific /folder/page Allow: /folder and Disallow: /folder Allow: /folder When rules clash, Google uses the least restrictive one /page.htm Allow: /page and Disallow: /*.htm Disallow: /*.htm The path is longer, so it is more specific / (home page) Allow: /$ and Disallow: / Allow: /$ The dollar sign matches only the home page Two symbols help you write exact rules. The star ( * ) matches any run of characters. The dollar sign ( $ ) marks the end of the address. Use them sparingly and test after every change. End of chapter 8 Next: Robots.txt examples you can copy → 09 Chapter 9 · 1 min Robots.txt examples you can copy These are the rules most sites need. Change the paths to match your own site. Allow everything User-agent: *
Disallow: An empty Disallow line blocks nothing. This has the same effect as having no file at all. Block one folder User-agent: *
Disallow: /checkout/ Every address that starts with /checkout/ is off limits to all crawlers. Block a folder but allow one file in it User-agent: *
Disallow: /downloads/
Allow: /downloads/price-list.pdf The more exact rule wins, so the price list can still be crawled. Block one type of file User-agent: *
Disallow: /*.xls$ The star stands for any text. The dollar sign marks the end of the address. Together they match every address that ends in .xls . Block one crawler only User-agent: GPTBot
Disallow: /

User-agent: *
Allow: / Here one named crawler is kept out and all others are welcome. Add your sitemap Sitemap: https://www.example.com/sitemap.xml Use the full address. You can list more than one sitemap, each on its own line. End of chapter 9 Next: Robots.txt for WordPress → 10 Chapter 10 · 1 min Robots.txt for WordPress If your site runs on WordPress, you can usually edit robots.txt from an SEO plugin such as Yoast SEO, without touching files on the server. A common starting point looks like this: User-agent: *
Disallow: /wp-admin/
Allow: /wp-admin/admin-ajax.php
Disallow: /?s=

Sitemap: https://www.example.com/sitemap_index.xml This keeps crawlers out of the admin area and out of internal search results. It still allows the one admin file that some themes and plugins need on the public site. Do not block the folders that hold your styles and scripts. Google warns that blocking files a page needs can stop it from understanding the page properly. End of chapter 10 Next: Robots.txt examples for different kinds of sites → 11 Chapter 11 · 1 min Robots.txt examples for different kinds of sites The right rules depend on the site. These are starting points to adapt, not templates to paste. An online store Stores often create thousands of addresses from filters and sorting options, such as ?sort=price . These near-copies waste crawl effort. User-agent: *
Disallow: /cart/
Disallow: /checkout/
Disallow: /*?sort=
Disallow: /*?filter= Keep your category and product pages open. Block only the parameters that create copies, and check them first so you do not block pages that rank. A blog or company site Small sites need very little. Block the admin area and internal search, add the sitemap, and stop there. A site under development Do not use robots.txt to hide a test site. A blocked address can still appear in Google if someone links to it. Protect it with a password. Then, when you launch, check that you did not carry the “block everything” rule across to the live site. End of chapter 11 Next: Do you need a robots.txt file? → 12 Chapter 12 · 1 min Do you need a robots.txt file? No. Google says that unless you write rules, every file on your site may be crawled. A site with no robots.txt works, and Google treats it as having no crawl limits. You need the file when you want to keep crawlers away from certain sections, to point to your sitemap, or to set rules for specific bots such as AI crawlers. Most sites do have one. The HTTP Archive’s Web Almanac 2025 looked at a July 2025 crawl of more than 16 million websites. It found that 85% of requests for robots.txt returned a valid 200 status, up from 84% in 2024, and that about 13% returned a 404, which means no file. The Almanac warns that a 200 only shows that a file exists. It does not show that the rules inside are right. End of chapter 12 Next: What happens if your robots.txt is missing or broken? → 13 Chapter 13 · 1 min What happens if your robots.txt is missing or broken? It depends on the error. Google’s documentation sets out how Googlebot treats each status code: What the server returns What Google does 200 (success) Reads and follows the file as served Redirect (3xx) Follows at least five hops, then treats the file as a 404 Client error (4xx, except 429) Acts as if no robots.txt exists and assumes there are no crawl limits Server error (5xx) For the first 12 hours, stops crawling the site and keeps trying to fetch the file. For the next 30 days, uses the last good copy while it keeps trying. After 30 days, if the site is available, it behaves as if there is no file. If the site has general availability problems, it stops crawling This is why a 5xx error on robots.txt is more dangerous than a missing file. A missing file means no limits. A server error can pause crawling of the whole site. Google also caches the file for up to 24 hours and may keep an old copy longer when it cannot refresh it. Errors are not rare. In the 2024 Web Almanac, Lighthouse audits found that 8.43% of desktop pages and 7.40% of mobile pages failed the check for a valid robots.txt file. Check yours in the robots.txt report in Search Console. End of chapter 13 Next: Is robots.txt a law or a lock? → 14 Chapter 14 · 1 min Is robots.txt a law or a lock? Neither. It is a voluntary standard, published as RFC 9309. Google says that its crawlers and other respectable crawlers follow the rules, but the file cannot force any crawler to obey, and some crawlers do not follow it. Do not use robots.txt to protect private information. Use a password or other access control for that. Also remember that anyone can read your robots.txt, so do not list paths you want to keep secret. End of chapter 14 Next: Should you block images with robots.txt? → 15 Chapter 15 · 1 min Should you block images with robots.txt? You can. Google’s documentation says that for media files, robots.txt can manage crawl traffic and can keep image, video and audio files out of Google Search results. It will not stop other sites or people from linking to the file. Do not block image, script or style files that Google needs to understand your pages. If the page is harder to render without them, Google may not analyze it well. End of chapter 15 Next: How do you fix robots.txt problems? → 16 Chapter 16 · 1 min How do you fix robots.txt problems? When pages are missing from Google or the wrong ones appear, work through this table: What you see Likely cause What to do Whole site missing from Google A Disallow: / rule for all crawlers Remove the rule, then request a recrawl in Search Console A blocked page still shows in results, with no description Other sites link to it, so Google knows the address To remove it, use noindex or a password, and unblock it so Google can see the tag Pages look broken in Google’s preview Styles or scripts are blocked Allow the folders those files sit in A new rule does not seem to work Google keeps a copy of the file for up to 24 hours Wait a day, then check again The rule blocks too much or too little A path is missing a slash, or letters are the wrong case Check the path against the real address and test it Google cannot read the file The server returns an error for robots.txt Fix the server so the file returns a normal response In Search Console, the robots.txt report shows the file Google found and any lines it could not use. A page marked as blocked by robots.txt in the page indexing report should be one you chose to block. End of chapter 16 Next: What are the most common robots.txt mistakes? → 17 Chapter 17 · 1 min What are the most common robots.txt mistakes? Blocking the entire site. The directive Disallow: / under User-agent: * stops all crawling. This is often left over from a test site. Using it to hide pages. Blocked pages can still be indexed. Use noindex instead. Blocking files a page needs. Google warns against blocking style and script files if the page is hard to understand without them. Putting the file in a folder. It only works at the root. Forgetting subdomains. Each one needs its own file. Letting the file break. If your server returns an error for robots.txt, Google stops crawling the site for the first 12 hours. It then uses the last good copy for up to 30 days. Making it too big. Google reads only the first 500 kibibytes. End of chapter 17 Next: Robots.txt best practices → 18 Chapter 18 · 1 min Robots.txt best practices Keep the file short. Fewer robots.txt rules mean fewer mistakes. Block sections, not single pages. Use one rule for a folder where you can. Add the sitemap directive. It helps crawlers find your important pages. Write a comment above each rule. Say why it is there, so the next person does not have to guess. Check Search Console. A page marked as blocked by robots.txt there should be one you meant to block. Review the file after every launch or migration. Test sites often carry a rule that blocks everything. End of chapter 18 Next: Robots.txt and your sitemap → 19 Chapter 19 · 1 min Robots.txt and your sitemap A robots.txt file tells crawlers where not to go. An XML sitemap tells them what you want found. They work together. Google says sitemaps are a good way to show which content you want crawled, as opposed to which content it can or cannot crawl. Put the full sitemap address in your robots.txt file, and make sure no page in your sitemap is blocked by a Disallow rule. A page that is both listed and blocked sends mixed signals. End of chapter 19 Next: Robots.txt checklist before you publish → 20 Chapter 20 · 1 min Robots.txt checklist before you publish Run through this list every time you change the file: The file is named robots.txt and sits at the root of the site. It is plain text in UTF-8, saved from a text editor, not a word processor. No rule blocks pages you want to rank, or the style and script files they need. There is no Disallow: / under User-agent: * unless you mean it. Each path starts with a slash and has the right letter case. Your sitemap address is listed in full. You decided on purpose whether to allow AI search crawlers. You tested the file in a private browser window and in Search Console. Each subdomain has its own file. End of chapter 20 Next: Robots.txt and AI crawlers → 21 Chapter 21 · 1 min Robots.txt and AI crawlers AI tools read the web too, and each one has its own crawler name. You can allow or block them in robots.txt like any other crawler. Crawler name Who runs it What it is for OAI-SearchBot OpenAI Showing sites in ChatGPT search answers GPTBot OpenAI Collecting content that may be used to train its models Google-Extended Google Controls use of your content for Gemini training and grounding Two facts matter here. OpenAI says sites that block OAI-SearchBot will not be shown in ChatGPT search answers. Google says Google-Extended does not affect your place in Google Search. So decide on purpose. If you want AI answers to name and cite your business, do not block the search crawlers. Many sites now set AI rules. In the Web Almanac 2025, GPTBot was named in the robots.txt files of 4.5% of desktop sites, up from 2.9% in 2024. ClaudeBot rose from 1.9% to 3.6%, CCBot (Common Crawl) was at 3.5% and Google-Extended at 3.4%. The Almanac counts sites that name a crawler, and a rule can allow it as well as block it, so these are not the share of sites that block it. The Almanac’s authors called the growth one of the fastest expansions of named user agents in robots.txt in recent memory. End of chapter 21 Next: Robots.txt or a meta robots tag: which one? → 22 Chapter 22 · 1 min Robots.txt or a meta robots tag: which one? They do different jobs. Use the one that fits the goal. Your goal Use this Stop crawlers wasting time on a section Robots.txt Keep one page out of search results A noindex meta tag Keep an image or video file out of search results Robots.txt Keep a PDF out of search results A noindex header Keep something private A password Robots.txt works on whole sections of a site. A meta robots tag works on one page at a time. End of chapter 22 Next: Wrapping up → 23 Chapter 23 · 1 min Wrapping up Robots.txt is short, but it controls how every crawler meets your site. Keep it simple. Block only what has no search value. Never use it to hide pages. Test it after every change. If your pages are not being crawled or indexed and you are not sure why, the robots.txt file is the first place to look. It is also the first thing our technical SEO services check. To see how AI tools find and cite a site, read about AI search optimization . Back matter Glossary A to Z C Crawler A program a search engine or AI tool uses to read web pages. Also called a bot or spider. D Disallow A rule that tells a crawler not to open a path. N Noindex A tag or header that tells search engines not to show a page in results. S Sitemap A file that lists the pages you want search engines to find. U User agent The name a crawler gives itself, such as Googlebot. Rules in robots.txt are addressed to user agents. Questions FAQs Do I need a robots.txt file? Not always. Without one, crawlers assume they may crawl the whole site. A small site with no private or duplicate sections can work without it. Most sites still add one to block admin pages and point to the sitemap. Can robots.txt remove a page from Google? No. It only stops crawling. Google says a blocked page can still appear in results if other pages link to it. To remove a page, use a noindex tag, a password, or delete the page. Where should I put my robots.txt file? At the root of the site it is for, such as https://www.example.com/robots.txt. Crawlers do not look for it in folders. Each subdomain needs its own file. How long do robots.txt changes take to work? Google usually keeps a copy of the file for up to 24 hours. So a change can take about a day to be noticed. OpenAI also says its search systems can take about 24 hours to adjust. What happens if robots.txt returns an error? If the file is missing (a 404 error), Google treats the site as having no crawl limits. If the server fails (a 5xx error), Google stops crawling the site for the first 12 hours, then uses the last good copy for up to 30 days. What is the maximum size of a robots.txt file? Google reads the first 500 kibibytes of the file. Anything after that is ignored. If your file is close to that size, combine rules or move blocked content into one folder. Should I block AI crawlers in robots.txt? It depends on your goal. Blocking OAI-SearchBot keeps your site out of ChatGPT search answers. Blocking GPTBot or Google-Extended only limits use of your content for AI training. If you want AI tools to cite you, allow the search crawlers. Does Google support crawl-delay in robots.txt? No. Google lists crawl-delay as a field it does not support. Google supports User-agent, Allow, Disallow and Sitemap. What is the best robots.txt for SEO? There is no single best file, because the right rules depend on your site. A good robots.txt for SEO is short: it blocks admin areas, internal search and pages that make endless near-copies, leaves everything useful open, and lists your sitemap. Test it after every change. What does Disallow: / mean in robots.txt? It tells the crawlers named in that group not to crawl any page on the site. It is useful on a private test site and a serious mistake on a live one. If your live site is missing from Google, check for this line first. Does robots.txt affect crawl budget? It can, on very large sites. Google says crawl budget matters mainly for sites with about 1 million pages or more, or about 10,000 pages or more that change daily. On those sites, blocking pages you never want crawled saves effort. Small sites usually do not need to worry about it. Do I need a robots.txt file? No. Google says that unless you write rules, all files may be crawled. You need the file to keep crawlers out of certain sections, point to your sitemap or set rules for specific bots. In the Web Almanac 2025, 85% of robots.txt requests returned a valid 200 status. What happens if my robots.txt returns a server error? Google's documentation says that for the first 12 hours it stops crawling the site and keeps trying to fetch the file. For the next 30 days it uses the last good copy. After 30 days, if the site is available, it acts as if there is no file. A 4xx error, except 429, is treated as no file. How many sites block AI crawlers in robots.txt? The Web Almanac 2025 found GPTBot named in 4.5% of desktop sites' robots.txt files, up from 2.9% in 2024, and ClaudeBot in 3.6%, up from 1.9%. These figures count sites that name the crawler, which can mean a block or an allow. copy_text: Home Blog Digital Marketing Sensory Marketing: Know How 5 Senses Marketing Works… Explainer Digital Marketing Sensory Marketing: Know How 5 Senses Marketing Works Best for Businesses R Reinforce Lab team Published 20 Feb 2025 Updated 13 Apr 2025 Sensory marketing or sensory appeal is one of the effective methods of advertising where the 5 senses marketing approach is applied mainly. Sensory market research seeks to understand consumers’ views of a product and their whole experience. According to Science of Sensory Marketing , a certain sensory appeal can alter how a person views an object or activity when connected with that sensory experience. So, a sensory marketing strategy can be one of the best choices. As marketing is increasing, trying marketing that plays with people’s senses can help you keep ahead for sure. I know this sensory appeal sounds quite unorthodox, but trust me, things will be much easier once you understand its algorithm. For your business at the same time, for your potential customers for sure! As a marketer, you should apply various marketing techniques to see which is suitable for your business, right? Here you will get another sensational marketing technique; you can say, called sensory branding or marketing. So let’s get started then! What Is Sensory Marketing? Most individuals may be unfamiliar with this notion and wonder, “What is sensory marketing?” Although there are several methods for sense marketing definition, the sensory marketing concept remains consistent. Simply said, marketing with sense is the implementation of a marketing plan with emotional connections that appeal to customers. Sense marketing’s definition appeals to the five senses of the audience: sight, sound, touch, taste, and smell. The marketing tool of sensory marketing entails a variety of ways to reach your customers’ senses. And they are influencing their behavior depending on how your brand and tactics make them feel aside from traditional marketing. Using media senses in advertising and marketing campaigns may significantly impact your audience for your product or service. Also, their choice to purchase your goods is how sensorial emotional appeal works. Like sense marketing definition, now see something directly connected with this sensorial emotional appeal! Five Senses Sensory Marketing are – Marketers use marketing with senses to catch their target audiences more perfectly. Obviously, marketing with sense helps a lot in retargeting your potential consumers as its effects are intense emotional connections. Five senses of sensory marketing that marketing use as a marketing tool in its best ways are – 1. Sensory Marketing with Sight Here marketers attract consumers with unique or brand-related – Colors Images Text Graphics Video Light In this way, they properly use the sense marketing definition. 2. Sensory Marketing With Sounds Using this type of sense can attract consumers most and marketers use – Voice Overs Sound Effects Thematic Music To let consumers know about a specific brand so that they can remember faster after hearing that tune or music anywhere anytime. 3. Sensory Marketing With Scent Smelling works best in case of memorizing anything and brands use this option much fruitfully with – Environmental Scents Fragrances Food Scents The more unique smell the more brand awareness you can get and this is how marketing with scent works. 4. Sensory Marketing with Touch Touching sense can be remembered years after years so marketers never fail to use this sensory marketing tactic. Marketing with touch does not mean you will have to allow your products for touching randomly, instead, it works with – Comfort Collateral Hands-On Tests So people can simply judge w2hat they are offering in person and trust me this system, works best! 5. Sensory Marketing with Taste People’s sense of taste with taste buds is the best thing that you can use for your promotions. And how do marketers usually do that? See the ways – Samples New Flavors This way people can get the varieties in their product selection which helps them to see what they should choose. Why Is Sensory Marketing Important? There are thousands of reasons available for your business to define it as a sensory marketing brand. But for that, you must apply a suitable sensory branding strategy; otherwise, it will not work. Here are 5 reasons why sensory testing is essential! 01. Sensory marketing is a go-to approach since it is all about improving the consumer experience This sort of marketing mainly plays with the senses of the audience. So this marketing approach includes things that can give comfort to audiences. As a result, consumers absorb more of this type of marketing method. Ultimately businesses with sensory marketing can improve the consumer experience. 02. Mainly, the sensory appeal offers a whole experience Sensory marketing brands take the advantage of people’s 5 senses. So ultimately they can easily win people’s hearts if the approach can be applied perfectly at the same time uniquely. Offering marketing methods including satisfying customers’ 5 senses can work better than any other technique. That is why it is one of the biggest important issues to go for this theory as it gives the whole experience to any consumer. 03. It can stand out as a distinctively engaging method of capturing the audience’s attention While blending marketing sense with people’s emotions can easily catch people’s attention. If you know the proper strategy and how things work in this marketing method then things will be easier enough. Trust me marketing brands of sensory appliances use this method in order to get much engagement and they became succeeded. So if you can get proper ideas on how sensory marketing works nothing can stop your business! 04. Build the relationship between brand and consumer by exciting all the senses and producing emotions Customers want to interact with businesses that do good or make them feel good and also sense of taste good. And you can simply make them feel something by using sensory marketing. Customers who are emotionally committed to a brand are less likely to switch to a competitor brand. You’ve gained their trust and will be rewarded with higher client retention. 05. Sensory Ads text with multisensory stimulation improves genuine taste judgments Consumers’ senses are aroused when they can eat, smell, or listen to your sensory appeal; Following sense marketing definition, the brain combines information from these many sensory inputs guarantees. That the tasting experience with a sense of taste is always multimodal. As a result, consumers can readily sense how your offerings are as marketing experts. And they will remain loyal to your business regardless of what happens. Brands that Employ Sensory Marketing Examples Companies that use sensory marketing in their branding strategies never fail to tempt their target audiences, which is a thousand times true. Let’s learn about some examples used by marketing experts that will surely realize how effective sensory marketing is! So starting with – Apple Customers may interact with the company through very immersive in-store experiences. The stores, which are decked in Apple’s distinctive white, are a visual feast, All of their retail stores or shops are crammed with products you can touch, play with, and experience. Apple stores are an essential aspect of Apple’s sensory marketing approach. As well as a sense of marketing definition to expose people to the lifestyle Apple gadgets promote. MASTERCARD Mastercard is leveraging sensory appeal to establish a new identity for credit card users — the “sonic identity,” to be precise. When a customer completes a transaction, they hear the sonic sound. The sound is intended to represent the meeting of the red and yellow circles in Mastercard’s logo. That noise creates a sense of security and consistency – because of the familiar sound, customers know their transactions were successful. Customers can nevertheless get a fictitious visual experience. Marriott Hotels Marriott Hotels employed a virtual reality headset to transport its guests to holiday places where Marriott has a presence. By allowing them to see famous spots as well as experience odors and noises connected with the area. VR and AR bring a visual layer to marketing, which is critical for companies but much more appeal to customers. It takes a visual or text ad and enhances it in such a manner that it becomes more interactive and tailored for customers or clients. Using an AR app can assist clients in deciding whether they want to visit this place in person and use Marriott as a service provider. If you want your clients to believe in your brand, you must first create an emotional appeal to them. Airbnb, for example, does this brilliantly with its “Belong Anywhere” marketing. Consider this: the deeper you can connect emotionally with your readers, the they will likely remember your brand. This, in turn, will allow you to appeal to their other media senses as well. 2. Recreate Advertising with a Sense of Smell In South Korea, Dunkin’ Donuts employed sensory marketing by releasing a coffee fragrance into the air while playing their business jingle. Even if this sounds a little far-fetched for your company, there are still techniques to appeal to your clients’ sense of scent. Placement of scented advertisements in major publications and the use of a signature fragrance in your businesses are two clever possibilities. Smell is a strong sense, and studies have shown that pleasant fragrances may boost mood by 40%. Find a way to include smell in your brand to stick with the sense marketing definition. However, when employing scent in your advertising, be sure that the aroma is not overpowering. While fragrance has the ability to evoke happy memories, it also has the ability to repel your audience. I approached this feeling with caution and purpose. 3. Include Sound Effects in Senses Marketing In advertising, sound may take numerous forms. It may be the State Farm jingle “Like a nice neighbor…” or a catchphrase you can’t get out of your brain. Today, sensory advertising necessitates that all firms and retail stores use sound in their branding initiatives. If something appears tough, know there is always a way to do it. Consider the lingerie behemoth Victoria’s Secret, which plays classical music in its stores to make clients feel as though they are part of an exclusive shopping experience. According to a 2018 survey by Mood Media, 75 percent of customers will stay in a business if they love the music. 4. Create Touch Appealing To The Senses Touch is a powerful sensation that most companies can quickly capitalize on. There is almost always a method for your brand to benefit from texture. This may be choosing substantial, high-quality card paper for your postal adverts. Or going above and above to ensure your items feel lovely in the customer’s hand. Whatever method you use, make sure that you are not neglecting this critical sensory opportunity in your marketing. 5. Make Sense Marketing Visually Appealing Of course, sight is one of the most potent senses in the world of advertising. Fortunately, it’s also one of the most superficial marketing senses to master. To emphasize the importance of sight, ensure that your company’s website is visually appealing to clients, or employ an expert to create your social media or advertising visuals. Color is an essential component of sight, and companies such as Coca-Cola and Virgin Airlines have used color to build brand awareness for their goods. The logos of these companies are instantly recognizable all across the world. If you don’t already have a color scheme for your company, now is a great time to create one. Hire a professional web design company if you don’t feel comfortable doing it on your own. Since color says so much about your brand, this is one marketing step that’s well worth investing in. title: SEO Mistakes to Avoid: 12 Common Mistakes | Reinforce Lab
meta: SEO mistakes to avoid: 12 common SEO errors in fix order, on-page and technical checklists, hiring red flags and a free 60-minute audit you can run today.
h1_text: SEO Mistakes to Avoid: 12 Common SEO Mistakes and How to Fix Them
lede: Short answer
copy_text: Home Blog Search Engine Optimization SEO Mistakes to Avoid: 12 Common SEO Mistakes… Checklist Search Engine Optimization SEO Mistakes to Avoid: 12 Common SEO Mistakes and How to Fix Them By Jamil Ahmed Published 4 Mar 2025 Updated 16 Nov 2026 13 min read Contents (26) What data shows how common SEO mistakes are? Mistake 1: Optimizing for a keyword, not for the search task Mistake 2: A noindex tag or a robots block you did not mean Mistake 3: Content that search engines cannot see Mistake 4: Duplicate pages and mixed canonical signals Mistake 5: Weak titles and meta descriptions Mistake 6: A messy heading structure Mistake 7: Thin or copycat content Mistake 8: Keyword stuffing and pages that compete with each other Mistake 9: Weak internal links and orphan pages Mistake 10: Slow, unstable pages Mistake 11: Images without useful descriptions, and heavy files Mistake 12: Markup that does not match the page, and no measuring Why does Google show a different title or description than mine? A bonus mistake: blocking the bots that feed AI answers What are the biggest SEO mistakes? Do 404 errors hurt SEO? Common on-page SEO mistakes to avoid Common technical SEO mistakes to avoid Mistakes to avoid when hiring an SEO company Which free tools help you find these mistakes? How should you order the fixes? A free 60-minute audit Worked example: a small services site Our interest in this topic Final thoughts Short answer The most common SEO mistakes are basic: a stray noindex tag, content search engines cannot see, duplicate or missing titles and headings, thin copycat pages, weak internal links and slow pages. Fix access and indexing first, then relevance and content, then structure, speed and polish, and measure the result in Search Console and in leads. Key takeaways Fix access and indexing first. A stray noindex tag or robots block stops everything else from working. The 2025 Web Almanac found titles on 98.6% of desktop pages but meta descriptions on 67.7%, an H1 on 71% and canonical tags on 68%. SE Ranking's audits found images without descriptions on 74.43% of sites and duplicate titles on 53.69%. These are audited sites, not all sites. Google's recommended Core Web Vitals targets at the 75th percentile are LCP 2.5 seconds, INP 200 milliseconds and CLS 0.1. Thin or copycat content is a content problem, not a tag problem. Add first-hand evidence, examples or data. Pick one preferred URL for each page and avoid mixed canonical, sitemap and robots signals. Run a free 60-minute audit with Search Console, a crawler and PageSpeed Insights, and keep it as a habit. The most common SEO mistakes are not clever tricks gone wrong. They are basic problems that stop a page from being found, understood or chosen: a stray noindex tag, content that loads only in the browser, duplicate or missing titles, thin pages that repeat what others say, weak internal links and slow pages. Check access and indexing first, then relevance and content, then speed and polish. This checklist covers 12 mistakes in the order we would fix them. For each, you get how to spot it, how to fix it and the data behind it. We cite only sources we could read at the publisher, and we say when a figure comes from a vendor’s own audits. It replaces our older post on the same topic. What data shows how common SEO mistakes are? Two public data sets help. They measure different things, so do not mix them. The 2025 Web Almanac (HTTP Archive). It analyzes millions of web pages. It found title tags on 98.6% of desktop pages, but meta descriptions on only 67.7%, H1 headings on 71%, and canonical tags on 68%. It found a noindex directive on 3.5% of desktop pages and 2.4% of mobile pages, and structured data on 50% of pages. These are page-level facts for the crawled sample, mostly home pages, and a noindex on some pages is often intended. SE Ranking’s audit data. SE Ranking, an SEO software vendor, published the share of audited websites with each issue. It reported that 74.43% had images without descriptions, 53.69% had duplicate titles, 65.38% had missing meta descriptions, 54.67% had missing H1 headings and 50.58% had pages blocked by noindex. These are sites that ran an audit with its tool, which may skew toward sites with problems, so read them as a guide to what audits find, not as the share of all sites. The pattern is that basic elements are widespread, and still often missing or wrong. That is why a plain checklist pays. Mistake 1: Optimizing for a keyword, not for the search task How to spot it: the page gets impressions but few clicks, people leave quickly, or the top results are a different kind of page. The problem: a page can use the right phrase and still answer the wrong question. Someone searching for a checklist wants steps. Someone searching for a service wants scope, proof and price. The fix: before you write or update a page, classify the task: learn, compare, diagnose, do or buy. Look at the kinds of pages that rank for the query, and match the format and depth. Then answer the main question first and the natural follow-up questions after it. Our guide to ranking in AI Overviews shows the same answer-first approach. Mistake 2: A noindex tag or a robots block you did not mean How to spot it: a page is missing from Google even though it is live. Open Search Console’s Page Indexing report and look for “Excluded by noindex tag” and “Blocked by robots.txt”. In WordPress, check Settings, Reading, “Discourage search engines” and the robots setting in your SEO plugin. The fix: remove the tag or rule on pages that should be found, then request indexing. This is the most costly mistake, because nothing else helps while it is there. A noindex on 3.5% of desktop pages in the Web Almanac sample is often right, for example on thank-you pages, so check page by page. Our robots.txt guide explains what the file can and cannot do. Mistake 3: Content that search engines cannot see How to spot it: use the URL Inspection tool in Search Console and compare the rendered HTML with what you see in the browser. Or fetch the page without a browser and look for the main text in the response. The fix: make the main text, links and headings available in the HTML that is served, or reliably rendered. Google can process JavaScript, but other crawlers may not. In December 2024, Vercel reported that none of the major AI crawlers it tested rendered JavaScript. Avoid “load more” buttons for content you want indexed, and use normal links. Mistake 4: Duplicate pages and mixed canonical signals How to spot it: several URLs show the same content, such as with and without “www”, with tracking parameters or in print versions. In Search Console, look for “Duplicate without user-selected canonical”. The fix: pick one preferred URL for each page. Link to it, list it in your sitemap, and point canonical tags to it. The Web Almanac describes canonical tags as strong hints, not commands, and found them on 68% of desktop pages in 2025. Do not send mixed signals, such as a page that is in your sitemap, canonicalized to another URL and blocked from crawling at once. Use redirects for old duplicate URLs. Mistake 5: Weak titles and meta descriptions How to spot it: run a crawl and sort by title. Look for repeated titles, missing ones and titles that are too long or empty of meaning. The Web Almanac found titles on almost every page, so the issue is quality, not presence. SE Ranking’s audits found duplicate titles on 53.69% of sites, and missing meta descriptions on 65.38%. The fix: write a distinct, accurate title for each page that names its subject, and a description that states what the reader gets. Google may rewrite either one if it does not match the page, so keep both honest. Avoid stuffing keyword lists. Mistake 6: A messy heading structure How to spot it: check each page for one clear H1, then H2s for the main sections and H3s for parts of them. The Web Almanac found an H1 on 71% of desktop pages, and only 66% had a non-empty H1, so many pages lack a clear main heading. SE Ranking’s audits found missing H1s on 54.67% of sites and multiple H1s on 54.52%. The fix: use one H1 that names the page’s subject, then a logical outline. Use headings as a table of contents, not as places to repeat the keyword. A clear outline helps readers scan and helps systems pull the right passage for an answer. Mistake 7: Thin or copycat content How to spot it: the page says what the top results say, in fewer words, with nothing new. It has few links and no examples, data or experience. The fix: add something others lack: first-hand experience, a worked example, a template, original data, an expert quote or a clear decision rule. Google’s guidance for AI features says unique, expert-led content with a point of view will likely matter more over time than other tips. Make fewer, stronger pages instead of many thin ones. Google’s spam policy on scaled content abuse lists using generative AI tools to produce many pages without adding value as an example. Mistake 8: Keyword stuffing and pages that compete with each other How to spot it: the same phrase appears in every heading and alt text, or two pages of your own alternate in results for the same query. The fix: use the keyword where it fits and write for the reader. For pages that compete, merge them into the strongest page, redirect the weaker ones and update links. Pick one page for each main intent. Mistake 9: Weak internal links and orphan pages How to spot it: crawl your site and list pages with no or one internal link, and links whose text says “read more” or “click here”. SE Ranking’s audits found internal linking issues on a large share of sites, including 69.32% with pages that have no inbound links. The fix: link new pages from related older pages as soon as you publish, use clear, short anchor text and link to the final URL, not a redirect. Keep important pages within a few clicks of the home page. Our guide to entity SEO shows how clear links and names also help machines understand your topics. Mistake 10: Slow, unstable pages How to spot it: check field data in Search Console’s Core Web Vitals report and in PageSpeed Insights. Google’s web.dev gives these recommended thresholds, measured at the 75th percentile of page loads: Largest Contentful Paint within 2.5 seconds, Interaction to Next Paint of 200 milliseconds and Cumulative Layout Shift of 0.1. The fix: find the biggest cause for each template. Common ones are oversized images, render-blocking scripts, many third-party tags and images without set dimensions that make the layout jump. Speed does not replace relevance, but a very slow page can block the task. Mistake 11: Images without useful descriptions, and heavy files How to spot it: list images with missing alt text and files over a few hundred kilobytes. SE Ranking’s audits found images without descriptions on 74.43% of sites. The fix: write alt text that says what the image shows, in plain words, for people who cannot see it. Leave it empty for purely decorative images. Compress files and set width and height. Do not fill alt text with keywords. Mistake 12: Markup that does not match the page, and no measuring How to spot it: run key pages through Google’s Rich Results Test. Check that the markup matches what the page shows. The Web Almanac found structured data on 50% of pages, mostly as JSON-LD in the HTML. The fix: mark up only what is visible and true, such as Article, Organization and Product, and keep it current. Google says structured data is not required for its AI features, though it helps with rich results. Then measure. Use Search Console for impressions, clicks, indexing and, for AI features, the Generative AI performance report. Skipping measurement lets old problems return unseen. Our AI search audit guide covers the AI side of the check. Why does Google show a different title or description than mine? Google builds title links and snippets from the page and may replace what you supplied when it does not describe the page well. The Web Almanac notes that title rewrites in search results are widespread, yet title tags are still present on almost every page. So write titles that match the visible page, give the main heading, title and opening answer the same purpose, and put a clear definition or answer near the top of the page. If Google keeps changing your title, compare it with your H1 and with how other sites link to the page. The rewrite is often a sign that your title promises something the page does not deliver. A bonus mistake: blocking the bots that feed AI answers Security plugins and CDN settings sometimes block crawlers without anyone noticing. OpenAI says sites that opt out of OAI-SearchBot will not be shown in ChatGPT search answers, and that a robots.txt change can take about 24 hours to apply. Check that the search bots you want, such as Googlebot, Bingbot and OAI-SearchBot, are not blocked on pages you want found. Training bots such as GPTBot are a separate choice. Our AI search audit guide shows how to test each bot. What are the biggest SEO mistakes? If you only fix a few things, fix these first, because each one can keep a page out of search results or hide it from buyers: A noindex tag or robots block on pages you want found. Content that search engines cannot see, such as text that only loads after a script runs. Pages that do not match what the searcher wants. Important pages that return an error, or redirect to the wrong place. Pages with no internal links pointing to them. Do 404 errors hurt SEO? A 404 means “page not found.” Google says it does not use content from URLs that return a 4xx status, does not index them, and removes already indexed 4xx URLs from its index. It also crawls them less often over time. So a 404 is not a penalty. It is the right answer for a page that is gone on purpose. The harm comes from the pages it removes. If a page that earned links or traffic starts returning a 404, you lose what that page earned. Here is how to handle it: Page moved: use a 301 redirect to the closest matching page. Page gone for good, with no close match: leave a 404 or 410 and make sure no internal link points to it. Page should exist: restore it and fix the cause. Error shown, but the page looks normal: check for a “soft 404,” where the page says “not found” but returns a 200 status. To find them, open the Page indexing report in Google Search Console, or crawl the site with a tool. On a large site, fix the error pages that have links or traffic first. Common on-page SEO mistakes to avoid On-page mistakes live on the page itself. They are usually the fastest to fix. The most common ones are: A title or meta description that is missing, duplicated or does not match the page (mistake 5). Headings that skip levels or carry no meaning (mistake 6). Thin or copycat copy that adds nothing new (mistake 7). Keyword stuffing, or several pages aimed at the same search (mistake 8). No internal links to or from the page (mistake 9). Images with no description, or files that are too large (mistake 11). Common technical SEO mistakes to avoid Technical mistakes stop pages from being found, shown or used. Check these first, because they can undo good content: A noindex tag or robots block you did not mean (mistake 2). Content that loads only in the browser, so crawlers cannot see it (mistake 3). Duplicate pages and mixed canonical signals (mistake 4). Slow, unstable pages on phones (mistake 10). Markup that does not match what the page shows, and no measuring (mistake 12). Mistakes to avoid when hiring an SEO company Many SEO problems start with the wrong hire. Google’s own advice for hiring an SEO is a useful checklist: Never accept a ranking guarantee. Google says no one can guarantee a number one ranking, and warns against anyone who claims a special relationship with Google. Ask for examples and a plan. Ask for past work, the results they expect, the timeframe and how they measure success. Give read access first. For an audit, Google advises read access to Search Console and not write access at the start. Insist on explanations. Be careful if a company is secretive or will not say what it plans to do. You are responsible for what firms you hire do to your site. Do not trust cold emails. Be wary of firms that email you out of the blue. Never agree to link to them or to buy link schemes. Which free tools help you find these mistakes? Tool What it finds Search Console, Page Indexing report Noindex, robots blocks, duplicates, soft 404 errors, pages not indexed Search Console, URL Inspection What Google fetched and rendered, and the chosen canonical Search Console, Core Web Vitals report Field data on loading, responsiveness and layout shift by URL group PageSpeed Insights Lab and field speed data and the largest causes Rich Results Test Markup errors and eligibility for rich results A site crawler Titles, headings, status codes, redirects, orphan pages and link anchors Bing Webmaster Tools Indexing in Bing, which matters for tools that use Bing, and AI citation data Any basic crawler will do for a small site. Paid suites help at scale, such as when you have thousands of pages, but they do not replace a person who reads the results and decides what matters. How should you order the fixes? Priority Mistakes Why first 1. Access and indexing 2, 3, 4 If a page cannot be crawled or indexed, nothing else matters. 2. Relevance and content 1, 7, 8 The page must answer the right question better than others. 3. Structure and signals 5, 6, 9 Clear titles, headings and links help people and systems understand the page. 4. Experience and polish 10, 11, 12 Speed, images and markup support a good page. They do not rescue a weak one. A free 60-minute audit 10 minutes: open Search Console’s Page Indexing report and fix noindex and robots problems on pages that matter. 10 minutes: inspect three key pages with URL Inspection and compare the rendered text with the live page. 15 minutes: crawl the site with any crawler, and sort by title, H1, status code and inbound links. 10 minutes: read the Core Web Vitals report and pick the worst template. 10 minutes: review your top five pages against the search task and write what is missing. 5 minutes: list the first three fixes, with an owner and a date. Worked example: a small services site This is an illustration, not a client result. Imagine a 40-page site for a local accounting firm. The audit finds a noindex tag left on its services page after a redesign, a blog that loads posts only after a “load more” click, 12 pages with the same title, and a home page with three H1s. The team fixes access first by removing the noindex tag and adding normal links to blog posts. It then rewrites 12 titles and merges two competing posts. In week four it adds internal links from the blog to the services page, and compresses the largest images. It tracks indexed pages, impressions and inquiries against a baseline taken before the work. The result may be small or large, and it is measured, not assumed. Our interest in this topic Reinforce Lab sells SEO and AI search services. Nothing here is paid placement. Jamil Ahmed, who wrote this guide, is a Semrush Ambassador, and Reinforce Lab uses affiliate links for some tools. Read our FTC and affiliate disclosure . Our technical SEO service covers these checks, and you can get your free diagnostic . Final thoughts Fix what stops a page from being found first, then what makes it worth choosing, then what makes it pleasant and fast. Keep a short audit habit, since a stray tag or a redesign can undo months of work. Measure the result in Search Console and in leads, not only in rankings. Back matter Glossary A to Z N Noindex A tag that tells search engines not to show a page in results. C Canonical tag A hint that names the preferred URL when several pages have the same content. C Crawl When a program visits your pages to find content and links. O Orphan page A page that no other page on your site links to. C Core Web Vitals Google's measures of loading speed, responsiveness and visual stability. I Information gain New, useful material that a page adds beyond what others already say. Frequently asked questions What are the most common SEO mistakes? Blocking or noindexing pages by accident, content that search engines cannot see, duplicate or missing titles and headings, thin or copycat content, weak internal links, keyword stuffing, slow pages, images without descriptions and markup that does not match the page. What is the biggest SEO mistake? An unintended noindex tag or robots block, because nothing else helps while a page cannot be indexed. Check Search Console's Page Indexing report for pages excluded by noindex or blocked by robots.txt. How do I find SEO mistakes on my website? Use Search Console for indexing, URL Inspection for rendering, a crawler for titles, headings, status codes and internal links, PageSpeed Insights or the Core Web Vitals report for speed, and the Rich Results Test for markup. How common are missing meta descriptions and H1 tags? The 2025 Web Almanac found meta descriptions on 67.7% of desktop pages and an H1 on 71%. SE Ranking's audited sites showed missing meta descriptions on 65.38% and missing H1s on 54.67%. The two data sets measure different things. Does keyword stuffing still hurt SEO? Yes. Google's spam policies list keyword stuffing as a manipulation technique. Use the keyword where it fits and write for the reader's question. What are the Core Web Vitals thresholds? Google's web.dev recommends LCP within 2.5 seconds, INP of 200 milliseconds and CLS of 0.1, measured at the 75th percentile of page loads and segmented by mobile and desktop. Do duplicate titles matter? They make pages hard to tell apart in results and can signal thin or duplicated content. SE Ranking found duplicate titles on 53.69% of audited sites. Give each page a distinct, accurate title. Is AI-written content an SEO mistake? Not by itself. Google says appropriate AI use is not against its guidelines. Generating many pages without adding value for users is listed as scaled content abuse. Add original value and check every fact. How often should I run an SEO audit? Run a short check monthly and a fuller audit each quarter and after any redesign, migration or plugin change, since a stray tag or setting can undo months of work. Do I need paid tools to avoid SEO mistakes? Not to start. Search Console, URL Inspection, PageSpeed Insights, the Rich Results Test and any basic crawler cover most checks. Paid tools help at scale. What are common on-page SEO mistakes? Missing or duplicate titles and descriptions, a messy heading structure, thin or copycat content, keyword stuffing, pages that compete with each other, weak internal links and images with no description. What are common technical SEO mistakes? An accidental noindex tag or robots block, content that crawlers cannot see, duplicate pages with mixed canonical signals, slow or unstable pages and markup that does not match the page. What mistakes should I avoid when hiring an SEO company? Do not accept ranking guarantees, secrecy or cold emails. Ask for examples, a plan and how success is measured, start with read-only access to Search Console, and never agree to link schemes. Do 404 errors hurt SEO? Not by themselves. Google drops URLs that return a 404 from its index and crawls them less. The harm comes when a page that earned links or traffic starts returning a 404. Redirect moved pages, and leave a 404 or 410 for pages that are gone for good. Are 404 errors bad for SEO? A 404 is the correct response for a page that no longer exists, so it is not a penalty. It is bad when it hits a page that had links, traffic or internal links. Fix those with a 301 redirect or by restoring the page. What are the biggest SEO mistakes? Blocking pages from search by accident, hiding content from crawlers, ignoring search intent, leaving important pages broken or redirected wrongly, and having no internal links to key pages. What SEO mistakes should I avoid in 2026? The same core mistakes still apply: accidental noindex, unreadable content, weak titles, thin pages and slow pages. Add one more: do not block the crawlers that feed AI answers if you want to be cited there. How do I fix SEO errors? Find them with Google Search Console or a crawl, sort them by the pages that have links or traffic, and fix the ones that block indexing first. Then recheck after the next crawl.
