It helps patients, healthcare professionals and business buyers find accurate, approved information, under strict advertising and review rules. Give every search one page owner, map audiences and markets, bring search into medical, legal and regulatory review early, show checkable evidence and measure in stages. 01 Pharma SEO uses ordinary SEO methods, but ownership, claims, evidence and approval time carry more weight. 02 Rules differ by country, product and audience, so decide the audience and market for every page first. 03 Give every target search one page owner, and map keywords by audience and intent, with a named reviewer. 04 Bring SEO into medical, legal and regulatory review early, so wording is agreed once. 05 Show the author, reviewer, sources and review date on every health page. 06 Check what AI tools say about your key questions each quarter, and fix the source pages first. 07 Plan for several months before pages go live and six to twelve months before judging results. Pharma SEO, also called pharmaceutical SEO or life sciences SEO, is search engine optimization for pharmaceutical and life sciences companies. It helps patients, caregivers, healthcare professionals and business buyers find accurate, approved information about conditions, medicines, research and suppliers. It works inside strict advertising rules, so the plan and the approvals have to be built together. SEO is one part of pharma digital marketing, which also includes paid search, email, social media and field teams. This guide covers the organic search part. It explains what pharma SEO is, how it differs from ordinary SEO, which rules shape it, and how to run it in eight steps. It includes worked examples, a 90-day plan, questions to ask a pharma SEO company and the mistakes that cost teams the most time. It is not legal advice. Your medical, legal and regulatory team makes the final call on every claim. 01 Chapter 1 · 1 min What is pharma SEO? Pharma SEO means making regulated health and company information easy to find in Google and in AI answers, without weakening the evidence or the review process behind it. The mechanics are the same as in any SEO: pages, links, technical health and content that answers real questions. What changes is who owns each page, which statements are allowed and how long a change takes to approve. It covers four kinds of site: Manufacturer and brand sites. Corporate pages, pipeline pages, product information and disease education. Contract and supply sites. Contract manufacturers, active ingredient suppliers, packaging and testing firms that sell to other companies. Pharmacy and distribution sites. Wholesalers, specialty pharmacies and online pharmacies. Research and education sites. Trial information, medical education and patient groups. End of chapter 1 Next: How does pharma SEO differ from general SEO and healthcare SEO? → 02 Chapter 2 · 1 min How does pharma SEO differ from general SEO and healthcare SEO? General SEO Healthcare SEO Pharma SEO Typical site Any business Clinics, practices, hospitals Manufacturers, suppliers, pharmacies, research bodies Main audience Customers Local patients Patients, caregivers, prescribers, business buyers, investors What you may say Few limits beyond consumer law Professional and advertising rules Tight rules on claims, risk information and who may see product information Review before publishing Editor Clinician or practice owner Often medical, legal and regulatory review (MLR) Local search Sometimes Central Rare, except pharmacies Proof Google looks for Helpful, original content Named clinicians, reviews Named experts, cited sources, dates, consistent facts Healthcare SEO helps a practice get found by patients nearby. Pharma SEO is about explaining conditions, treatments, evidence and suppliers to many different audiences, under rules that differ by country and by audience. End of chapter 2 Next: Which rules shape pharma search content? → 03 Chapter 3 · 2 min Which rules shape pharma search content? You do not need to be a lawyer to plan SEO, but you do need to know why the review step exists. These are the public sources we checked. Each applies differently to different products and markets, so treat them as background and ask your regulatory team. Source What it says in plain words Why it matters for SEO US FDA, draft guidance on online platforms with space limits If a firm makes a benefit claim for a prescription drug, it should also give risk information in the same space and a way to reach the full risk information. The FDA notes that guidance documents do not create legal requirements by themselves. A title tag or meta description that states a benefit may need risk information too. Short text does not remove the duty. US FDA, guidance on presenting risk information Prescription drug promotion should give a fair balance of benefit and risk information. A product page cannot be built around benefits and leave safety for a link nobody sees. US FTC, Health Products Compliance Guidance Marketers are responsible for claims that are stated and for claims reasonably implied. Health claims need strong scientific support. An image, a heading or a comparison table can make a claim. Check the whole page, not only the text. UK MHRA guidance on advertising medicines The ban on advertising prescription-only medicines to the public applies to social networks as well as to traditional media. Public pages about prescription-only medicines need care in the UK. Disease information and product promotion are treated differently. EU Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 88 Member States must prohibit advertising prescription-only medicines to the general public. Patient-facing product pages are restricted across the EU. Pages for healthcare professionals follow different rules. Google, helpful content guidance Google asks for experience, expertise, authority and trust, and holds topics that affect health to the highest standard. It calls these Your Money or Your Life topics. Named authors, reviewers, sources and dates are not extras for pharma pages. They are what Google looks for. One point sits above the rest. Rules differ by country, by product type and by audience. A page that is fine for healthcare professionals in one market may not be fine for the public in another. Decide the audience and market for every page first. End of chapter 3 Next: Who searches, and what do they want? → 04 Chapter 4 · 2 min Who searches, and what do they want? A pharma site often serves six audiences. Each searches in its own words, so mixing them in one keyword list produces pages that rank for the wrong searches. Audience What they search (examples) Page that fits Patients symptoms of a condition, how a treatment works, side effects Plain-language disease education, with sources and a review date Caregivers managing a medicine for a parent, what to ask the doctor Practical guides and question lists Healthcare professionals mechanism of action, dosing, trial results, prescribing information Evidence pages, clearly marked as for professionals Business buyers contract manufacturer for sterile injectables, active ingredient supplier Capability pages, certifications, case studies, contact forms Researchers and journalists trial name, publication, company pipeline Pipeline, publications and media pages Investors and partners company results, partnerships Corporate and investor pages Some numbers show why this matters. In the US National Health Interview Survey, 58.5% of adults used the internet to look for health or medical information in July to December 2022 (a sample of 14,020 adults, reported by the CDC’s National Center for Health Statistics). In a Pew Research Center survey of 3,014 US adults from August to September 2012, 59% had looked online for health information in the past year, and 8 in 10 of them started at a general search engine. The Pew survey is older, so treat it as a sign of search behavior and not as a current figure. Professionals are also online. IQVIA’s 2025 survey of more than 33,000 healthcare professionals in 38 countries found that one-to-one face-to-face meetings still made up 40% of preferred channels in the US and the largest EU markets plus the UK, and that email preference reached a new peak of 15%. That mix is why search, email and owned pages sit next to field work and do not replace it. End of chapter 4 Next: What is the difference between branded and unbranded search? → 05 Chapter 5 · 1 min What is the difference between branded and unbranded search? Branded searches include a product or company name. Unbranded searches are about a condition, symptom or treatment class and do not name a brand. They play different roles. Unbranded search builds trust early. A patient who reads a clear explanation of a condition may remember the source. Branded search is mostly navigation. People look for prescribing information, patient resources or contact details. The link between the two needs care. For prescription medicines, disease education that links straight to product promotion can change how regulators view the education page. Treat internal links on these pages as a compliance question, and ask your regulatory team how the two page types may connect. End of chapter 5 Next: How to do pharma SEO: 8 steps → 06 Chapter 6 · 4 min How to do pharma SEO: 8 steps Step 1: Give every search one page owner List the searches you want to win. For each one, name the single page that should answer it, the audience and the page type. Service pages, guides, glossary entries and product pages can all stay live, but each needs a clear job. If Search Console shows five pages getting impressions for the same phrase, Google cannot tell which one is meant to answer. Step 2: Map your audiences and markets Choose the audiences from the table above that matter to your business. Note the country for each. A page for UK patients, a page for EU professionals and a page for US prescribers are three different pages with three different review paths. Step 3: Build a keyword map by intent Use a keyword tool and your own Search Console data. Group the searches by audience and by what the searcher wants: to learn, to compare or to contact. Add a column for who must approve the page. Do not target a keyword on a page that cannot say what searchers want to know, for example a price or a claim that is not allowed. Search (example) Audience Intent Page Reviewer [condition] symptoms Patients Learn Disease education page Medical, regulatory [drug class] mechanism of action Professionals Learn Evidence page for professionals Medical, legal, regulatory contract manufacturer sterile injectables Business buyers Compare, contact Capability page Quality, legal [company] clinical trials Researchers Learn Pipeline and trials page Medical, regulatory Step 4: Design the page before you write it Review can remove risk from a page. It cannot give a page a purpose it never had. Before drafting, fix these fields for each page: Audience and market The one question the page answers Claims it will make, and the source for each Approved wording and required safety text Author, reviewer, owner and next review date Put the answer at the top in two or three plain sentences. Then add detail. Step 5: Bring SEO into the review process early Many teams run review first and add SEO after. That turns a small title change into another approval round. Instead, share the keyword map and the page design with medical and regulatory colleagues before drafting, so wording is agreed once. Plan production around real approval times, publish durable pages first and keep a log of approved text that can be reused. Some agencies report approval cycles of several weeks. Check your own, because they vary by company and by content type. Step 6: Fix the technical basics Crawling and indexing. Make sure public pages can be crawled and indexed. Gate professional-only content clearly, and do not rely on gated pages as landing pages. Speed and mobile. Professionals often search on a phone between appointments. Site structure. Group pages by condition, audience and product, and link them in a logical path. Titles and headings. Use the words your audience uses. Check each title for claims. Structured data. Schema markup tells machines what a page is, such as an article, an organization or a medical web page. Google documents the types it supports. Use markup to describe the page honestly, and do not expect it to lift rankings by itself. Images. Add plain alt text, and check that images do not imply a claim. Step 7: Show evidence people can check Authority comes from what a reader can verify. On every page show: The author, with relevant experience The medical or scientific reviewer, with the review date Links to the sources for each important statement, preferring primary sources such as regulators, guidelines and peer-reviewed papers A visible updated date, with changes logged when guidance changes The scope: who the page is for and what it does not cover Label worked examples as real, anonymized or illustrative. That does not weaken a page. It stops the page from promising evidence it does not have. Step 8: Measure in stages Stage Question Where to look Discovery Are the right pages indexed and getting impressions? Search Console Ownership Does the intended page get the impressions for its searches? Search Console, by query and page Ranking Are pages moving to positions where clicks happen? Rank tracking Engagement Do the right visitors read and take the next step? Analytics: scroll, clicks, form fills Quality Are pages current, sourced and approved? Content log and review dates End of chapter 6 Next: Worked example 1: a disease education page → 07 Chapter 7 · 1 min Worked example 1: a disease education page This example is illustrative. A company develops a treatment for a chronic skin condition and wants an unbranded education page for patients in one market. Decision Choice Search “[condition] symptoms” and “what causes [condition]” Audience and market Adult patients, one country Page job Explain the condition in plain words and say when to see a doctor Top of page A three-sentence answer with the author and reviewer named Body Symptoms, causes, types, when to seek care, questions to ask a doctor Sources Clinical guidelines and a national health service page, linked What it avoids Product names, benefit claims and links to product pages, unless the regulatory team has approved how the two connect Review Medical and regulatory, with the keyword map shared first Measure Impressions and clicks for the condition searches, and time on page End of chapter 7 Next: Worked example 2: a contract manufacturer → 08 Chapter 8 · 1 min Worked example 2: a contract manufacturer This example is also illustrative. A contract manufacturer of sterile injectables sells to other companies and has one general “services” page. Audit. The page is indexed but ranks for nothing, because it lists capabilities in one paragraph. Keyword map. Four searches: sterile injectable contract manufacturing, fill and finish services, small batch clinical supply, and the company name. Pages. One capability page for each, with equipment lists, batch sizes, quality certifications the company actually holds, an anonymized project example and a contact form. Evidence. Named quality head as reviewer, certification numbers and dates, and a changelog. Measure. Enquiries from organic search tagged by page and tracked into the sales system. The result is a site that answers a buyer’s detailed questions before the first call. Search volume for this kind of term is small, but each visit comes from a qualified buyer. End of chapter 8 Next: How do you write titles and descriptions in a regulated field? → 09 Chapter 9 · 1 min How do you write titles and descriptions in a regulated field? Titles and meta descriptions are the first words a searcher reads, and they are short. That makes them easy to get wrong. A few rules keep them safe and useful: Describe the page, do not promote. “Understanding [condition]: symptoms, causes and when to see a doctor” is safer than a line about results. Avoid benefit words for products. Words such as “effective” or “proven” can read as claims. If a product is named, ask what risk information must sit with it. Name the audience. “For healthcare professionals” in a title sets the right expectation and filters out the wrong clicks. Keep them stable. Once approved, a title should not change often, because each change may need review. End of chapter 9 Next: How should internal links work? → 10 Chapter 10 · 1 min How should internal links work? Internal links tell Google which pages matter and how topics connect. In pharma they also shape how a regulator or reviewer reads a page. Plan them with the same care as the text. Link disease education pages to each other and to related patient resources. Link professional pages to evidence, trial and prescribing resources, not to patient pages. For prescription products, agree with your regulatory team whether and how education pages may point to product pages. Use clear link text that says where the link goes. Avoid “click here”. Write the linking rules down, so new pages follow them without a new debate. End of chapter 10 Next: How do you handle content for healthcare professionals? → 11 Chapter 11 · 1 min How do you handle content for healthcare professionals? Clinical data pages are valuable for authority, and they carry the highest accuracy risk. Some companies place them behind a professional check. That is a legitimate choice, but it has an SEO cost: search engines cannot read gated pages. A workable pattern is to keep a public, indexable page that explains what the resource is, who it is for and what it covers, and to gate only the material that requires it. The public page can rank and send the right visitors to the next step. Make sure the public text follows the same approval rules as any other page. End of chapter 11 Next: What about pharmacies and distributors? → 12 Chapter 12 · 1 min What about pharmacies and distributors? Pharmacies and distributors often win with local and trust signals more than with long articles. Check these basics: A complete Google Business Profile with the correct name, address, phone number and hours Licence and registration details on the site, in plain view Pages for each service, such as repeat prescriptions or delivery, written in plain language Clear information on what the pharmacy can and cannot advertise about prescription-only medicines in its country Reviews that you ask for fairly and answer without sharing any patient detail End of chapter 12 Next: Can pharma companies use AI to write content? → 13 Chapter 13 · 1 min Can pharma companies use AI to write content? Google has said that using AI is not against its guidelines when the result is helpful and made for people, and that using it mainly to manipulate rankings breaks its spam policies. For pharma the bigger point is accuracy and responsibility. An AI tool can invent a dose, a study or a safety statement that sounds right. Your company is responsible for every claim on its pages. If you use AI in drafting, keep these rules: Give it approved source material, not open questions. Have a qualified person check every fact against the source. Run the normal medical, legal and regulatory review. Name the human author and reviewer on the page. Keep a record of the sources used. End of chapter 13 Next: What content types work in pharma SEO? → 14 Chapter 14 · 1 min What content types work in pharma SEO? Content type Audience Search value Review effort (our judgment) Disease education Patients, caregivers High: condition searches Medium: avoid implied promotion Evidence summaries Professionals High for medical terms High: study data must be exact Mechanism of action explainers Professionals Medium: niche but strong authority Medium Capability pages Business buyers High for commercial terms Medium: certifications must be current Glossary entries Everyone Medium: short definitions Low to medium Pipeline and trial pages Researchers, investors Medium High Expert interviews Professionals Medium: builds trust Medium: check disclosures End of chapter 14 Next: Pharma SEO and AI search → 15 Chapter 15 · 1 min Pharma SEO and AI search People now ask AI tools and Google’s AI answers about conditions and medicines. These tools summarize pages, and they can get facts wrong. For pharma this is a risk as well as a chance. Put the answer first. A short, direct opening is easy for people and for machines to use. Keep facts consistent. Names, indications and safety wording should match across your pages and your listings. Cite your sources on the page. Pages that show where each statement came from are easier to trust. Check what AI tools say. Ask them the questions your audiences ask. Record any wrong or unsafe answer, and fix the source pages first. Know the limits. No method guarantees that an AI tool will cite you, and regulatory rules still apply to your own pages. End of chapter 15 Next: How long does pharma SEO take? → 16 Chapter 16 · 1 min How long does pharma SEO take? Google says some changes show in hours and others take months, and it suggests waiting a few weeks before judging a change. Pharma adds approval time before anything goes live. Plan for six to twelve months before you judge the program, and for a few months before the first pages are live. End of chapter 16 Next: A 90-day plan to start → 17 Chapter 17 · 1 min A 90-day plan to start Days Work Output 1 to 14 Audit indexing, page ownership and technical health; list audiences and markets Starting point and a fix list 15 to 30 Build the keyword map; agree page designs and approved language with the review team Map and page models agreed once 31 to 60 Fix the technical basics; write and submit the first three to five pages for review Pages in approval 61 to 90 Publish approved pages; set up measurement; test AI answers for your key questions First pages live and a monthly report End of chapter 17 Next: Should you hire a pharmaceutical SEO company? → 18 Chapter 18 · 1 min Should you hire a pharmaceutical SEO company? Some teams run SEO in-house with medical writers and a technical lead. Others use an agency for strategy, technical work and reporting. Whichever you choose, the same questions apply. Ask any pharmaceutical SEO company or agency: Which audiences and markets have you worked in, and which rules do you plan around? How will you work with our medical, legal and regulatory team, and when does SEO enter the process? Who writes and who reviews the content, and what are their qualifications? How do you report results, and can you tie them to enquiries or other business goals? How do you earn links? Google lists buying links to affect rankings as link spam. How do you check AI answers about our products? What is in the written scope, and how can we end the contract? Be careful with anyone who promises a ranking date or guarantees approvals. Nobody controls Google, and your own regulatory team controls approvals. Reinforce Lab also offers search services to pharmaceutical companies, so read this guide with that in mind. It was written by a team whose founder trained as a pharmacist and worked in pharmaceutical marketing. End of chapter 18 Next: Common pharma SEO mistakes → 19 Chapter 19 · 1 min Common pharma SEO mistakes Adding SEO after review. A small change then triggers a new approval round. Mixing audiences. One keyword list for patients, professionals and buyers makes pages that serve none. Gating the wrong pages. If professional content is the landing page, public searchers find nothing to read. Writing benefit-led titles. A title or description can carry a claim. Linking education straight to promotion. Ask your regulatory team first. No author, reviewer or date. Health pages without them lose trust. Copying competitor pages. Duplicate pages do not earn authority. Letting facts drift. Out-of-date doses and indications are a risk for patients and for you. Buying links. Short-term gain, long-term risk. End of chapter 19 Next: A quick checklist → 20 Chapter 20 · 1 min A quick checklist One page owner for each target search Audiences and markets listed, each page tied to one Keyword map with a reviewer for every page Page designs and approved wording agreed before drafting Author, reviewer, sources and dates visible on every health page Professional-only content clearly marked, and public pages indexable Titles and descriptions checked for claims Technical basics fixed and measured AI answers about your key questions checked each quarter Monthly report that ties search to business goals End of chapter 20 Next: Final thoughts → 21 Chapter 21 · 1 min Final thoughts Pharma SEO works when search and regulatory teams plan together from the start. Pick the audience, name the page that owns each search, show evidence a reader can check and measure in stages. The first few pages take longest. After that, the approved models make every new page faster to publish and safer to maintain. Back matter Glossary A to Z B Branded search A search that includes a product or company name. F Fair balance Presenting risk information with comparable content and prominence to benefit claims in prescription drug promotion. M MLR review Medical, legal and regulatory review: the approval step many pharmaceutical companies use before content is published. U Unbranded search A search about a condition, symptom or treatment class that names no brand. Y YMYL Your Money or Your Life: Google's term for topics that can affect health, money or safety, held to a higher quality standard. Questions FAQs What is pharma SEO? Pharma SEO is search engine optimization for pharmaceutical and life sciences companies. It helps patients, healthcare professionals and business buyers find accurate, approved information, while following advertising and review rules that are stricter than in most industries. How is pharma SEO different from healthcare SEO? Healthcare SEO mostly helps clinics and practices get found by local patients. Pharma SEO serves manufacturers, suppliers, pharmacies and research bodies, speaks to several audiences at once and works under tight rules on claims, risk information and who may see product information. Can pharmaceutical companies do SEO for prescription medicines? Yes, within the rules of each market. Rules differ by country, product and audience. In the EU and UK, advertising prescription-only medicines to the public is prohibited, so patient-facing pages focus on disease information and approved material. Your regulatory team decides what each page may say. How does medical, legal and regulatory review affect SEO? Review decides what a page may say, so it affects both speed and wording. Bring SEO in early: share the keyword map and page design before drafting, agree approved wording once and publish durable pages first, so small changes do not trigger new approval rounds. Can pharma companies target healthcare professionals with SEO? Yes. Professionals search for mechanism of action, dosing, trial data and prescribing information. Keep a public indexable page that explains what a resource is and who it is for, and gate only the material that needs it, because search engines cannot read gated pages. What are the best keywords for pharma SEO? They depend on the audience. Patients search conditions, symptoms and treatment questions. Professionals search clinical and scientific terms. Business buyers search suppliers and capabilities. Build a keyword map by audience and intent, and record who must approve each page. Can pharma companies use AI to write content? Google says AI use is not against its guidelines when the content is helpful and made for people. For pharma, accuracy and responsibility matter most: give AI approved sources, have a qualified person check every fact, run normal review and name the human author and reviewer. Do AI answer engines cite pharma product pages? They can draw on pharma pages, and they can also get facts wrong. Put clear answers at the top, keep facts consistent across pages, cite your sources and check what AI tools say about your key questions every quarter. No method guarantees a citation. How long does pharma SEO take? Google says some changes show in hours and others take months. Pharma also needs approval time before pages go live. Plan for a few months before the first pages are live and six to twelve months before you judge the program. How do I choose a pharma SEO company? Ask which audiences and markets they know, how they work with your medical, legal and regulatory team, who writes and reviews content, how they report results, how they earn links and what the written scope and exit terms are. Be wary of promised ranking dates. Set a goal for each audience, decide audiences and markets first, map the rules, build approved content modules, choose a few sequenced channels, plan safety reporting and privacy, and measure in layers. 01 Rules differ by country, product and audience, so decide the audience and market for every asset first. 02 Start with one owned, one direct and one reach channel, and add more only when you can review and staff them. 03 Write approved content modules once and reuse them, so reviewers approve a block, not every page. 04 Any channel the company runs or sponsors can produce safety reports, so plan how to capture them. 05 Disclose paid relationships. The FDA named undisclosed paid influencer promotion as a concern in 2025. 06 Measure reach, engagement, behavior and business results in layers, and count qualified engagement, not total opens. 07 Search is the base for many other channels, so make the main pages easy to find and trust. Pharma digital marketing is the use of digital channels to reach patients, caregivers, healthcare professionals and business buyers with information about conditions, medicines and services. It covers websites, search, email, social media, paid media, webinars and more. Every channel sits inside advertising rules, so the plan and the approvals have to be built together. This guide explains what pharma digital marketing is, which rules shape it, how to choose channels, and how to build a program in eight steps. It includes worked examples, a measurement model, a 90-day plan and questions to ask an agency. It is not legal advice. Your medical, legal and regulatory team decides what each asset may say. For the organic search part of the mix, see our guide to pharma SEO . 01 Chapter 1 · 1 min What is pharma digital marketing? Pharma digital marketing uses the same tools as digital marketing in other industries, applied to regulated products and services. A company may promote a prescription medicine to prescribers, share disease information with the public, sell active ingredients to manufacturers or support a patient program. The tools are familiar. The limits on what each channel may carry are not. Three things make it different from general digital marketing: Who may see what. Prescription medicine promotion is aimed at professionals in many markets, while the public sees disease information. What you may claim. Benefit claims need risk information, evidence and approval. How long it takes. Review, safety reporting and data privacy add steps that other industries skip. End of chapter 1 Next: Why does digital marketing matter for pharmaceutical companies? → 02 Chapter 2 · 2 min Why does digital marketing matter for pharmaceutical companies? Professionals and patients both look for information online before they speak to a person. A prescriber may search for clinical data between appointments. A patient may search for a condition before seeing a doctor. A business buyer may compare suppliers before the first call. If your company is not there with accurate information, other sources fill the gap, and they may not be accurate. Digital channels also let teams measure engagement and reach people between field visits. They do not replace field teams or medical affairs. They connect with them. The numbers point the same way, with limits: Patients search. In the US National Health Interview Survey, 58.5% of adults used the internet to look for health or medical information in July to December 2022 (14,020 adults, CDC’s National Center for Health Statistics). Spend is moving to digital. eMarketer estimated that US pharma would spend $19.45 billion on digital advertising in 2024, which it put at 88% of the wider healthcare industry’s digital ad spend. Its 2025 forecast for healthcare and pharma digital ad spend was $24.77 billion, up 13.3%. These are forecasts from one research firm. Budgets are shifting. Axtria analyzed 140 marketing mix studies across 70 US brands. Digital’s share of pharma marketing spend rose from 6% in 2018 to 22% in 2022, while the field force channel was still the largest at 62% of spend in 2022. Professionals prefer a mix. IQVIA’s 2025 survey of more than 33,000 healthcare professionals in 38 countries found that face-to-face meetings were 40% of preferred channels in the US and the largest EU markets plus the UK, and email reached a new peak of 15%. Veeva, which sells software to the industry, reported in a 2024 ebook that 84% of healthcare professionals prefer to keep or increase the share of virtual interactions with biopharma companies. No source here says that digital replaces in-person work. They show a blend, so plan for both. End of chapter 2 Next: Which rules shape pharma digital marketing? → 03 Chapter 3 · 2 min Which rules shape pharma digital marketing? These are the public sources we checked. Each applies differently by product, audience and country, so use them as background and ask your regulatory team. Source What it says in plain words What it means for digital work US FDA, announcement of 9 September 2025 The FDA said it was sending thousands of letters to pharmaceutical companies about misleading ads and about 100 cease-and-desist letters, and starting rulemaking on how risk information is provided in broadcast and digital ads. It also said digital and social media, including undisclosed paid influencer promotion, have blurred the line between editorial content and advertising. It said it was using AI and other tools to review drug ads. Expect closer review of digital and social promotion in the US. Disclose paid relationships, and treat every post as an ad if the company pays for it. US FDA, draft guidance on online platforms with space limits If a firm makes a benefit claim for a prescription drug, it should include risk information in the same space and a way to reach the full risk information. The FDA notes that guidance documents do not create legal requirements by themselves. Short formats such as search ads and social posts do not remove the duty. If a format cannot carry the risk information, do not make the benefit claim in it. US FDA, guidance on presenting risk information Prescription drug promotion should present a fair balance of benefit and risk information. Risk information has to be comparable in content and prominence to the benefits, on every page and in every asset. US FTC, Health Products Compliance Guidance Marketers are responsible for claims that are stated and for claims reasonably implied. Health claims need strong scientific support. An image, a heading or an influencer’s tone can make a claim. Review the whole asset. UK ABPI Code of Practice and MHRA The ABPI Code prohibits advertising prescription-only medicines to the public. The MHRA says the ban applies to social networks in the same way as to traditional media. Company-sponsored digital activity, including social media, falls under the Code. Public-facing UK content about prescription-only medicines is limited to disease information and approved public information. Professional content follows the Code. EU Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 88 Member States must prohibit advertising prescription-only medicines to the general public. Patient-facing product promotion is restricted across the EU. National codes add detail. One point sits above the rest. Rules differ by country, product type and audience, so decide the audience and market for every asset first. A tactic that is normal in one market can be a breach in another. End of chapter 3 Next: Who are you trying to reach? → 04 Chapter 4 · 1 min Who are you trying to reach? Audience What they need Typical channels Healthcare professionals Clinical data, dosing, safety, prescribing information, education Professional website, verified professional networks, approved email, webinars, remote or digital detailing Patients Condition information, when to see a doctor, support options Unbranded disease education sites, search, video, patient groups Caregivers Practical help managing a condition or medicine Guides, question lists, support program pages Business buyers Capabilities, certifications, capacity, quality records Capability pages, search, LinkedIn, trade media, events Researchers, partners and investors Pipeline, publications, results Corporate site, media releases, professional networks End of chapter 4 Next: Which channels work in pharma digital marketing? → 05 Chapter 5 · 1 min Which channels work in pharma digital marketing? Channel Best for Main caution Website Every audience, with separate paths Keep professional and public content clearly separate; add author, reviewer and dates Search (SEO) Disease education, professional evidence, supplier searches Titles and descriptions can carry claims; see our pharma SEO guide Paid search Disease awareness, over-the-counter products, supplier terms Platform health advertising policies differ by country; check them and the rules for your product Email Professionals and patients who opted in Keep consent records; follow privacy law; refer medical questions to medical information Professional networks and media Reaching verified professionals Ask for audience verification and reporting you can check Webinars and virtual meetings Education, with credible speakers Keep it educational; follow rules on hospitality and speaker payments Remote or digital detailing Extending field reach Same approval as a face-to-face call; log content shown Social media Awareness, education, company news, hiring Space limits make risk information hard; company channels fall under the rules; plan for comments and safety reports Influencers and creators Disease awareness in some cases Disclose paid relationships; the FDA has named undisclosed paid promotion as a concern Apps and tools Education, adherence support Treat claims and data collection as regulated Start small. Pick one owned channel, one direct channel and one reach channel, and add more only when you can review, staff and measure them. Each channel needs review and someone to handle responses. End of chapter 5 Next: How to build a pharma digital marketing strategy: 8 steps → 06 Chapter 6 · 3 min How to build a pharma digital marketing strategy: 8 steps Step 1: Set one clear goal for each audience Write a goal that matches how each audience acts. For professionals it might be more qualified visits to evidence pages. For patients it might be more people finding accurate condition information. For business buyers it might be more qualified enquiries. Avoid one goal for everyone, because a single number hides what works. Step 2: Decide audiences and markets first For each asset, name the audience and the country. Public content in one market, professional content in another and a supplier page for buyers are three different jobs with three different review paths. Step 3: Map the rules to the plan Sit with your medical, legal and regulatory team before you choose channels. Ask which formats can carry the required risk information, which channels are allowed for each product and market, and what must be reported. It is faster to learn this at the start than after the creative is made. Step 4: Build content in approved modules Write approved building blocks once: a short disease explanation, a mechanism-of-action summary, a safety statement, a set of answers to common questions. Reuse them across channels. Each block has a source, a reviewer and a review date. This cuts review time, because reviewers approve a block once, not every page. Step 5: Choose a few channels and sequence them Match the channel to the audience and to what you may say there. Run education before promotion, and let each touchpoint hand over to the next. A professional who attends a webinar should get a follow-up that answers the questions they asked, not a generic email. Step 6: Plan for safety reporting and comments Any channel the company runs or sponsors can produce information about side effects or product complaints. Set up a way to capture and pass it on to the safety team within the required time. ABPI guidance on pharmacovigilance treats company-sponsored digital activities, including social media, as in scope. Decide in advance who watches comments and what they do. Step 7: Respect privacy and consent Email, tracking and retargeting use personal data. Privacy law, such as GDPR in Europe and HIPAA in the US where it applies, limits what you may collect and how you may use it. Do not put health data into advertising tools. Keep consent records, and ask privacy counsel before you set up tracking. Step 8: Measure in layers Layer Examples Take care Reach Verified professionals reached, impressions Easy to count, easy to over-report Engagement Visits to key pages, webinar attendance, email clicks, return visits Count qualified people, not total opens Behavior Meeting requests, enquiries, enrolments in a patient program Track with consent Business Sales or prescription trends in engaged segments compared with similar segments Not a perfect test; do not claim credit for all growth Sales in pharma happen through doctors, pharmacies and distributors, so you rarely see a straight line from a click to a sale. Agree definitions with finance before launch, and compare against a baseline or a matched group where you can. End of chapter 6 Next: Worked example 1: launching education for a specialist treatment → 07 Chapter 7 · 1 min Worked example 1: launching education for a specialist treatment This example is illustrative. A company is preparing a specialist treatment for a rare condition in one European market. Decision Choice Audiences Specialists first; patients and caregivers through unbranded condition information Rules No public promotion of the prescription-only product; professional content follows the national code Owned channel A professional section with evidence summaries, trial information and prescribing information, with verification Direct channel Approved email to specialists who opted in, with webinar invitations Reach channel Verified professional network placements pointing to the professional section Public content An unbranded condition guide, with sources and a review date, linking only where the regulatory team agrees Safety Adverse event link on every professional page and a named owner for comments Measure Qualified specialist visits, webinar attendance and return visits, meeting requests tied to the field team’s records End of chapter 7 Next: Worked example 2: a supplier looking for new buyers → 08 Chapter 8 · 1 min Worked example 2: a supplier looking for new buyers This example is also illustrative. A producer of active pharmaceutical ingredients sells to generic manufacturers and has an old brochure site. Goal. More qualified enquiries from manufacturers in three regions. Content. One page for each ingredient family, with specifications, regulatory file status the company actually holds, audit history and a contact form. Each page has a named quality head as reviewer. Channels. Search for supplier terms, LinkedIn for the quality and sourcing roles, and presence at two trade events with a landing page for each. Rules. Claims about regulatory status must match the records; no health claims; privacy rules for the contact form. Measure. Enquiries tagged by channel and page, followed into the sales system through to qualified opportunities. The channels are small, and each visit comes from a qualified buyer. This kind of site often does better than a broad campaign. End of chapter 8 Next: Where does SEO fit? → 09 Chapter 9 · 1 min Where does SEO fit? Search is the base for many other channels. People find disease education, professional evidence and supplier pages through Google and, more and more, through AI answers. Strong search pages also make paid and email work better, because the landing pages are clear. If you do one thing first, make the main pages easy to find and easy to trust. Our pharma SEO guide covers the steps in detail. End of chapter 9 Next: What is omnichannel marketing in pharma? → 10 Chapter 10 · 1 min What is omnichannel marketing in pharma? Multichannel means you use several channels. Omnichannel means the channels work as one conversation. A professional who reads an evidence page, attends a webinar and later meets a representative should feel that each step knew about the one before it. To make that real, you need three things: Shared plans. Marketing, field and medical teams agree the sequence and who owns each touchpoint. Connected records, within consent. A follow-up should reflect what the person asked about. Limits. Stop sending what someone already has, and keep the number of messages low. Professionals have little time. Start with two channels that hand over to each other, such as a webinar and a follow-up email. Add more once that works. End of chapter 10 Next: What should you know about paid media? → 11 Chapter 11 · 1 min What should you know about paid media? Paid search and display can reach people quickly. They also have the tightest limits. Platforms such as Google publish advertising policies for health and medicines, and those policies differ by country. Some products or markets may need approval before ads run. Check the current policy for each platform and country, and ask your regulatory team whether a benefit claim fits in the ad space. Safe uses include disease awareness ads, supplier and capability ads, and over-the-counter products where the rules allow. For prescription products, the main tool is often search: make sure professionals and patients find accurate, approved pages when they look for your company or condition. Whatever you run, keep the landing page in line with the ad. If the ad says one thing and the page says another, reviewers and platforms will both notice. End of chapter 11 Next: How should pharma teams handle social media and influencers? → 12 Chapter 12 · 1 min How should pharma teams handle social media and influencers? Social media is hard for prescription products because posts are short and risk information takes space. The FDA’s draft guidance says a benefit claim in a space-limited post should come with risk information and a way to reach more, and the FDA’s 2025 announcement says it is concerned about undisclosed paid influencer promotion. A cautious approach: Use company social channels for company news, hiring, education and approved unbranded content. Do not make benefit claims for a prescription product in a format that cannot carry risk information. Disclose every paid relationship clearly, in a way the audience sees. Brief creators in writing, review their posts before they go live and keep a record. Have a plan for comments, safety reports and misinformation about your products. End of chapter 12 Next: How is AI changing pharma digital marketing? → 13 Chapter 13 · 1 min How is AI changing pharma digital marketing? AI tools help with research, drafts, translation and reporting. They can also invent a dose or a study that sounds right. The FDA has said it is using AI to review drug ads, which means errors can be found faster. Keep humans in charge: Give AI tools approved source material, not open questions. Have a qualified person check every fact against the source. Run normal medical, legal and regulatory review. Keep a record of the sources and the reviewer. People also ask AI tools about your conditions and medicines. Check what they say about your key questions, and fix the source pages if an answer is wrong. End of chapter 13 Next: How does the plan change by product type? → 14 Chapter 14 · 1 min How does the plan change by product type? The same channel can be right for one product and wrong for another. Sort your products first. Product type What the public may see Digital focus Prescription medicine In many markets only disease information, not product promotion Professional channels, unbranded education, search for conditions, patient support pages where allowed Over-the-counter medicine Product advertising within consumer rules and platform policies Search, video, retail media, social, reviews handled with care Medical device or diagnostic Claims must match the clearance or approval Professional education, demos, case information, procurement pages Ingredient, contract or service supplier Business-to-business communication Search, capability pages, LinkedIn, trade events, case studies End of chapter 14 Next: What is the difference between HCP and patient marketing? → 15 Chapter 15 · 1 min What is the difference between HCP and patient marketing? Professional and patient audiences want different things and are held to different rules. Do not run them as one funnel. Professional marketing is about evidence and time. Prescribers want clear data, short formats and sources. They often search on a phone between visits. Content should be easy to scan and easy to verify. Patient and caregiver marketing is about understanding and trust. People want plain words about a condition, what to ask the doctor and where to find support. In many markets this has to stay at the level of disease information for prescription products. Keep the two clearly separate on your site and in your messages. Professional content that appears on public pages without context can be misread, and public pages that read like promotion can cause a regulatory problem. End of chapter 15 Next: How should email and CRM work? → 16 Chapter 16 · 1 min How should email and CRM work? Email is a workhorse channel for professionals and patients who ask to hear from you. It also carries the most privacy risk. A few rules keep it useful: Get clear consent and record it. Say what people will receive and how often. Segment by audience and interest. A specialist in one therapy area does not need news about another. Send help, not only promotion. Evidence summaries, event invitations and guides earn opens. Route medical questions to medical information, not to marketing. Make it easy to opt out and honor the request quickly. Keep health data out of marketing tools unless privacy counsel has approved the set-up. End of chapter 16 Next: What makes a good webinar or virtual event? → 17 Chapter 17 · 1 min What makes a good webinar or virtual event? Webinars work when the topic is useful and the speakers are credible. They fail when they feel like a long advertisement. For a professional event: Choose a clinical question the audience already has. Pick independent or well-known speakers, and disclose any payment. Plan the slides and the questions with the review team in advance. Record the event only if the recording is also approved. Follow up with the people who asked questions, using approved answers. Capture any safety information raised during the event and pass it on. End of chapter 17 Next: How much should you spend? → 18 Chapter 18 · 1 min How much should you spend? There is no standard budget. It depends on your products, your markets and your goals. In its 2025 announcement the FDA Commissioner said that drug companies spend up to 25% of their budget on advertising, which shows how large the spend can be for big brands. That figure says nothing about what a smaller company should spend. A sensible way to set a budget: Start from the goal for each audience. Cost the review time and the safety reporting set-up, which are easy to forget. Fund the owned pages first, because every other channel points to them. Add one paid or direct channel and measure it for a quarter. Move money to the channels that show qualified engagement, not only reach. End of chapter 18 Next: A 90-day plan to start → 19 Chapter 19 · 1 min A 90-day plan to start Days Work Output 1 to 14 List audiences, markets, goals and rules; audit your site, search and current channels Starting point and constraints 15 to 30 Agree channels with the review team; draft the approved content modules Channel plan and module list 31 to 60 Build the owned pages; set up consent, safety reporting and measurement; submit first assets for review Assets in approval 61 to 90 Launch one owned, one direct and one reach channel; report; decide what to add First results and a next-quarter plan End of chapter 19 Next: How to choose a pharma digital marketing agency → 20 Chapter 20 · 1 min How to choose a pharma digital marketing agency Whether you hire an agency or build a team, the same questions apply. Ask any pharma digital marketing agency: Which markets, products and audiences have you worked with, and which rules do you plan around? When do you bring your plan to our medical, legal and regulatory team? How do you handle safety reports and comments on social channels? How do you handle consent and personal data? Who writes and reviews content, and what are their qualifications? How do you report results, and how do you link them to business outcomes? What is in the written scope, and how can we end the contract? Be careful with anyone who guarantees approvals or results. Your own regulatory team controls approvals. Reinforce Lab also offers search and AI visibility services to pharmaceutical companies, so read this guide with that in mind. It was written by a team whose founder trained as a pharmacist and worked in pharmaceutical marketing. End of chapter 20 Next: Common pharma digital marketing mistakes → 21 Chapter 21 · 1 min Common pharma digital marketing mistakes Starting with channels, not rules. The format may not be allowed for your product. One message for every audience. Patients, professionals and buyers need different content and different review. No plan for safety reports. A comment about a side effect is a report to handle. Counting opens and views as success. Measure qualified engagement and business results. Too many channels at once. Each needs review and staffing. Undisclosed paid posts. This is a named concern for the FDA. Health data in ad tools. Privacy rules apply. Ignoring search. Many journeys begin with a search. End of chapter 21 Next: A quick checklist → 22 Chapter 22 · 1 min A quick checklist Goal, audience and market set for each asset Rules reviewed with the regulatory team before channels are chosen Approved content modules with sources, reviewers and review dates One owned, one direct and one reach channel to start Safety reporting and comment handling in place Consent and privacy checked for email, tracking and forms Paid relationships disclosed Measurement in four layers, agreed with finance AI answers about your key questions checked each quarter End of chapter 22 Next: Final thoughts → 23 Chapter 23 · 1 min Final thoughts Pharma digital marketing works when rules, content and measurement are planned together. Pick the audience, pick a few channels, write approved building blocks once and measure what matters to the business. The first assets take longest. After that, approved modules make every new campaign faster and safer to run. Back matter Glossary A to Z F Fair balance Presenting risk information with comparable content and prominence to benefit claims in prescription drug promotion. H HCP Healthcare professional, such as a doctor, nurse or pharmacist. O Omnichannel marketing Channels that work as one connected conversation, so each step reflects the one before. P Pharmacovigilance The collection and review of information about side effects and other safety issues with medicines. U Unbranded content Information about a condition that does not name a product. Questions FAQs What is pharma digital marketing? Pharma digital marketing uses digital channels such as websites, search, email, social media, paid media and webinars to reach patients, caregivers, healthcare professionals and business buyers with information about conditions, medicines and services, within advertising and review rules. How is pharma digital marketing different from pharma SEO? Pharma SEO is one part of it: making accurate pages easy to find in search. Pharma digital marketing also covers email, social media, paid media, events, detailing and measurement across all channels. Is advertising prescription medicines to the public legal? It depends on the country. In the US, direct-to-consumer advertising is allowed but must present fair balance between benefits and risks. In the UK and the EU, advertising prescription-only medicines to the public is prohibited. Your regulatory team decides what each market allows. Can pharmaceutical companies run Google Ads? Often yes, for suitable products and content, but Google publishes health and medicines advertising policies that differ by country and may require approval. Check the current policy for each country and ask your regulatory team whether the ad can carry required risk information. Can pharma companies use influencers? Only with great care. The FDA's 2025 announcement named undisclosed paid influencer promotion as a concern. Disclose every paid relationship, brief creators in writing, review posts before they go live and keep records, and follow the rules for your product and market. What is omnichannel marketing in pharma? It means channels work as one connected conversation, so each step reflects the one before. Multichannel simply means using several channels. Omnichannel needs shared plans between marketing, field and medical teams, and connected records within consent. How do you measure pharma digital marketing? Measure in layers: reach, engagement, behavior and business results. Count qualified engagement, not total opens. Because sales happen through doctors and pharmacies, compare engaged segments with similar segments, and agree definitions with finance before launch. How should companies handle side-effect reports on social media? Treat any channel the company runs or sponsors as a possible source of safety information. Set up a way to capture it, pass it to the safety team within the required time, and decide who watches comments. ABPI pharmacovigilance guidance treats company-sponsored digital activity, including social media, as in scope. How much do pharmaceutical companies spend on digital marketing? There is no standard figure. In its 2025 announcement, the FDA Commissioner said drug companies spend up to 25% of their budget on advertising. That reflects large brands. Set your own budget from goals per audience, review costs and the channels that show qualified engagement. How do I choose a pharma digital marketing agency? Ask which markets and rules they know, when they involve your regulatory team, how they handle safety reports, consent and data, who writes and reviews content, how they report results and what the written scope and exit terms are. Be wary of guaranteed approvals or results. What is pharmaceutical content marketing? It is creating educational content for health professionals, patients or buyers, within the rules for promotion. Medical, legal and regulatory review comes before anything is published.
