Check it in about 30 minutes: write 10 buyer prompts, run them in three tools in fresh sessions, log six fields per answer and score mention rate, citation rate, share of voice and accuracy. Repeat monthly, because AI answers change from run to run. 01 AI brand visibility is several measures: mention rate, citation rate, share of voice, accuracy and sources. 02 A 30-minute test uses 10 prompts (4 category, 3 comparison, 3 branded) in three tools and a six-column sheet. 03 SparkToro found less than a 1 in 100 chance of the same brand list twice, so one run is a sample, not a verdict. 04 Do not track position in an AI list. Track the share of runs in which you appear. 05 Split results by prompt type: a good total can hide gaps in category questions. 06 Fix wrong facts first, then repeat the same prompts each month and report an average and a range. AI brand visibility is how often AI tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Google AI Mode name, describe or link to your brand when people ask questions about your market. You can get a first reading in about 30 minutes with a spreadsheet and three browser tabs. This guide gives you the test, the scoring, two worked examples and a plan to repeat it each month. It also tells you what a 30-minute test cannot do. AI answers change from run to run, so one check is a sample, not a verdict. A large study by SparkToro found that AI tools almost never give the same list of brands twice. So we show you how to read a first test fairly and how to build a trend over time. 01 Chapter 1 · 1 min What is AI brand visibility? AI brand visibility is a set of separate questions, not one number. A tool may name you but not link to you. It may link to you but describe you wrongly. It may name your competitors and leave you out. Measure each question on its own: Mention rate: in what share of answers is your brand named? Citation rate: in what share of answers does the tool link to a page of yours? Share of voice: of all the brands named across your test, what share is yours? Accuracy: when you are named, is the description right? Sources: which pages does the tool cite, and are they yours or someone else’s? Ahrefs lists similar measures in its AI visibility audit guide: mentions, citations, share of voice, and a check of accuracy, tone and whether you are the lead recommendation. Some tools combine these into one “AI visibility score”. Treat a combined score with care until you know what goes into it. End of chapter 1 Next: Why does one test not tell the full story? → 02 Chapter 2 · 2 min Why does one test not tell the full story? AI tools write each answer fresh. The same question can give different brands on different runs, in different orders. SparkToro and Gumshoe tested this in a study published in January 2026. About 600 volunteers ran 12 prompts through ChatGPT, Claude and Google’s AI Overviews and AI Mode, for nearly 3,000 runs in all. The main findings were: There was less than a 1 in 100 chance that ChatGPT or Google’s AI would give the same list of brands in any two responses to the same prompt. There was less than a 1 in 1,000 chance of seeing the same list in the same order. Even so, some brands came up again and again across dozens of runs. Appearing in most runs of a prompt showed a brand the tool tended to link with that question. The authors draw two lessons. First, a “position in AI answers” figure is not meaningful, since the order is close to random. Second, the share of runs in which you appear is a reasonable measure, if you run each prompt many times. Our 30-minute test gives you a baseline sample. To turn it into a real rate, you repeat it, which we cover below. Google makes a related point for its own tools. It says no third-party tool has access to its internal ranking or AI systems, and it tells site owners to use the Generative AI performance report in Search Console to see how their content does in its AI features. End of chapter 2 Next: How do you run the 30-minute test? → Reinforce Lab service · SEO & AI Search Audit Want a bigger test with a written 90-day plan? Reinforce Lab starts with a free diagnostic of your Google and AI search visibility and a 90-day plan. See the AI search audit → Or get a free diagnostic first 03 Chapter 3 · 3 min How do you run the 30-minute test? You need a spreadsheet, a notepad and the ability to open ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity. If you can only test two tools, test the two your buyers use most. Here is the time budget. Step Time What you do 1. Write the prompts 5 minutes Write 10 buyer questions in three groups 2. Run them 15 minutes Paste each into three tools and copy the answers 3. Log the results 5 minutes Fill six columns for each answer 4. Score and read 5 minutes Work out four numbers and note the gaps Step 1: Write 10 prompts (5 minutes) Use three groups. The mix matters, because a tool may know you well when asked by name and still leave you out of a category question. Category prompts (4): questions where no brand is named. Example: “What is the best invoicing software for a small accounting firm?” Comparison prompts (3): you against a named competitor, or two competitors. Example: “How does [your brand] compare with [competitor]?” Branded prompts (3): questions about you. Example: “What does [your brand] do, and who is it for?” Take the wording from real sources: sales calls, support emails, the “People also ask” box and the questions prospects send you. Write the way a buyer writes, not the way your product page reads. Keep the prompts fixed once you pick them, because changing them makes later comparisons useless. Step 2: Run them in three tools (15 minutes) Open each tool in a fresh session. Where you can, turn off memory and personalization, or use a private window and log out, so your own history does not shape the answer. Paste each prompt, wait for the full answer and copy it into your sheet. Use the web search mode if the tool offers one, since that is how many buyers use it. For Google, run the same question in a logged-out window and check whether an AI Overview appears. Not every question triggers one. Pew Research found in March 2025 that about 18% of Google searches in its study produced an AI summary, and that longer and question-style searches produced them more often. If no overview appears, write “none” and move on. Step 3: Log six columns (5 minutes) For each answer, record: Named: yes or no. Linked: does the answer link to a page on your domain? Position: first, middle, last or not applicable. Treat this as a rough note only, given the random order. Competitors named: list them. Accuracy: right, partly wrong or wrong, checked against your own facts. Cited pages: copy every URL the tool shows, yours or not. If you have time, add a seventh note: the tone. Mark each mention positive, neutral or negative. “The best option for beginners” and “the expensive option” are both mentions, but they do very different work for you. Ahrefs lists sentiment and framing, differentiation and whether you are the lead recommendation as things to check in an AI visibility audit. Step 4: Score it (5 minutes) Work out four numbers. Mention rate = answers that name you, divided by all answers. Citation rate = answers that link to your domain, divided by all answers. Share of voice = your mentions, divided by all brand mentions across every answer. Accuracy rate = answers about you that are right, divided by answers that name you. Then list the cited pages that are not yours. That list shows where the tools get their facts about your market. End of chapter 3 Next: Worked example 1: an HR software company → 04 Chapter 4 · 1 min Worked example 1: an HR software company This is an illustration, not a client result. Imagine a company that sells HR software to firms with 50 to 200 staff. It runs 10 prompts in three tools, so 30 answers in all. It is named in 6 of the 30 answers. Mention rate: 6 divided by 30, which is 20%. A page on its own domain is linked in 2 answers. Citation rate: about 7%. Across all 30 answers, the tools name 84 brands in total, and 6 of those mentions are the company. Share of voice: 6 divided by 84, about 7%. Of the 6 answers that name it, 4 describe it correctly. Accuracy rate: about 67%. The breakdown by prompt type tells more than the totals. The company is named in all 3 branded answers in one tool but in only 1 of the 12 category answers. The wrong descriptions all repeat one error: they say the company serves “enterprises only”, based on a review page from three years ago. The fixes follow from the data. The team corrects the old review page by contacting the site. It updates its own “who we serve” page with a clear first sentence and a date. It writes one page that answers the category question “what HR software suits a firm with 100 staff”, with real pricing ranges and a named source for the legal points. It then repeats the test a month later with the same 10 prompts. End of chapter 4 Next: Worked example 2: a cybersecurity consultancy → 05 Chapter 5 · 1 min Worked example 2: a cybersecurity consultancy This is another illustration. Imagine a consultancy that sells security reviews to mid-sized companies. It runs the same test: 30 answers. It is named in 14 of 30 answers. Mention rate: about 47%. It is linked in 3 answers. Citation rate: 10%. All 9 branded answers name it. Only 5 of the 21 other answers do. At first the 47% looks healthy. The split shows the real position. The tools know the brand when asked by name, but they rarely recommend it for category and comparison questions. The cited pages for those questions are two review sites and a trade association list, and the consultancy is on none of them. The plan is not to rewrite its own pages. It is to earn a place where the tools already look. The team checks which review sites list its competitors, applies to be listed, and offers the trade body a short, original guide with data from its own reviews. It also adds a direct answer to its main service page. The lesson is to split your results. A good total can hide a gap in the questions that matter most for new buyers. End of chapter 5 Next: How do you read your results? → 06 Chapter 6 · 1 min How do you read your results? What you see What it usually means First fix Not named anywhere, even for branded prompts The tools have little or no information about you Check access, indexing and basic brand facts across your site and profiles Named for branded prompts only The tools know you but do not link you to your category Build category pages and earn mentions on sites the tools cite Named but described wrongly An old or wrong source is being used Update your page and the third-party page the tool cites Named but never linked The tool uses other sites for facts about you Add direct answers and clear facts to your own pages Competitors named often, you rarely They appear on more pages the tools trust Study the cited pages and plan real outreach Different results on each run Normal variation Repeat the test and use the rate, not one run Check access early. Ahrefs notes that some content delivery networks block AI crawlers by default, so a site can be hidden from some tools without anyone deciding it. Make sure robots.txt, your firewall and your CDN allow the crawlers you want. For Google, a page must be indexed and eligible to show with a snippet to appear as a supporting link in its AI features. End of chapter 6 Next: How do you turn the test into a trend? → 07 Chapter 7 · 1 min How do you turn the test into a trend? Repeat it. A baseline plus four monthly rounds with the same prompts gives you a rate and a range, which is far more useful than one number. Keep the prompts fixed. Add new ones in a second list, so the trend stays clean. Use the same tools and conditions. Same fresh-session method, same country, same month day. Run important prompts more than once. If you can spare time, run each prompt three times per tool. If you appear in one of three, that is inconsistent visibility, which is different from appearing in all three. Record the average and the range. Report “named in 3 to 5 of 10 runs”, not “named”. Add competitors. Track three to five, since share of voice is a ratio. Note what changed. A new page, a press story or a model update can explain a shift. When your list grows past 30 to 40 prompts or covers several markets, a paid tool saves time, because it can run many prompts often. Be careful with any tool that sells a “ranking position in AI answers”. Given the order findings above, that figure has little meaning. Look for tools that report the share of runs in which you appear, show the full answers and name the sources. End of chapter 7 Next: What should you do after the test? → 08 Chapter 8 · 1 min What should you do after the test? Work from the gaps, not from a generic list. Fix wrong facts first. A wrong answer about your price, service or location costs more than a missed mention. Update your page and the cited third-party page. Add direct answers. Put a clear answer in the first sentences of your key pages and name your sources. Make brand facts consistent. Match your name, services, location and leaders across your site, profiles and listings. Close content gaps. Where the tools answer a buyer question and cite others, write one useful page. Earn mentions where tools already look. Use the cited-page list to plan outreach with a real story or real data. Check traffic. In analytics, look for visits from AI tool domains such as chatgpt.com or perplexity.ai. Check your own data to see which domains appear. Our guides on generative engine optimization , GEO vs SEO and AEO vs SEO cover the page-level work in more detail. End of chapter 8 Next: Why does my brand show up in one tool and not another? → 09 Chapter 9 · 1 min Why does my brand show up in one tool and not another? Each tool builds its answers from its own sources and methods, so a brand can be visible in one and missing in another on the same day. Google’s AI Overviews and AI Mode draw on Google’s search index, and Google says a page must be indexed and eligible to show with a snippet to be a supporting link. Other tools use their own crawls and partner indexes. Ahrefs has measured the difference. In its study, on average only about 12% of the citations from AI assistants also ranked in Google’s top 10 for the original prompt, and Perplexity was the outlier at nearly one in three. Ahrefs also found that the most cited brands differ between Google AI Overviews, ChatGPT and Perplexity. So do not blend the tools into one number too early. Score each tool on its own first, then compare. A pattern such as strong in one tool and weak in two others points to a source problem. You may be present on the pages that one tool trusts and absent from the pages the others use. The cited-page list from step 3 shows which pages those are. End of chapter 9 Next: What is a good AI share of voice? → 10 Chapter 10 · 1 min What is a good AI share of voice? There is no reliable public benchmark. Share of voice depends on how many brands the tools name for your prompts, and that number differs a lot between markets. In a market where the tools name three brands per answer, a share near 33% is average. In a market where they name 15, a share near 7% is average. So compare yourself with the competitors in your own test, and with your own baseline from last month. A few rules keep the number honest: Use the same prompts and tools each time. Count a brand once per answer, however many times the answer repeats its name. Track three to five named competitors, so you can see who gains when you lose. Look at the number by prompt type. Your share on category questions matters most for new buyers. Be wary of any article that gives a “good” percentage without saying how it was measured. Without the prompt set, the tools and the market, a benchmark means little. End of chapter 10 Next: Can analytics track AI mentions? → 11 Chapter 11 · 1 min Can analytics track AI mentions? Only in part. Analytics tools such as Google Analytics can show visits that arrive from an AI tool, if the tool sends a referrer. They cannot show a mention that sent no click. Pew Research found that people clicked a link inside a Google AI summary in only 1% of visits in its March 2025 data, so many mentions will never appear in your reports. That is why the prompt test matters. It measures the part analytics cannot see. Use both together: Prompt tests show whether you are named, linked and described correctly. Referral visits show how many people clicked through, and what they did next. Branded search and direct visits may rise when mentions build awareness, but they have other causes, so treat a rise as a clue and not as proof. A lead source question on your forms, such as “how did you hear about us”, can catch buyers who say they used an AI tool. Search Console is part of this too. Google counts traffic from its AI features in the normal Search Console reports and also offers a Generative AI performance report. Use it for Google’s tools. For ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity, the prompt test and your referral data are what you have. End of chapter 11 Next: Which tools should you test, and are free checkers worth using? → 12 Chapter 12 · 1 min Which tools should you test, and are free checkers worth using? Start with the tools your buyers use. For most businesses that means ChatGPT, Google (AI Overviews and AI Mode) and Perplexity. Add Gemini if your buyers work in Google’s tools. Add Claude if your buyers are technical or use it for research. This is a judgment call, so check with your customers, and keep the same set each month. Several vendors offer free checkers. Ahrefs has a free AI visibility checker that needs no signup. It queries ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Copilot and Google AI Overviews and shows total mentions, mentions by platform and the most cited domains and pages. Semrush has a free AI search visibility checker that you can use three times a day without an account. Both vendors sell paid tools, so treat these as a free preview. A free checker is useful for a quick second opinion on your manual results. It is not a program. It tests a limited set of prompts that the tool chose, not the questions your own buyers ask. That is why the manual test above starts from your own sales and support questions. Prompt choice matters as much as the tool. If you pick 20 prompts that happen to favor your brand, you will look strong, and if you pick 20 that do not, you will look invisible. End of chapter 12 Next: What if your brand never appears? → 13 Chapter 13 · 1 min What if your brand never appears? First, check the branded prompts. If a tool cannot describe you even when asked by name, the problem is basic. Work through these in order: Access. Check that robots.txt, your firewall and your CDN allow the crawlers you want, and that your key pages are indexed in Google. Basic facts. Make sure your site clearly says who you are, what you sell, where you work and who runs the company, with the same facts on your profiles and listings. Third-party presence. Check whether you appear on the review sites, directories and lists that the tools cite for your category. Category pages. Check whether you have a page that answers the main buyer question directly. Set expectations honestly. An Ahrefs author writes that, in their experience, established brands with strong SEO can see early wins in weeks to months, while new brands with little online authority may need 12 to 18 months. That is one practitioner’s view, not a measured rule, but it shows why a new brand should not expect quick results. End of chapter 13 Next: Can you report one AI visibility score? → 14 Chapter 14 · 1 min Can you report one AI visibility score? You can, but it hides the cause of any change. A single score blends mentions, links, accuracy and tools that behave differently. If it moves, you will not know why. For your team or your board, report the four numbers by prompt type and by tool, plus a short note on what changed. Add a single combined score only as a summary, and write down how it is calculated. Branded search volume is a useful clue but it is not a replacement. It can rise when people hear about you in AI answers, and it can rise for many other reasons. Use it next to the prompt test, not instead of it. End of chapter 14 Next: What are the common mistakes? → 15 Chapter 15 · 1 min What are the common mistakes? Testing once. One run is a sample. The SparkToro study shows how much lists vary. Chasing order. Whether you are first or third in a list changes from run to run. Focus on whether you appear. Testing only branded prompts. You will look better than you are. Include category and comparison questions. Changing the prompts each month. You cannot compare results if the questions differ. Logging in while testing. Memory and history can change the answer. Trusting one tool’s score. Keep mentions, citations and accuracy separate. Ignoring wrong answers. Inaccurate answers can cost deals, so track accuracy. Buying mentions. Google says seeking fake mentions is not as helpful as it might seem. End of chapter 15 Next: A simple template for your sheet → 16 Chapter 16 · 1 min A simple template for your sheet Create one sheet with these columns and one row per prompt, per tool, per run: Column What to enter Date and tool For example, 14 Nov, ChatGPT with search Prompt group Category, comparison or branded Prompt The exact text Named Yes or no Linked Yes or no, plus the URL Competitors named A short list Accuracy Right, partly wrong or wrong Cited pages Every URL shown A second tab can hold the four scores for each month. That tab is the one you show to your team. End of chapter 16 Next: A 90-day plan → 17 Chapter 17 · 1 min A 90-day plan Days 1 to 30: baseline Run the 30-minute test. Log everything. Fix wrong facts and access problems that you find. Choose three to five competitors to track. Days 31 to 60: fix and fill Update your five key pages with direct answers and sources. Write one or two pages for the gaps. Correct third-party pages where you can. Repeat the test. Days 61 to 90: earn and compare Pitch one or two real stories to the sites the tools cite. Run the test a third time. Compare the rates with your baseline and decide what to repeat. End of chapter 17 Next: How Reinforce Lab approaches AI brand visibility → 18 Chapter 18 · 1 min How Reinforce Lab approaches AI brand visibility Reinforce Lab sells AI search and SEO services, so weigh this section with that in mind. Our free diagnostic works the same way as the test above, with a larger prompt set, repeated runs, competitor tracking and a written 90-day plan. You can read about our SEO and AI search audit , or get your free diagnostic . End of chapter 18 Next: Final thoughts → 19 Chapter 19 · 1 min Final thoughts You do not need a paid tool to learn where you stand in AI search visibility. Ten prompts, three tools and a sheet will show whether you are named, linked and described correctly. Treat the first result as a baseline, repeat it each month and read the rate, not a single run. The cited-page list is the most useful output, because it shows where to earn your next mention. Back matter Glossary A to Z A AI brand visibility How often AI tools name, describe or link to your brand. B Baseline The first set of results you compare later tests against. C Citation rate The share of answers that link to a page of yours. M Mention rate The share of answers that name your brand. P Prompt The question or request you type into an AI tool. S Share of voice Your brand mentions divided by all brand mentions in the test. Questions FAQs What is AI brand visibility? AI brand visibility is how often AI tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Google AI Mode name, describe or link to your brand when people ask questions about your market. It is measured with mention rate, citation rate, share of voice and accuracy. How do I check if ChatGPT mentions my brand? Write 10 buyer questions, run each in a fresh ChatGPT session with memory off, and record whether your brand is named, linked and described correctly. Repeat in other tools and run the same prompts each month. How long does an AI visibility check take? A first baseline takes about 30 minutes with 10 prompts in three tools. A reliable trend takes repeated runs over several weeks, because AI answers change between runs. Why do AI tools give different answers each time? They generate each answer fresh. SparkToro and Gumshoe found less than a 1 in 100 chance that ChatGPT or Google's AI would give the same list of brands twice for the same prompt, so measure the share of runs in which you appear. What is AI share of voice? Your brand mentions divided by all brand mentions across the answers in your test. It shows how you compare with competitors for the same questions. Do I need a paid tool to track AI visibility? Not to start. A spreadsheet and three tools give a baseline. A paid tool helps once you track more than about 30 to 40 prompts or several markets. Avoid tools that sell a ranking position in AI answers, because list order is close to random. Can Google Analytics show visits from AI tools? It can show referral visits from AI tool domains such as chatgpt.com or perplexity.ai if those tools send a referrer. Check your own data to see which domains appear. Google also reports its AI feature traffic in Search Console. How often should I re-run the test? Monthly is a sensible minimum for manual testing. Keep the same prompts and tools, and report an average and range over at least four rounds before drawing conclusions. What do I do if an AI tool says something wrong about my brand? Note the prompt, the answer and the cited sources. Update your own page, correct or contact the third-party page the tool relies on, and add a clear, dated statement of the fact on your site. Why am I named for branded questions but not for category questions? The tools know your name but do not link you to your category. Build pages that answer category questions directly and earn mentions on the review sites and lists that the tools already cite. Are free AI visibility checkers worth using? Yes, as a quick second opinion. Ahrefs and Semrush both offer free checkers. They test a limited set of prompts the tool chose, not your buyers' real questions, and both vendors sell paid tools, so use them as a preview and keep a manual test as your baseline. What if my brand never appears in any AI answer? Check branded prompts first, then access and indexing, basic brand facts across your site and profiles, presence on the review sites and lists the tools cite, and whether you have a page that answers the main buyer question. New brands with little authority may need much longer than established ones. An AI brand visibility tool shows how often AI answers name, describe or link to your brand, and how that compares with your competitors. It runs a fixed set of buyer questions through tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Google’s AI Overviews, then records the answers. A good one shows the full answer, the sources behind it and the trend over time. A weak one gives a single score you cannot check. This guide is for B2B marketing teams that are deciding whether to buy one. It explains what these tools track, what they cannot do, what the entry plans of two well-known tools cost, and a checklist for choosing. It includes two worked examples and a 14-day test you can run before you sign anything. If you want to try the method by hand first, start with our 30-minute AI brand visibility test . 01 Chapter 1 · 1 min What is an AI brand visibility tool? An AI brand visibility tool is software that asks AI search tools a list of questions on a schedule and records whether your brand appears in the answers. The software owner chooses the prompts, the engines and the competitors. The tool then reports results such as mention rate, citations, share of voice and sentiment. You will see other names for the same thing: AI visibility platform, AI search visibility tool, GEO tool, AEO tool, LLM tracking tool and AI brand monitoring. The names overlap. What matters is what the product records and how you can check it. Two versions exist. The first is a simple monitor that reports where you appear. The second adds advice, such as which page to change or which site to approach. Decide early which one you need. A monitor is enough to find out if you have a problem. You need more once you know what to fix and who will fix it. End of chapter 1 Next: What do these tools track? → 02 Chapter 2 · 2 min What do these tools track? Most tools report the same core measures. Ahrefs lists mentions, citations, impressions and AI share of voice in its AI visibility audit guide. Semrush lists an AI visibility score, mentions, citations, platform coverage, top cited pages, topics and a competitor comparison for its free checker. Here are the measures in plain words: Measure The question it answers Watch out for Mentions In what share of answers is my brand named? A mention is not a link. Check that the tool counts them separately. Citations In what share of answers does the tool link to a page of mine? Ask to see the exact URL for each one. Share of voice Of all brand mentions in my test, what share is mine? Each vendor calculates it differently. Ask for the formula. Sources cited Which pages do the tools cite in my market? This list is often the most useful output, because it shows where to earn mentions. Sentiment Is the brand described in a good, neutral or bad way? Read a sample of the answers yourself. Automated scoring can miss tone. Accuracy Are the facts about us right? Most tools do not check this for you. Plan to check by hand. History Is the trend going up or down? Ask how long results are kept. Some tools also report a “position” or “rank” inside an answer. Be careful with it. See the next section. End of chapter 2 Next: What can these tools not do? → Reinforce Lab service · SEO & AI Search Audit Want the test done for you, with a written plan? Reinforce Lab starts with a free diagnostic of your Google and AI search visibility and a 90-day plan. See the AI search audit → Or get a free diagnostic first 03 Chapter 3 · 2 min What can these tools not do? AI answers are not like search results, so no tool can offer the certainty a rank tracker gives. Four limits matter most. Answers change from run to run SparkToro and Gumshoe ran a study in January 2026 with about 600 volunteers and 12 prompts across ChatGPT, Claude and Google’s AI Overviews and AI Mode. They found less than a 1 in 100 chance of getting the same list of brands twice for the same prompt, and less than a 1 in 1,000 chance of the same order. Their conclusion was that a “ranking position in AI” figure is not meaningful, while the share of runs in which you appear is a reasonable measure. A good tool therefore repeats each prompt and reports a rate, not a single screenshot. No tool sees inside Google Google says that no third-party tool has access to its internal ranking or AI systems, and it warns about tools that claim to use internal Google metrics. For its own AI features, Google points to the Generative AI performance report in Search Console. That report is free, so use it as your first Google signal. A score is a snapshot Answers vary by prompt wording, country, model version and date. A score from one day tells you little. Repeated measurements tell you whether a change lasts. Tools do not fix anything on their own A dashboard shows a gap. Someone still has to write the page, correct the facts or earn the mention. Decide who owns that work before you buy. The software is the cheap part. End of chapter 3 Next: Why do B2B teams track AI visibility at all? → 04 Chapter 4 · 2 min Why do B2B teams track AI visibility at all? Because buyers use AI tools, and surveys show it, with a catch: each survey asks a different question, so the numbers are not interchangeable. Here are three, with what each one actually measured. Forrester: 94% of business buyers report using AI somewhere in the buying process, up from 89% a year earlier (Buyers’ Journey Survey 2025, published January 2026). That counts any use at any stage. Gartner: in a survey of 645 B2B buyers in August and September 2025, 45% said they used generative AI during a recent purchase, mainly to gather information on vendors and products. Buyers used an average of seven information sources. 69% preferred to validate AI-generated insights with a sales rep. 6sense: its 2026 report, based on 4,611 recent B2B buyers, found that 81% use an LLM somewhere in an evaluation, down from 94% the year before. Only 26% use an LLM to discover vendors. Before contacting a seller, 21% said LLMs influenced their view of vendors, against 34% who cited their own existing knowledge and 32% who cited internal discussions. Read together, they say that most buyers touch AI, a smaller share use it to find new vendors, and it often sorts and checks what buyers already know. 6sense also found that buyers chose the vendor they favored before contacting a seller 82% of the time, and that 92% of eventual winners were on the initial shortlist. That is why being named in AI answers matters before the first sales call: it helps get you onto the shortlist and keeps you on it. Treat the figures as a reason to measure, not as proof that AI answers will win deals for you. End of chapter 4 Next: Are AI visibility tools, trackers and monitoring tools the same thing? → 05 Chapter 5 · 1 min Are AI visibility tools, trackers and monitoring tools the same thing? Mostly yes. Vendors use different labels for the same job: AI brand visibility tool, AI search visibility tool, AI visibility tracker, AI brand monitoring, LLM tracking tool and GEO tool. Each one runs a set of prompts in AI tools such as ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini and Google AI Overviews. It records whether your brand appears, and it reports mentions, citations, share of voice and sentiment. The real differences are which AI tools it covers, how often it runs your prompts, how it handles competitor benchmarking and what reporting you get. Several SEO platforms, including Semrush and Ahrefs, list AI visibility features too. Ask whether you need a separate tracker at all. What are the best AI brand visibility tools? There is no single best one, and we do not rank vendors here. The best fit depends on the AI tools you need covered, how many prompts you track, whether you need competitor benchmarking, the reports you must send, and the price. Use the checklist and the 14-day test below, on your own prompts, before you pay for a year. End of chapter 5 Next: What kinds of tools exist? → 06 Chapter 6 · 1 min What kinds of tools exist? Type What it is Good for Free and built-in Google Search Console’s Generative AI report. Free checkers from Ahrefs (no signup, queries ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Copilot and AI Overviews) and Semrush (three free uses a day, no account). A first look and a second opinion Add-ons to SEO suites Ahrefs Brand Radar and the Semrush AI Visibility Toolkit. Teams that already use these suites Dedicated trackers Stand-alone products such as Otterly and Peec, which run your prompts daily. Teams that want prompt-level history and competitor views Enterprise platforms Products such as Profound and Scrunch, which comparison guides describe as aimed at large or regulated organizations. Check each vendor for its pricing. Large and regulated organizations We read the Ahrefs and Semrush pages and the Otterly and Peec pricing pages ourselves. We did not test the others. Comparison guides name them, and many of those guides are written by tool vendors, so treat their rankings with care. End of chapter 6 Next: How much do AI visibility tools cost? → 07 Chapter 7 · 1 min How much do AI visibility tools cost? Prices vary a lot. Here is what two stand-alone trackers listed on their own pricing pages when we read them in November 2026: Tool and plan Monthly price Prompts Price per prompt a month Peec AI, Starter $95 50 about $1.90 Peec AI, Pro $245 150 about $1.63 Peec AI, Advanced $495 350 about $1.41 Otterly, Lite $29 See note See note Otterly, Standard $189 See note See note Otterly, Premium $489 See note See note Both tools also offer a custom enterprise plan. The Peec per-prompt figures are our own arithmetic from its listed prices. For Otterly, the prompt counts shown in the page text differ from the counts in the page’s own description, so we do not quote them. Check the current counts on the page before you compare. Also note that entry plans track only some of the engines. Peec’s page says to choose three models, and Otterly’s lists three of seven engines on each of its first three plans. The lesson is simple. The monthly price is not the cost. Count prompts, engines, markets and users, and add the staff time to act on the results. End of chapter 7 Next: How do you choose one? A 10-point checklist → 08 Chapter 8 · 2 min How do you choose one? A 10-point checklist Comparison guides use similar criteria. These ten are our version. The first five decide whether the data is useful. The last five decide whether you can use it. Engines. Does it cover the tools your buyers use, on the plan you would buy? A vendor may list an engine that your plan does not include. Google AI Mode and AI Overviews. Are both covered? Check the plan. Mentions and citations kept apart. A brand named without a link and a link without a name are different events. The full answer. Can you read the whole answer and every source, not only a score? History per prompt. Can you see how one prompt changed over weeks? Prompt control. Can you add your own buyer questions, or are you stuck with the vendor’s list? Competitors. Can you track three to five named rivals for the same prompts? Exports and alerts. Can you export the data and get a warning when a prompt that was working drops? Price per prompt and trial. Is there a trial, and what happens when you pass the prompt limit? Who acts on it. Does the tool point to the page or source to fix, and do you have a person to do it? Ask every vendor the same questions and write the answers in one sheet. If a vendor will not show a full answer with its sources, treat that as a warning. End of chapter 8 Next: Worked example 1: a B2B software company runs a 14-day test → 09 Chapter 9 · 1 min Worked example 1: a B2B software company runs a 14-day test This is an illustration, not a client result. Imagine a company that sells scheduling software to clinics. It wants to know if it needs a paid tool. It writes 25 buyer prompts: 10 for the category, 8 for comparisons and 7 for brand questions. It names three competitors. On day 1 it runs the 25 prompts by hand in three AI tools and saves the answers. It is named in 4 of 75 answers, which is about 5%. It tries Google Search Console and sees AI feature data for its pages. On days 2 to 7 it tests two trial accounts with the same 25 prompts. It scores each tool from 0 to 2 on the ten points above. Tool A scores 16 of 20 and shows full answers, sources and history. Tool B scores 11 of 20. It gives a single visibility score, does not show full answers, and counts a mention and a link as one event. On days 8 to 14 it compares the tools’ numbers against its hand checks. Tool A matches within a few answers. Tool B reports a mention rate that is nearly twice what the team saw by hand. The team picks Tool A on the entry plan, because it can read every answer. The company does not treat the tool as the end of the job. It lists the five pages most often cited for its category, a review site and four blogs, and plans one real story for two of them. End of chapter 9 Next: Worked example 2: a small consultancy decides it does not need a paid tool → 10 Chapter 10 · 1 min Worked example 2: a small consultancy decides it does not need a paid tool Again, this is an illustration. Imagine a three-person consultancy that sells compliance training. It has 12 buyer questions and no budget for software. It tests the 12 questions monthly in three AI tools by hand, which takes about an hour. It also runs the free Ahrefs and Semrush checkers as a second opinion and watches the Search Console AI report. For a paid tool at $95 a month, it would get 50 prompts, so it would use under a quarter of the allowance. After three months the team sees that its results are stable, and that the work it needs is writing and outreach, not more data. The lesson is that the right tool depends on the size of your prompt list and your team. A spreadsheet can be enough when the list is short, and software saves time when the list is long or covers several markets. End of chapter 10 Next: How do you run a 14-day proof-of-value test? → 11 Chapter 11 · 1 min How do you run a 14-day proof-of-value test? Use this before you sign a contract, especially an annual one. Days 1 to 2: write the prompts. Write 20 to 30 real buyer questions without your brand name. Add two or three competitors and your country. Days 2 to 3: run a hand baseline. Ask 5 to 10 of the prompts yourself in each engine and save the answers. Days 3 to 10: run the trials. Use the same prompts and competitors in every trial. Days 10 to 12: check the data. Compare each tool with your hand baseline. Open ten answers and confirm that the brand and sources shown are real. Days 12 to 13: test the follow-up. Can the tool tell you what to fix, or only that there is a gap? Day 14: decide. Score each tool on the ten points. Count the real cost, including staff time. Run the test over a period when nothing big changes on your site, so you do not mix tool noise with real change. End of chapter 11 Next: How do you monitor brand mentions in ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity? → 12 Chapter 12 · 1 min How do you monitor brand mentions in ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity? People search for this in many ways: track brand mentions in ChatGPT, AI brand monitoring, LLM brand monitoring, or tools for monitoring brand visibility in AI interfaces. They all describe one job. You pick a fixed set of questions your buyers ask, run them in each AI tool on a schedule, and record what each answer says about you. Five things matter when you monitor: Mentions: does your brand name appear in the answer? Citations: does the answer link to your site or to a page that names you? Accuracy: are the facts about your prices, services and locations right? Sentiment: is the wording about you positive, neutral or negative? Competitors: who else is named for the same question? Check which AI tools a vendor covers. Common ones include ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Claude, Grok, Microsoft Copilot and Google AI Overviews, and coverage differs by vendor. A paid tool automates the running and the logging. It does not change what the AI tools say. If you want a Perplexity brand mention monitoring tool, a tool that watches ChatGPT and Gemini together, or a tool for AI Mode, check each vendor’s list of covered AI tools and how often it runs your prompts. Coverage differs. End of chapter 12 Next: How do you track brand mentions in ChatGPT without a paid tool? → 13 Chapter 13 · 1 min How do you track brand mentions in ChatGPT without a paid tool? You can run a simple test by hand. It is slower than a tool, but it shows you whether paying for one is worth it. List 15 to 25 buyer prompts. Use the questions your customers ask, such as “best [your category] for [your buyer].” Run each prompt in ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini and Google AI Mode. Use a new chat each time. Record the result in a sheet: prompt, tool, date, whether your brand appeared, its position, the sources cited, the competitors named and whether the facts were right. Repeat weekly at the same time with the same prompts. Read trends, not single answers. Answers change by person, place and time, so treat each run as a sample. If the sheet shows you rarely appear, fix the pages and facts the answers rely on first. A tool will only measure the same problem faster. End of chapter 13 Next: Why should you track AI brand visibility? → 14 Chapter 14 · 1 min Why should you track AI brand visibility? Because buyers now ask AI tools to shortlist vendors, and you cannot see those answers in a normal rank report. Tracking tells you whether you are named, whether the facts are right and who is named instead of you. Without it you are guessing. Tracking does not prove the answers cause sales, so treat it as one input next to leads and revenue. End of chapter 14 Next: What should you do after the tool finds a gap? → 15 Chapter 15 · 1 min What should you do after the tool finds a gap? Fix wrong facts first. A wrong price or service description costs more than a missed mention. Read the cited pages. The pages that AI tools cite for your category show where your competitors are mentioned and you are not. Add direct answers. Put a clear answer, a named source and a date near the top of your key pages. Earn mentions where tools already look. Pitch real stories and real data to those sites. Repeat the test monthly and report a rate with a range, not one number. Our guides on generative engine optimization , GEO vs SEO and AEO vs SEO cover the page-level work. End of chapter 15 Next: What else do B2B teams ask? → 16 Chapter 16 · 2 min What else do B2B teams ask? How are these tools different from SEO tools? A rank tracker records the position of your page in a list of results. An AI visibility tool records whether your brand appears inside a written answer, with which sources. The two answer different questions, and you need both. Ahrefs describes GEO as building on SEO, and Google says its AI features rest on the same ranking and quality systems as Search. Strong SEO still helps you get retrieved. The AI tool then shows whether you were named. Can an SEO suite do the job? Often, for a first look. Ahrefs and Semrush both offer AI visibility features and free checkers. A stand-alone tracker may offer more prompt control and history. Compare what each one shows against the ten points above rather than assuming that a bigger suite is better. Should you use more than one tool? One tool with the right engines is usually enough. Use your hand test as a second opinion. Ahrefs found that the most cited brands differ between Google AI Overviews, ChatGPT and Perplexity, so check that your one tool covers the engines your buyers use rather than adding a second tool. How often should you sample? There is no standard. SparkToro’s study found that a brand shows up across many runs of the same prompt even when the list changes each time, so the more runs you have, the better the rate. A tool can run daily. By hand, monthly is a sensible minimum. Report an average and a range, and do not react to one day. Do these tools show what real people ask? No. They run the prompts that you or the vendor chose. AI platforms do not share what users ask, so there is no public prompt volume like the search volume in keyword tools. Search Engine Land makes this point in its guide to measuring GEO. Build your prompt list from sales calls, support emails and the questions prospects send you. Can a tool prove revenue impact? Not on its own. A tool shows that you appeared in answers. It cannot see the private conversation, so it cannot show who read the answer or what they did next. To estimate impact, combine the tool with referral visits from AI tool domains in your analytics, a “how did you hear about us” field on forms, and your sales team’s notes. Treat the link to revenue as a clue and not as proof. End of chapter 16 Next: What are the common mistakes? → 17 Chapter 17 · 1 min What are the common mistakes? Buying before testing by hand. You cannot judge a tool’s data without a baseline. Trusting one score. Keep mentions, citations and accuracy separate. Chasing a rank in AI answers. The order in answers is close to random. Buying the cheapest plan without checking the limits. Prompts, engines and markets decide what you can learn. Tracking only branded questions. You will look better than you are. Include category and comparison questions. Treating the tool as the program. The person who acts on the results matters more than the software. Using a vendor’s own “best tool” list as proof. Many such lists are written by vendors. End of chapter 17 Next: Our interest in this topic → 18 Chapter 18 · 1 min Our interest in this topic Reinforce Lab sells search and AI search services. We do not sell an AI visibility tracking tool, and nothing here is paid placement. Jamil Ahmed, who wrote this guide, is a Semrush Ambassador, and Reinforce Lab uses affiliate links for some tools. Read our FTC and affiliate disclosure . Our free diagnostic works like the test above, with a larger prompt set, repeated runs and a written plan. You can read about our SEO and AI search audit or get your free diagnostic . End of chapter 18 Next: Final thoughts → 19 Chapter 19 · 1 min Final thoughts Start with a hand test and the free tools. Buy software when your prompt list or your markets outgrow a spreadsheet. Choose on what you can verify: full answers, sources, history and a price that includes the work after the dashboard. And plan who will act on the results, because that is where visibility changes. Back matter Glossary A to Z C Citation An answer that links to a page of yours. E Engine An AI search product such as ChatGPT, Gemini or Perplexity. M Mention An answer that names your brand. P Prompt The question you type into an AI tool. P Proof of value A short trial that checks a tool against your own hand test. S Share of voice Your brand mentions divided by all brand mentions in the test. Questions FAQs What is an AI brand visibility tool? Software that runs a fixed list of buyer questions through AI tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Google's AI Overviews on a schedule and records whether your brand is named, linked or described correctly, compared with competitors. What do AI visibility tools track? Most report mentions, citations, share of voice, sources cited, sentiment and history. Ahrefs and Semrush both list mentions, citations and share of voice or a visibility score. Check that a tool keeps mentions and citations separate. How much do AI visibility tools cost? It varies. In November 2026, Peec AI listed $95, $245 and $495 a month for 50, 150 and 350 prompts, and Otterly listed $29, $189 and $489 a month. Both offer custom enterprise plans. Prompts, engines, markets and staff time decide the real cost. Are AI visibility scores accurate? They are directional. SparkToro and Gumshoe found less than a 1 in 100 chance that ChatGPT or Google's AI would give the same list of brands twice for one prompt, so a score from one day is a snapshot. Look for repeated runs and a trend. Do I need a paid AI visibility tool? Not to start. Test 20 to 30 buyer questions by hand, use Search Console's Generative AI report and the free Ahrefs and Semrush checkers. Buy software when your prompt list or markets outgrow a spreadsheet. Can an AI visibility tool show my rank in AI answers? Some report a position, but the order of brands in AI answers is close to random, so it is not a reliable measure. Use the share of runs in which you appear instead. Do AI visibility tools fix problems automatically? No. They show gaps. Someone still has to correct facts, write pages and earn mentions, so decide who owns that work before you buy. Which AI engines should a B2B tool cover? The ones your buyers use, on the plan you would buy. For most B2B teams that means ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews and AI Mode, Perplexity and Gemini. Entry plans often cover only some engines, so check the plan. How many B2B buyers use AI to research vendors? It depends on the question asked. Forrester found 94% use AI somewhere in buying, Gartner 45% on a recent purchase, and 6sense 81% use an LLM in an evaluation but only 26% to discover vendors. How do I test an AI visibility tool before buying? Write 20 to 30 buyer prompts without your brand name, run a hand baseline, trial each tool with the same prompts and competitors, compare the tool with your baseline, open ten answers to confirm the sources are real, and score each tool on a fixed checklist. What is the best AI brand visibility tool? There is no single best one. The right choice depends on the AI tools covered, the number of prompts, competitor benchmarking, reporting and price. Run a 14-day test on your own prompts before you pay. Can I check my AI visibility for free? Yes, by hand. List 15 to 25 buyer prompts, run them in ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini and Google AI Mode, and record whether your brand appears, the sources cited and whether the facts are right. Repeat weekly. Are AI visibility tools the same as GEO tools and LLM trackers? Mostly. The labels vary, but each one runs prompts in AI tools and reports mentions, citations, share of voice and sentiment. They differ in coverage, frequency, benchmarking and reporting. How do you track AI visibility? Pick a fixed set of buyer prompts, run them on a schedule in the AI tools your buyers use, record mentions, citations and accuracy, and compare trends over weeks, not single answers. How do I track brand mentions in ChatGPT? Write 15 to 25 questions your buyers ask. Run each one in a new ChatGPT chat, and record whether your brand appears, what is said and which sources are cited. Repeat weekly with the same questions. A paid tool does the same thing at larger scale. What are AI brand monitoring tools? They are tools that run a set of prompts in AI tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity and record whether and how your brand appears. Some also track sentiment and competitor mentions. Vendors also call them AI visibility trackers or LLM brand monitoring tools. How do you track brand visibility in Google AI Mode? Run your buyer questions in AI Mode in a new session and record the answer, the brand names and the sources shown. Answers vary by person, place and time, so repeat the test and look at trends. If you buy a tool, ask the vendor whether it covers AI Mode. Why should I track AI brand visibility? It shows whether AI tools name your brand, whether they state your facts correctly and which competitors they name instead. You cannot see this in a normal rank report. What are the best AI search visibility tools? There is no single best one. Compare the AI tools each covers, how many prompts you can track, whether it benchmarks competitors, its reports and its price, then test two or three on your own prompts for 14 days. What are LLM tracking tools? LLM tracking tools run your prompts in AI tools and record whether your brand appears, which sources are cited and how answers change over time. They are the same kind of product as AI visibility trackers. lede: How to rank in AI Overviews: what Google says, what studies found, a 10-step checklist, what does not matter, worked examples, a way to check your results and a 30-day plan.
copy_text: Home Blog AI Growth Systems How to Rank in AI Overviews: A Practical… Guide AI Growth Systems How to Rank in AI Overviews: A Practical Checklist for Google How to rank in AI Overviews: what Google says, what studies found, a 10-step checklist, what does not matter, worked examples, a way to check your results and a 30-day plan. Jamil Ahmed Published 20 Oct 2026 Updated 16 Nov 2026 17 Chapters 12 Min read A to Z Glossary 01 What are Google AI Overviews, and when do they appear? 2 min 02 What does Google say you need to do? 1 min 03 Do you need to rank on page one first? 1 min 04 How to rank in AI Overviews: a 10-step checklist 3 min 05 What does not matter? 1 min 06 Worked example 1: a software company’s “what is” page 1 min 07 Worked example 2: a consultancy that is cited for definitions but not comparisons 1 min 08 How do you optimize for AI Overviews? 1 min 09 What does it mean to rank in an AI Overview? 1 min 10 How does Google choose its sources? 1 min 11 Does this work for product pages or only for informational content? 1 min 12 How long does it take to see changes? 1 min 13 How do you check whether AI Overviews cite you? 1 min 14 What are the common mistakes? 1 min 15 A 30-day plan 1 min 16 How Reinforce Lab approaches AI Overviews 1 min 17 Final thoughts 1 min Chapter 01 of 17 0% read Chapters 0% 01 What are Google AI Overviews, and when do they appear? 02 What does Google say you need to do? 03 Do you need to rank on page one first? 04 How to rank in AI Overviews: a 10-step checklist 05 What does not matter? 06 Worked example 1: a software company’s “what is” page 07 Worked example 2: a consultancy that is cited for definitions but not comparisons 08 How do you optimize for AI Overviews? 09 What does it mean to rank in an AI Overview? 10 How does Google choose its sources? 11 Does this work for product pages or only for informational content? 12 How long does it take to see changes? 13 How do you check whether AI Overviews cite you? 14 What are the common mistakes? 15 A 30-day plan 16 How Reinforce Lab approaches AI Overviews 17 Final thoughts About 12 min in total Short answer To rank in Google AI Overviews, a page must be indexed and eligible to show with a snippet. Google says there are no extra technical requirements. Answer the question early, cover the related questions, back claims with named sources, earn real mentions on other sites and check your results monthly. Ranking in normal results helps, but Ahrefs found only about 38% of cited pages ranked in the top 10 in March 2026. 01 Google says a page needs to be indexed and snippet-eligible, with no extra technical requirements and no special markup. 02 AI Overviews trigger mostly on questions and long searches: Ahrefs found 21% of keywords overall and 57.9% of question searches. 03 About 38% of pages cited in AI Overviews ranked in the top 10 in March 2026, down from about 76% in July 2025. 04 Cover the main question and its follow-ups in depth, but do not make a page for every wording, which Google treats as spam. 05 Brand mentions and fan-out coverage correlate with citation in Ahrefs studies. Correlation is not proof of cause. 06 Page length, llms.txt and special schema do not matter. Check your results monthly and read the trend. To rank in Google AI Overviews, your page must be indexed and eligible to show in Google Search with a snippet. Beyond that, Google says there are no extra technical requirements and no special tricks. What helps is the same work that helps any page: answer the question clearly, cover the related questions, back your claims with sources, and be talked about by other sites. Ranking well in normal results also helps, but it is no longer enough on its own. This guide gives you a checklist of ten steps, with the data behind each one and the limits of that data. It also covers how to check whether Google cites you, what does not matter, two worked examples and a 30-day plan. We cite only studies we could read at the source, and we say when a finding is a correlation and not a cause. 01 Chapter 1 · 2 min What are Google AI Overviews, and when do they appear? An AI Overview is a short AI-written summary at the top of some Google results, with links to the pages it drew on. Google says AI Overviews and AI Mode may use “query fan-out”: the tool splits your question into several related searches and gathers supporting pages for each one. Google also says an AI Overview only shows when its systems decide it adds something to classic Search, so many searches do not trigger one. Studies agree that they appear far more often on questions and long searches. Two examples, with different samples: Ahrefs analyzed 146 million search results and found that AI Overviews showed on 21% of keywords. They showed on 57.9% of question searches and on 46.4% of searches with seven or more words. “Why” questions had the highest rate, at 59.8%. Of the keywords that triggered one, 99.9% were informational. The Pew Research Center tracked the browsing of 900 US adults in March 2025. About 18% of the Google searches in its sample produced an AI summary. That share was 8% for searches of one or two words and 53% for searches of ten words or more. The two figures differ because the samples and methods differ. Both point the same way: AI Overviews are mostly about informational and question-style searches. If your pages target buying searches, such as “pricing” or “near me”, expect fewer of them to be affected. Pew also found that people clicked a regular result in 8% of visits to pages with an AI summary and 15% of visits to pages without one, and clicked a link inside the summary in 1% of visits. Google says clicks from pages with AI Overviews are higher quality. Look at conversions and not only clicks. End of chapter 1 Next: What does Google say you need to do? → 02 Chapter 2 · 1 min What does Google say you need to do? Google’s documentation on AI features is short and plain: To be shown as a supporting link, a page must be indexed and eligible to show in Google Search with a snippet. There are no additional technical requirements. The usual SEO basics still apply: allow crawling, link pages together, give people a good page experience, keep important content in text, and keep structured data matched to the visible text. You do not need new machine-readable files, AI text files, special markup or special schema.org types. Preview controls such as nosnippet , data-nosnippet , max-snippet and noindex apply to AI formats. More restrictive settings limit how your content can be used. Google’s guide asks for unique, non-commodity content with a point of view and first-hand experience. It warns that making separate pages for every variation of a question, mainly to influence AI answers, breaks its scaled content abuse policy. Google also reports AI feature traffic in the normal Search Console performance data and in a Generative AI performance report. Use those for your own measurement. End of chapter 2 Next: Do you need to rank on page one first? → Reinforce Lab service · AI Search Optimization Want to know if Google cites your pages? Reinforce Lab starts with a free diagnostic of your Google and AI search visibility and a 90-day plan. See AI search optimization → Or get a free diagnostic first 03 Chapter 3 · 1 min Do you need to rank on page one first? It helps, but the link is weaker than it used to be. In July 2025, Ahrefs found that about 76% of pages cited in AI Overviews also ranked in the top 10 for the same query, based on 1.9 million citations. In March 2026 it repeated the study with 863,000 keyword results and about 4 million AI Overview URLs and found about 38%. Ahrefs suggests that query fan-out explains part of the drop, because the tool draws on the results for related sub-questions. That is a guess, since Google does not publish the sub-questions. The lesson is to rank for the question and for its follow-ups. A page that answers a related sub-question can be cited even when it does not rank first for the main phrase. End of chapter 3 Next: How to rank in AI Overviews: a 10-step checklist → 04 Chapter 4 · 3 min How to rank in AI Overviews: a 10-step checklist 1. Check which of your searches trigger an AI Overview List 20 to 30 searches you want to be cited for. Run each in a logged-out window set to your country. Note which ones show an AI Overview. Work on those first. Skip the rest for now. 2. Make sure the page is eligible Check that the page is indexed, returns a normal 200 status, is not blocked by robots.txt or your CDN, and is not set to nosnippet or noindex . In Search Console, confirm that the page is indexed. Our guide to robots.txt for SEO covers the access side. 3. Answer the question early Put a direct answer in the first sentences under each question heading, in plain words. Then add detail. A reader and a tool can both use that answer without the rest of the page. 4. Write headings as real questions People search with questions, and AI Overviews trigger most often on them. Use the wording your buyers use. Take the questions from sales calls, support emails and the “People also ask” box. 5. Cover the related questions, on the right pages Ahrefs reports a study it ran with SurferSEO. Pages that ranked for the related fan-out searches were 161% more likely to be cited than pages that ranked only for the main phrase. The correlation between ranking for fan-out searches and being cited was 0.77. Treat that as a pointer, not a law. The practical step is to cover a topic in depth: write the main page, then pages for the real follow-up questions, and link them together. Write each page because a reader needs it. Do not create a page for every wording of a question. 6. Add evidence and what only you know Name your sources, add dates, and show first-hand experience: your own data, tests and results. Google’s guide asks for content that goes beyond common knowledge. A page that restates what everyone already says gives a tool no reason to choose it. 7. Build real mentions across the web Ahrefs found that branded web mentions had a correlation of 0.664 with AI Overview visibility in its study of 75,000 brands, and that mentions on highly linked pages had a correlation of 0.70 across 76.7 million AI Overviews. These are correlations, so they do not prove cause. Google adds that seeking fake mentions is not as helpful as it might seem. Earn mentions with real stories, real data and real expertise. 8. Use more than text where it fits Google says its AI features can bring in images and video, and that following its image and video guidance already counts. Ahrefs found that YouTube made up 18.2% of the AI Overview citations that did not rank in the top 100 for the same keyword, and 5.6% of all cited URLs in its 2026 study. If a video answers the question better than text, publish one, and write a clear title and description. 9. Keep pages fresh and markup honest Update facts and examples on your best pages and show an honest update date. If you use structured data, make sure it matches what the page shows. Google does not require special markup for AI Overviews, so do not expect markup alone to change your result. 10. Measure with repeated checks Check your list monthly: is an AI Overview shown, are you cited, and who is cited instead? Record the date and market. Use the Search Console reports for the Google side. Because AI answers vary from run to run, look at the trend over several checks and not at one result. End of chapter 4 Next: What does not matter? → 05 Chapter 5 · 1 min What does not matter? Page length. Ahrefs found a near-zero correlation (about 0.04) between word count and AI citations. Google says there is no ideal page length. Write until the question is answered. llms.txt and “chunking”. Google says it does not use llms.txt files and that you do not need to break content into tiny pieces for AI. Special schema. Google says no special schema.org markup is needed. FAQ markup also lost its rich result in Google Search on 7 May 2026. Rewriting only for AI. Google says AI systems understand synonyms and general meaning, so you do not need to write in a special way. End of chapter 5 Next: Worked example 1: a software company’s “what is” page → 06 Chapter 6 · 1 min Worked example 1: a software company’s “what is” page This is an illustration, not a client result. Imagine a company that sells expense software. Its page “what is expense management” ranks on page one, but an AI Overview shows for that search and does not cite it. The team reads the cited pages. They are short, answer in the first two sentences, name a source for a statistic and include a one-line definition. The company’s page opens with a long story about the company’s history. The fix is simple. It moves a two-sentence definition to the top, adds a named source for the one statistic it quotes, and adds a short list of the steps in a typical process. It also writes a page on a fan-out question that the cited pages cover, “how do expense approvals work”, and links the two. The team does not rewrite everything. It sets a monthly check of 25 searches, records whether it is cited, and watches the trend over three months. End of chapter 6 Next: Worked example 2: a consultancy that is cited for definitions but not comparisons → 07 Chapter 7 · 1 min Worked example 2: a consultancy that is cited for definitions but not comparisons Again, an illustration. Imagine a small consultancy that sells compliance training. It is cited in AI Overviews for three “what is” searches but not for any “X vs Y” or “best way to” searches, where buyers compare options. The team finds that the comparison searches cite review sites and a trade association page, and that the consultancy appears on neither. The plan has two parts. It writes one honest comparison guide with a table, named sources and a note on when each option fits. It also approaches the trade association with a short, original guide based on its own audits. Success is measured by whether the cited pages for those searches change over the next three checks. The lesson is to look at which sources are cited for each kind of search. Definitions, comparisons and how-to searches often cite different pages. End of chapter 7 Next: How do you optimize for AI Overviews? → 08 Chapter 8 · 1 min How do you optimize for AI Overviews? AI Overviews SEO is mostly ordinary SEO done well. The checklist above gives the steps. In short: make sure the page is indexed and can show a snippet, answer the question clearly under a matching heading, keep facts accurate and current, show who wrote the page and why they know the topic, and check whether Google cites you for your key questions. Content for AI Overviews works best when one page answers one question in plain words. End of chapter 8 Next: What does it mean to rank in an AI Overview? → 09 Chapter 9 · 1 min What does it mean to rank in an AI Overview? There is no rank number inside an AI Overview the way there is in a list of results. A page is either shown as a supporting link or it is not. Some sites are linked next to a sentence, some in a side panel and some at the bottom. So “ranking in AI Overviews” really means being cited, and sometimes being named in the text. Track whether you are cited, how often, and for which searches, not a position. End of chapter 9 Next: How does Google choose its sources? → 10 Chapter 10 · 1 min How does Google choose its sources? Google says its AI features rest on its core Search ranking and quality systems. It uses a method it calls retrieval-augmented generation: the system finds relevant, current pages in the Search index, reads the passages and writes an answer that links to the pages that support it. Google does not publish a list of ranking factors for AI Overviews, and no third-party tool can see inside its systems. What the studies add is a set of patterns, such as the share of cited pages that also rank, which we covered above. Use them as hints, and test on your own searches. End of chapter 10 Next: Does this work for product pages or only for informational content? → 11 Chapter 11 · 1 min Does this work for product pages or only for informational content? Mostly for informational content. Ahrefs found that 99.9% of the keywords that triggered an AI Overview in its study were informational, and that question searches triggered them far more than other searches. Product and pricing searches show them less often. That does not mean product pages are out of scope. Google asks you to keep Merchant Center and Business Profile information current, and to support text with good images and video. But for most businesses, the larger gains come from guides, comparisons and answers to buyer questions that sit around the product. End of chapter 11 Next: How long does it take to see changes? → 12 Chapter 12 · 1 min How long does it take to see changes? We found no reliable public figure, so we do not quote one. Pages must be recrawled before a change can show, and the answers themselves vary from run to run. Google also says that indexing and serving are not guaranteed, even when a page meets every requirement. A practical rhythm is to make a change, wait for the page to be recrawled, then check the same searches monthly for at least three months before you decide that it worked. End of chapter 12 Next: How do you check whether AI Overviews cite you? → 13 Chapter 13 · 1 min How do you check whether AI Overviews cite you? List your searches. Put the ones where you already rank on page one first. Run each in a logged-out window with your target country. Write down the date. For each, record whether an AI Overview appears, whether you are cited, which page, and who is cited instead. Copy every cited URL. The list shows who Google treats as a source in your market. Repeat monthly and compare. Keep AI Mode results separate from AI Overviews. Add Search Console’s Generative AI performance report for Google’s own numbers. Paid tools can run these checks daily. Our guide to AI brand visibility tools explains what to look for, and our 30-minute AI brand visibility test shows the hand method. End of chapter 13 Next: What are the common mistakes? → 14 Chapter 14 · 1 min What are the common mistakes? Chasing a trick. Google says there is no special optimization. Fix the basics first. Writing a page for every wording of a question. Google warns that this can break its spam policy. Burying the answer. A long introduction before the point gives a tool no clear passage. Quoting unsourced statistics. A claim with no source is easy to skip and easy to dispute. Ignoring the sources Google already cites. If you are on none of them, your own pages are only part of the answer. Judging by one check. Answers vary. Track a trend. Blocking snippets by accident. A nosnippet or noindex setting limits how your content can be used. End of chapter 14 Next: A 30-day plan → 15 Chapter 15 · 1 min A 30-day plan Week 1: list and baseline Pick 20 to 30 searches. Run them logged out and record which trigger an AI Overview and who is cited. Week 2: fix eligibility and openings Check indexing, status codes, robots.txt and snippet settings for your target pages. Move a direct answer to the top of each page. Week 3: fill the gaps Write one page for the most important follow-up question. Add a source and a date to your key claims. Plan one real story for a site that is already cited. Week 4: measure and decide Run the same checks again. Compare with week 1. Decide what to repeat. Then keep checking monthly. End of chapter 15 Next: How Reinforce Lab approaches AI Overviews → 16 Chapter 16 · 1 min How Reinforce Lab approaches AI Overviews Reinforce Lab sells search and AI search services, so weigh this section with that in mind. We start with a free diagnostic of your Google and AI search visibility, then build a plan. You can read about our AI search optimization service and our SEO and AI search audit , or get your free diagnostic . End of chapter 16 Next: Final thoughts → 17 Chapter 17 · 1 min Final thoughts There is no secret way to rank in AI Overviews. Be eligible, answer the question early, cover the follow-ups, show your evidence and earn real mentions. Then check your results on a schedule, because answers change. Do the basics well and the rest is measurement. Back matter Glossary A to Z A AI Overview A short AI-written summary shown at the top of some Google results, with links to the pages it used. C Citation A link to a page shown with an AI answer. C Correlation Two things that move together, which does not prove that one causes the other. E Eligible A page that is indexed and allowed to show with a snippet. Q Query fan-out One question split into several related searches to build a fuller answer. S Snippet The text Google shows for a page in its results. Questions FAQs How do you rank in Google AI Overviews? Make sure the page is indexed and eligible to show with a snippet, answer the question early, cover the related questions, add named sources and real expertise, earn real mentions on other sites, and check results monthly. Google says there are no extra technical requirements. Do you need to rank on page one to appear in AI Overviews? It helps but is not required. Ahrefs found about 76% of cited pages ranked in the top 10 in July 2025 and about 38% in March 2026, so pages ranking lower or not at all are also cited. What is query fan-out? Google says its AI features may split one question into several related searches and gather supporting pages for each. A page that answers a related sub-question can be cited even if it does not rank first for the main phrase. How often do AI Overviews appear? It depends on the sample. Ahrefs found them on 21% of keywords in 146 million results and on 57.9% of question searches. Pew found about 18% of Google searches in March 2025 produced an AI summary, and 53% of searches of ten words or more. Do I need special schema or llms.txt for AI Overviews? No. Google says there is no special schema.org markup to add and that it does not use llms.txt files. Keep any structured data matched to the visible text. Does page length affect AI Overviews? Ahrefs found a near-zero correlation of about 0.04 between word count and AI citations, and Google says there is no ideal page length. Write until the question is answered. Do brand mentions help? Ahrefs found correlations of 0.664 for branded web mentions and 0.70 for mentions on highly linked pages with AI Overview visibility. These are correlations, not proof, and Google says seeking fake mentions is not as helpful as it might seem. How do I check if AI Overviews cite my site? List 20 to 30 searches, run them logged out in your target country, and record whether an AI Overview appears, whether you are cited, which page, and who is cited instead. Repeat monthly and use Search Console's Generative AI performance report. Can I stop my content being used in AI Overviews? Google says preview controls such as nosnippet, data-nosnippet, max-snippet and noindex apply to its AI formats. More restrictive settings limit how your content is featured. How long does it take to see changes in AI Overviews? There is no reliable public figure. Pages need to be recrawled and answers vary from run to run, so check monthly for several months and read the trend. What is AI Overviews SEO? It is the work of making your pages eligible and useful for the AI summaries Google shows above results. It builds on normal SEO: indexed pages, clear answers, accurate facts and real expertise. How do you optimize for AI Overviews? Make sure the page is indexed, answer the question under a matching heading, keep facts correct, show the author and sources, and then check whether Google cites you. No special markup is required. What content works for AI Overviews? Clear, accurate pages that answer one question well, with definitions, steps, comparisons and named sources. Thin or copied pages rarely help.
