Start with the pages closest to a purchase, such as comparison, alternatives, integration and pricing pages. Then add problem and category content, fix technical issues such as JavaScript rendering, plan for AI search, and measure trials and pipeline, not only traffic. 01 Build decision-stage pages first: alternatives, versus, integration, use-case and pricing pages. 02 Decision-stage terms have low volume but high intent. Pick keywords by fit, difficulty and lead quality, not volume alone. 03 G2 found 79% of 1,169 B2B software buyers said AI search changed their research, and chatbots were the top shortlist influence at 17.1%. 04 One agency's client data shows SEO leads reaching sales at 51% against 26% for paid search. It is a vendor benchmark, not a target. 05 Check the raw HTML of your marketing pages. Major AI crawlers did not render JavaScript in Vercel's 2024 study. 06 Be accurate and dated on competitor comparisons, and show prices or the factors behind them. 07 Measure by trials, qualified leads and pipeline. No independent study gives a reliable SaaS SEO timeline. SaaS SEO is search engine optimization for software sold by subscription. Its job is to bring in buyers who are choosing a tool, and to turn them into trials, demos and customers. The best order is to start with the pages closest to a purchase, such as comparison, alternatives, integration and pricing pages. Then build content for earlier questions, fix the technical base and make sure AI search tools describe you correctly. This guide gives a ten-step plan for B2B software companies. It covers keyword research by funnel stage, the page types that convert, technical problems that SaaS sites have, how AI search changes the work, how to measure results, and when to hire help. We cite only studies and documents we could read at the source, and we say when a number comes from a vendor’s own client data. 01 Chapter 1 · 1 min What is SaaS SEO? SaaS SEO is the practice of making a software company’s site easy to find, understand and trust in search, for the questions that buyers ask while they decide what to buy. It covers the marketing site, the blog, the help center and any public pages of the product itself, such as templates and free tools. End of chapter 1 Next: How is SaaS SEO different from regular SEO? → 02 Chapter 2 · 1 min How is SaaS SEO different from regular SEO? The basics are the same: crawlable pages, clear content and good links. The differences come from how software is bought. Area Regular SEO SaaS SEO Buying cycle Often one visit and one decision Weeks or months, with several people involved Best keywords High volume, broad terms Lower volume, high intent terms such as “alternative”, “vs” and “pricing” Goal Traffic and sales Trials, demos and qualified leads, then retention Site structure One site A marketing site, an app, docs and a help center, often on different systems Competition Other sellers Review sites, comparison sites and large software brands Proof Reviews, photos Case studies, integrations, security pages, review-site ratings End of chapter 2 Next: Why does SaaS SEO matter now? → Reinforce Lab service · Enterprise SEO Strategy Want a SaaS SEO plan built around trials and pipeline? Reinforce Lab starts with a free diagnostic of your Google and AI search visibility and a 90-day plan. See enterprise SEO strategy → Or get a free diagnostic first 03 Chapter 3 · 2 min Why does SaaS SEO matter now? Two sets of data explain the stakes. They come from different sources and have different limits. Buyers research with AI. G2 surveyed 1,169 B2B decision-makers in April 2025 for its Buyer Behavior Report. It found that 79% said AI search had changed how they research, and 29% said they start research with AI search more often than Google. Generative AI chatbots were the top source influencing vendor shortlists, at 17.1%, ahead of software review sites at 15.1%. The sample is software buyers who answered G2’s survey, so it may lean toward people who use review sites. Organic search can convert well, on one vendor’s data. First Page Sage, an SEO agency, published funnel benchmarks from more than 50 B2B SaaS clients over a decade, mostly companies with $10M to $100M in revenue. In that data, SEO visitors became leads at 2.1% and paid search at 0.7%. Of the marketing-qualified leads, 51% from SEO and 26% from paid search became sales-qualified leads. These are one agency’s client numbers, with no sample size per row, and they assume strong execution. Use them as a rough guide, not a target. Search itself is also changing. The Pew Research Center tracked 900 US adults in March 2025 and found that people clicked a regular result in 8% of visits to pages with an AI summary and 15% of visits to pages without one. Google disputes that study’s method. The practical point is that being named in the answer matters as well as ranking under it. End of chapter 3 Next: A ten-step SaaS SEO plan → 04 Chapter 4 · 6 min A ten-step SaaS SEO plan Step 1: Define who you sell to and what job they hire you for Write down your ideal customer, the problem they have, the tools they use now and the reasons they switch. These notes feed every later step. The best source is your own sales calls, lost deals, support tickets and customer interviews, not a keyword tool. Step 2: Do keyword research by funnel stage Group keywords by what the buyer wants. The table shows page types and the query patterns they match. Stage Buyer question Page types Example query pattern Decision Which vendor, and at what price? Comparison, alternatives, pricing, integration, use-case, customer story “[competitor] alternative”, “[you] vs [competitor]”, “[category] for [role]” Consideration Which kind of tool fits us? Category guides, buying checklists, “best” lists, templates “best [category] software”, “[category] software for [use case]” Awareness What is this problem and how do I fix it? Guides, glossaries, research “how to reduce churn”, “what is [concept]” Decision-stage terms have low volume, and keyword tools often understate them, because buyers phrase the same need in many ways. Several agencies report that one comparison page ranks for hundreds of variants. Treat that as an agency observation. Check your own Search Console for queries with words like “vs”, “alternative”, “pricing” and “integration”, and look at those with a position between about 8 and 30, where Google already links the page with the intent. To choose what to build first, score each keyword on three things: does it match a problem your product solves, can you realistically rank for it now, and would a searcher be a qualified lead? Search volumes show why you must pick with care. In Semrush’s US database on 15 November 2026, “saas seo” has about 2,900 searches a month at a difficulty of 34, while “seo for saas” has about 1,300 at 33 and “saas seo strategy” about 590 at 27. Agency terms such as “saas marketing agency” run higher but are won by agencies and review sites, not by product pages. How do you find low-competition, high-intent SaaS keywords? Use four sources, in this order. Each one finds terms that a generic keyword list misses. Your competitors’ money pages. Put your three or four closest rivals into a keyword tool and filter their ranking pages for “vs”, “alternative”, “best”, “pricing” and “for”. That list shows what they have judged worth building. Your own conversations. Sales calls, lost deals, cancellation notes and support tickets give the exact words buyers use. No tool has these. Your product. Each feature, integration and use case on your own site is a possible page. An audit of your product pages often turns up dozens of candidates. Search Console. Filter queries for the same words and look at those where you already appear but rank below the top results. Then check difficulty in a tool and the search results themselves. If the top results are large review sites and big software brands, aim for a narrower phrase, such as a use case or an integration, where a focused page can win. Step 3: Build the bottom-of-the-funnel pages first These pages meet buyers when they are ready to choose. Build them in this order: Alternatives pages for the competitors your buyers leave. Name the usual reasons, such as price, missing features or team size, and show which option suits which reason, including options that are not you. Versus pages for two-name shortlists. Put a verdict near the top and a dated comparison table. Integration pages for each tool your product connects to. Say what syncs, in which direction, how often, on which plans and how to set it up. Use-case pages for each role or industry you serve, with real workflows and proof, not swapped nouns. A pricing page that states prices or the factors that set them. A page that hides everything behind “contact sales” gives search engines and AI tools little to quote. Be accurate and fair. Every claim about a competitor must be true on the day you publish, and you must date it. A comparison that admits where the rival wins is more believable and more likely to be quoted. Step 4: Add problem and category content Once the decision pages exist, write the guides and checklists that serve earlier questions. Group them into clusters around a few core topics, with one main page for each and supporting pages that link to it and to each other. Write for people first. Google warns that making separate pages for every small variation of a question, mainly to manipulate rankings or AI answers, breaks its scaled content abuse policy. Step 5: Use the product as a source of pages Templates, calculators, free tools and public help articles can attract links and searches that a blog cannot. Keep them useful on their own, and link them to the right product page. Step 6: Fix the technical base SaaS sites run into the same problems again and again: JavaScript rendering. If your marketing pages load their text in the browser, check the raw HTML. In December 2024, Vercel reported that none of the major AI crawlers it tested rendered JavaScript, and Google’s own guidance says JavaScript sites need extra care. Server-render or pre-render your public pages. App and marketing site on different hosts. Decide what belongs in search. Keep logged-in app pages out of the index, and keep your docs and help center crawlable. Parameters, filters and duplicate pages. Use canonical URLs and keep low-value pages out of the index. Speed and page experience on mobile and desktop. Clean redirects and sitemaps when you ship a redesign or a new docs system. Our technical SEO service covers these checks, and our robots.txt guide explains how to control what bots can reach. Step 7: Earn links and mentions in an honest way Links still matter for ranking, and mentions on other sites matter for AI answers. Good sources for a SaaS firm are integration partners, review sites such as G2 and Capterra, original research with real data, podcasts, and industry press. Do not buy reviews or links. Google says inauthentic mentions are not as helpful as they might seem. Step 8: Plan for AI search Many buyers now ask AI tools to build a shortlist, so the work above also needs to hold up there. Make sure the AI crawlers you want can reach your pages, keep your facts the same across your site and your profiles, and put short, sourced answers at the top of key pages. Then run a fixed list of buyer prompts each month and record whether you are named and cited. Our guides to generative engine optimization , checking if AI tools mention your brand and ranking in AI Overviews and running an AI search audit cover the details. For SaaS, the term “GEO for SaaS” has little search demand on its own, so we treat it as a section of SaaS SEO, not a separate subject. Step 9: Measure what matters to the business Traffic and rankings are leading signs. Judge the program by trials, demo requests, qualified leads and pipeline from organic search. Track: Visitor-to-lead and visitor-to-trial rates for each page type Leads that become sales-qualified, by landing page Impressions and clicks for decision-stage queries in Search Console Impressions in Google’s Generative AI performance report, and mentions across your prompt list Branded search, as a sign of awareness Compare yourself with your own past results first. Public benchmarks vary by source, and most come from a single vendor’s clients. Step 10: Refresh and repeat Update comparison, pricing and integration pages whenever the facts change. Review the plan every quarter against pipeline, not only against traffic. End of chapter 4 Next: Worked example: a small SaaS team reorders its plan → 05 Chapter 5 · 1 min Worked example: a small SaaS team reorders its plan This is an illustration, not a client result. Imagine a 25-person company that sells invoice approval software to accounting firms. Its blog has 60 posts on general finance topics and gets visits, but almost no demo requests. Its site has no comparison page and no integration page. The team lists the competitors named in its last 30 sales calls and the tools its customers connect, such as accounting packages. It plans eight pages: three alternatives pages, two versus pages and three integration pages, plus a rewrite of its pricing page. It writes each page in the plan above, with dated tables and named proof from two customers who agreed to be quoted. It pauses new blog posts for six weeks. It then tracks, for each new page, impressions and clicks in Search Console, demo requests, and how many of those leads reach a sales call. After 90 days it compares the pages with the blog posts on demo requests per visit. The point is not a promised lift. The point is to move effort toward pages that serve buyers and to measure the result against the team’s own history. End of chapter 5 Next: How do you measure SaaS SEO and build topical authority? → 06 Chapter 6 · 1 min How do you measure SaaS SEO and build topical authority? Pair two ideas. First, build topical authority: choose the few subjects your product owns, write one strong page for each, and support it with focused pages that link to it and to each other. Practitioners describe this as a pillar and cluster structure, and it also helps internal linking and AI answers. Second, measure business results by page type, not only organic traffic. A useful set is: impressions and clicks for decision-stage queries, visitors who start a trial or request a demo, leads that reach sales, the share of pipeline from organic search and the cost of the work against that pipeline. Review it each month with sales, since sales calls show which pages buyers read and which questions they still ask. If traffic rises and trials do not, the pages are attracting the wrong readers. End of chapter 6 Next: Should you hire a SaaS SEO agency or consultant? → 07 Chapter 7 · 1 min Should you hire a SaaS SEO agency or consultant? You can start in-house if you have a writer, a developer with time for technical fixes and someone who talks to customers. Hire help when you lack one of those, when you need a technical audit, or when you want a plan before you spend on content. Ask for the deliverables: a keyword and page map by funnel stage, a list of technical fixes in priority order, the comparison and integration pages, and a report tied to trials and pipeline. We did not find independent data on typical fees or timelines, so ask for written quotes and be careful with promises of rankings. Reinforce Lab works with B2B software companies on SEO content systems and enterprise SEO strategy . See how we work with B2B SaaS companies . End of chapter 7 Next: How long does SaaS SEO take? → 08 Chapter 8 · 1 min How long does SaaS SEO take? No independent study we found gives a reliable timeline. Decision-stage pages on a site that is already indexed can start to appear within weeks. New sites, competitive terms and link building take longer. First Page Sage reports about a seven-month break-even for B2B SaaS SEO, but that figure comes from its own clients and should be treated as a claim, not a rule. Judge progress by your own leading signs: impressions, then clicks, then trials. End of chapter 8 Next: What are the common mistakes? → 09 Chapter 9 · 1 min What are the common mistakes? Starting with a big blog. Traffic from general guides rarely turns into demos on its own. Ignoring comparison and integration pages. They are low in volume and high in intent. Chasing volume. A term with 50 searches from the right buyer can beat one with 5,000 from the wrong audience. Unfair or stale comparisons. A false or outdated claim can hurt trust and invite complaints. Hiding prices. Buyers and AI tools both look for them. Letting the app and the site fight each other. Decide what belongs in the index. Measuring only traffic. Tie the work to trials and pipeline. End of chapter 9 Next: Our interest in this topic → 10 Chapter 10 · 1 min Our interest in this topic Reinforce Lab sells SEO and AI search services to software and other companies. Nothing here is paid placement. Jamil Ahmed, who wrote this guide, is a Semrush Ambassador, and Reinforce Lab uses affiliate links for some tools. Read our FTC and affiliate disclosure . You can get your free diagnostic for a view of your site’s search and AI visibility with a written plan. End of chapter 10 Next: Final thoughts → 11 Chapter 11 · 1 min Final thoughts SaaS buyers choose slowly and check many sources, including AI tools. Meet them where the choice is made: with honest comparison, integration, use-case and pricing pages first, then guides, then the technical and AI search work that keeps everything findable. Measure by trials and pipeline, and keep the facts fresh. Back matter Glossary A to Z B Bottom of the funnel The stage where a buyer is ready to choose, close to a trial or a demo. D Decision-stage keyword A search from a buyer who is choosing a vendor, such as an alternative, a comparison or a price. I Integration page A page that explains how your product connects to another tool. M MQL and SQL A lead that fits your market, and a lead that has shown real buying interest and talks to sales. S SaaS Software as a service: software sold by subscription and used online. T Topic cluster A main page on one topic with supporting pages that link to it and to each other. Questions FAQs What is SaaS SEO? SaaS SEO is search engine optimization for software sold by subscription. It aims to bring buyers who are choosing a tool to your site and turn them into trials, demos and customers, across a long buying cycle. How is SaaS SEO different from regular SEO? The basics match, but SaaS buying takes weeks or months and involves several people. Keywords with intent such as alternative, vs and pricing matter more than volume, and the site often spans a marketing site, an app, docs and a help center. How do you start a SaaS SEO strategy? Define your ideal customer and their problem, mine sales calls and Search Console for decision-stage queries, then build alternatives, versus, integration, use-case and pricing pages before a large blog. Fix technical issues in parallel. What keywords should a SaaS company target first? Decision-stage terms such as competitor alternative, you vs competitor, pricing and integration pages, then category and use-case terms. They have lower volume but higher intent. Choose by fit, difficulty and the value of the lead. Does SaaS SEO still work with AI search? Yes, and it matters more to be named in the answer. G2 found 79% of 1,169 B2B software buyers said AI search changed how they research. Keep facts consistent, crawlers able to read your pages, and answers near the top of key pages. What is GEO for SaaS? It means making sure AI tools name and describe your software correctly. We treat it as one part of SaaS SEO: crawl access, consistent facts, sourced answers and a monthly check of a fixed prompt list. What are the technical SEO problems for SaaS sites? Common ones are content loaded only by JavaScript, app pages mixed with marketing pages, duplicate and parameter URLs, slow pages and broken redirects after a redesign. Vercel found major AI crawlers did not render JavaScript in 2024. How long does SaaS SEO take to work? We found no independent study with a reliable timeline. Decision-stage pages on an indexed site can start to show in weeks, while competitive terms and links take longer. Judge progress by impressions, clicks and trials. How much does SaaS SEO cost? We did not find independent data on typical fees, so ask any agency for written quotes and the deliverables. Compare them by what you receive: a page map, a technical fix list, the new pages and a pipeline report. Should a SaaS company hire an agency or do SEO in-house? Start in-house if you have a writer, a developer with time and someone who talks to customers. Hire help for audits, missing skills or a plan before spending on content, and be wary of ranking promises. h1_text: AI Search Audit: A 10-Step Checklist for Your Website
lede: An AI search audit: what it checks, a 10-step checklist for your website, a scoring sheet, two worked examples, the tools you can use and when to hire help.
copy_text: Home Blog AI Growth Systems AI Search Audit: A 10-Step Checklist for Your… Guide AI Growth Systems AI Search Audit: A 10-Step Checklist for Your Website An AI search audit: what it checks, a 10-step checklist for your website, a scoring sheet, two worked examples, the tools you can use and when to hire help. Jamil Ahmed Published 30 Oct 2026 Updated 15 Nov 2026 14 Chapters 17 Min read A to Z Glossary 01 What is an AI search audit? 1 min 02 How is an AI search audit different from an SEO audit? 1 min 03 Before you start: set the scope 1 min 04 The 10-step AI search audit checklist 9 min 05 How do you score the audit and decide what to fix first? 1 min 06 Worked example 1: a consulting firm finds a gap in the sources 1 min 07 Worked example 2: a site blocks the bot it wanted 1 min 08 Which tools can run an AI search audit? 1 min 09 How often should you repeat the audit? 1 min 10 What else do people ask? 1 min 11 When should you hire an agency for an AI search audit? 1 min 12 What are the common mistakes? 1 min 13 Our interest in this topic 1 min 14 Final thoughts 1 min Chapter 01 of 14 0% read Chapters 0% 01 What is an AI search audit? 02 How is an AI search audit different from an SEO audit? 03 Before you start: set the scope 04 The 10-step AI search audit checklist 05 How do you score the audit and decide what to fix first? 06 Worked example 1: a consulting firm finds a gap in the sources 07 Worked example 2: a site blocks the bot it wanted 08 Which tools can run an AI search audit? 09 How often should you repeat the audit? 10 What else do people ask? 11 When should you hire an agency for an AI search audit? 12 What are the common mistakes? 13 Our interest in this topic 14 Final thoughts About 17 min in total Short answer An AI search audit checks whether AI tools can reach your pages, read them, and name or cite your brand for the questions buyers ask. Check eligibility, bot access, HTML content and your facts, then run a fixed list of 10 to 15 buyer questions several times in each engine and map the sources behind the answers. Fix access and facts first, save a dated baseline and repeat each quarter. 01 Fix access first: indexed and snippet-eligible pages, bots not blocked by robots.txt or a CDN, and the main text in the HTML. 02 Bots differ: OpenAI says robots.txt may not apply to ChatGPT-User, and Perplexity says the same of Perplexity-User. 03 Run each prompt more than once: SparkToro found under a 1 in 100 chance of the same brand list twice, so look for a rate, not a rank. 04 Keep mentions and citations in separate columns. They need different fixes. 05 Map the sources behind the answers. Often they are directories, reviews and community sites, not your own pages. 06 Use free first-party data: Search Console's Generative AI performance report and Bing's AI Performance report. 07 Save a dated baseline and repeat each quarter and after any site or firewall change. An AI search audit checks three things: can AI search tools reach your pages, can they read and use what is on them, and do they name or cite you when buyers ask questions in your field. You can run a basic one in a day with free tools, a robots.txt file and a spreadsheet. The result is a baseline you can repeat, not a rank or a score you can trust on its own. This guide gives you a 10-step checklist for your website, a way to score it, and a sheet for recording what you find. It also covers the tools you can use, two worked examples, and when it makes sense to hire help. Every statistic comes from a page we read at the source, and we say what each study can and cannot show. 01 Chapter 1 · 1 min What is an AI search audit? An AI search audit is a structured check of how AI answer tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Perplexity and Google’s AI Overviews treat your site and your brand. It has two parts. The first is technical: access, rendering and clear facts on your pages. The second is observation: you run a fixed list of buyer questions through the tools and record whether you are named, linked and described correctly. You will also see the names “AI visibility audit” and “GEO audit”. They describe the same kind of work. Ahrefs and Semrush both publish their own versions, and the steps overlap. Ahrefs frames it around mentions, citations, impressions and share of voice. Semrush lists six steps, from a baseline to a check of site-level issues that affect AI access. End of chapter 1 Next: How is an AI search audit different from an SEO audit? → 02 Chapter 2 · 1 min How is an AI search audit different from an SEO audit? An SEO audit asks if your pages can rank. An AI search audit asks if your pages can be used as sources, and if your brand is described correctly in the answer. They share a base. A page that is blocked, not indexed or empty to a crawler fails both. But a page can rank well and still be missing from AI answers. The Pew Research Center shows why the second question matters. It tracked the browsing of 900 US adults in March 2025, and studied 68,879 Google searches, of which 12,593 produced an AI summary. People clicked a regular result link in 8% of visits to pages with an AI summary and 15% of visits to pages without one. They clicked a link inside the summary in 1% of visits. Google disputes the study’s method and says it directs billions of clicks to sites each day. Even so, the data suggests that being named in the answer matters as much as being linked below it. End of chapter 2 Next: Before you start: set the scope → Reinforce Lab service · SEO & AI Search Audit Want this audit done for you, with a written plan? Reinforce Lab starts with a free diagnostic of your Google and AI search visibility and a 90-day plan. See the AI search audit → Or get a free diagnostic first 03 Chapter 3 · 1 min Before you start: set the scope Write down four things before you run a single test. This keeps your baseline fair and lets you repeat the audit later. Engines. Pick the tools your buyers use. For most B2B teams that is ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews and AI Mode, Gemini and Perplexity. Claude is worth adding if your buyers are technical. Market and language. Use one prompt list and one baseline for each country. Brand names. List your company name, product names and the names of the founders or experts who should be linked to you. Competitors. Pick three to five. You need them to see what “good” looks like. End of chapter 3 Next: The 10-step AI search audit checklist → 04 Chapter 4 · 9 min The 10-step AI search audit checklist Do the steps in order. Steps 1 to 5 are about your site. Steps 6 to 10 are about what the AI tools say. If a step in the first group fails, fix it before you spend time on the second group, because a tool that cannot read your page cannot cite it. Score each step pass or fail. A partial pass is a fail until it is fixed. Step 1: Check that your pages are eligible and not excluded What to check. For Google, Google says a page must be indexed and eligible to show in Search with a snippet to appear as a supporting link in AI Overviews or AI Mode, and that there are no additional technical requirements. So check three things. First, the page is indexed, has one clear canonical URL and is in your sitemap. Second, it has no nosnippet or tight max-snippet setting you did not intend. Third, open Search Console and look at Settings, then “Search generative AI”. Google offers a control there with three choices: include your site, exclude it, or inherit from a parent property. The default is to include. If someone chose “exclude”, your site receives no impressions or traffic from those features. Pass if key pages are indexed, snippets are allowed and the control says include. Fix by removing the stray tag or changing the setting. Google lists no extra files or markup as a requirement for these features, so do not mark a missing llms.txt file as a failure for Google. That is our reading of Google’s page, not a promise about other tools. Step 2: Check crawler access, bot by bot What to check. Open yoursite.com/robots.txt . Then check your CDN, firewall and bot protection. AI companies run different bots for different jobs, and the rules are not the same for each. The table shows what each company says on its own pages. Bot Job, per its owner What the owner says about robots.txt OAI-SearchBot (OpenAI) Shows sites in ChatGPT search results Sites that opt out are not shown in ChatGPT search answers, though they can still appear as navigational links. A change can take about 24 hours to apply. GPTBot (OpenAI) Collects content that may train models Disallowing it says your content should not be used for training. It is a separate setting from OAI-SearchBot. ChatGPT-User (OpenAI) Visits a page when a user’s question needs it OpenAI says robots.txt rules may not apply, because a user starts the visit. Claude-SearchBot, Claude-User, ClaudeBot (Anthropic) Search quality, user questions, model training Anthropic says its bots honor robots.txt. Blocking the first two may reduce your visibility in Claude answers. PerplexityBot, Perplexity-User (Perplexity) Search index, and user-requested visits PerplexityBot follows robots.txt. Perplexity says Perplexity-User generally ignores it because a user asked for the fetch. Pass if none of the search bots is blocked on pages you want cited, and your firewall lets verified requests through without a challenge page. Fix the robots.txt rule first. Then check the CDN, because a rule there can block a bot that robots.txt allows. OpenAI and Perplexity both publish IP ranges you can allow. Blocking training bots is a separate choice. For OpenAI, allowing OAI-SearchBot while disallowing GPTBot is a setting OpenAI describes. If you need a refresher on the file itself, read our robots.txt guide . Step 3: Check that the content is in the HTML What to check. Fetch a key page without a browser and look for the main heading and body text in the raw response. A command such as curl -s https://yoursite.com/page/ | grep -i "your heading" works. Do not trust the rendered view in browser tools, because it runs scripts that crawlers may not run. Here is why this step matters. In December 2024, Vercel studied the crawlers hitting its network and the sites it hosts. It found that none of the major AI crawlers it tested rendered JavaScript, including OpenAI’s, Anthropic’s and Perplexity’s. ChatGPT’s crawler fetched JavaScript files in 11.50% of its requests and Claude’s in 23.84%, but did not run them. Googlebot, which Gemini uses, does render JavaScript. That is a snapshot from one network and one month, so test your own pages and do not rely on the number. Pass if the main text is in the first HTML response. Fix by server-rendering the key pages or serving them as static HTML. Step 4: Check your facts and your entity What to check. Write a one-page list of facts: legal and brand name, a one-sentence description, services, locations, leaders, prices or price ranges. Compare it with your home page, About page, LinkedIn page and the directories that matter in your field. Check that your structured data, such as Organization schema, if you use it, is valid and matches the visible text. Pass if the name and description match in at least three or four places and nothing contradicts your list. Fix the source that is wrong. AI answers often repeat an old directory line, so a wrong listing can cost you more than a weak page. Step 5: Check that your pages answer the question fast What to check. Take your five most important pages. For each, ask what a buyer would type: “what is it”, “who is it for”, “how much does it cost”, “how does it compare”. Look at the first two paragraphs. Is there one clear sentence that answers the question? Are there named sources, dates and real numbers where a claim needs proof? Is the author named? Is there a date? Pass if a short passage on the page answers the question without the rest of the page. Fix by moving the answer to the top and cutting the lead-in. Our guide on how to rank in AI Overviews has the full writing checklist. Step 6: Build a fixed prompt list What to do. Write 10 to 15 questions a real buyer would ask, in the words they would use. Do not use your brand name in most of them. Mix three kinds: category questions (“best way to automate X”), comparison questions (“A vs B”) and a few brand questions (“what is [brand]”). Pull the wording from sales calls, support tickets and your site search. Give each prompt an ID and freeze the list. If you change a prompt later, record it as a new one, or you will not be able to compare audits. The range of 10 to 15 is our recommendation for a first audit. Published guides range from 5 to 30. The point is a list small enough to finish and large enough to see a pattern. Step 7: Run every prompt several times, in each engine What to do. Run each prompt three times in each engine, in a fresh session, on the same day. Save the full answer and the sources it shows. Note the date, the engine and the mode. The reason is variation. SparkToro asked 600 volunteers to run 12 prompts through ChatGPT, Claude and Google’s AI features, a combined 2,961 times. It found less than a 1 in 100 chance that two responses to the same prompt gave the same list of brands, and about a 1 in 1,000 chance that two gave the same list in the same order. The lists also varied in length. SparkToro wrote that any tool reporting a “ranking position in AI” should not be trusted, and that visibility across dozens to hundreds of prompts, run many times, is a reasonable metric. Three runs is a compromise. It will not give you a precise rate. It will show you if a brand is named almost every time, sometimes, or never, and that is enough for a first baseline. Record each result in a sheet with these fields: Field What to write Prompt ID and text The exact wording Engine, mode and date So the run can be repeated Mentioned Is your brand named in the text? Yes or no Cited Is one of your pages shown as a source? Yes or no, with the URL Description The words used about you, and whether the tone is positive, neutral or negative Competitors named Which rivals appear in the same answer Other sources The other sites the answer links to Notes Wrong facts, old facts, odd claims Keep “mentioned” and “cited” in separate columns. A brand can be named without a link, or linked without being named, and each needs a different fix. Step 8: Check accuracy and tone What to do. Ask each engine direct questions about you: “What is [brand]?”, “What does [brand] cost?”, “Who is [brand] for?” Compare each answer with your list of facts from step 4. Log every mistake and note the source the engine gave for it, if it gave one. Pass if there is no material error, such as a wrong price, a retired service or the wrong audience. Fix by correcting the source the engine used. Do not argue with the engine. Fix the page, listing or article it reads from, then test again after a few weeks. Step 9: Map the sources behind the answers What to do. From your sheet, list every domain the engines cited for your prompts, and count how often each appears. Sort them into four groups: your own pages, third-party review and directory sites, community sites such as Reddit, and competitor pages. This map shows where the answers come from, and it is often not your site. Pew’s data on Google shows the same pattern at scale. In its sample, Wikipedia, YouTube and Reddit were the most cited sources in AI summaries and in regular results, and together made up 15% of the sources in AI summaries. For your field the mix will differ, so build your own map. Pass if you appear on at least two or three of the sources that keep showing up. Fix by earning a real place there: a complete profile, a customer review, a useful answer in a community thread, or a mention in an article the engines already cite. Do not post fake reviews or hide ads in forums. Step 10: Find the gaps, set a baseline and measure What to do. Compare your sheet with your competitors. Sort every gap into one of four types: Absent: you are not named or cited and the prompt matters to your sales. Mention only: you are named but no page of yours is cited. Wrong or weak: you are named, but with old facts or a poor description. Competitor edge: a rival is cited on a prompt where your page is as good or better. Then add the first-party data you can get for free. Google’s Generative AI performance report in Search Console shows how often links to your site were shown in AI Overviews and AI Mode, by page, country, device and date. Google says it reports impressions, and that this data is already counted in the main Performance report, so do not add the two. Bing Webmaster Tools has an AI Performance report, in public preview since February 2026, that shows total citations, average cited pages and page-level citation counts across Copilot and Bing’s AI summaries. Bing says its “grounding queries” are a sample and not the full set. Neither report covers ChatGPT, Claude or Perplexity, so your prompt sheet is still needed. Pass if you now have a dated baseline for each engine, whatever it shows. The step is to have something to compare with next time. End of chapter 4 Next: How do you score the audit and decide what to fix first? → 05 Chapter 5 · 1 min How do you score the audit and decide what to fix first? Count your passes out of ten. Treat the first five and the last five differently. Result What it means What to do Any fail in steps 1 to 3 Tools may not be able to reach or read your pages Fix these first. Nothing else matters until they pass. Fail in step 4 or 8 Your facts are wrong or inconsistent Correct the source pages and listings. These are quick wins. Fail in step 5 Your pages are hard to quote Rewrite the top of each key page. Start with the ones that sell. Fail in steps 6, 7, 9 or 10 You are missing from answers or from the sources that feed them Plan new content and outside mentions. This is slow work. Start now and expect weeks, not days. A simple way to rank fixes is by effort and reach. Fix first what takes little work and touches many prompts. Ahrefs sorts its findings into three actions: fix wrong information, build missing content, and influence the outside sources the AI relies on. That is a useful frame for your plan. End of chapter 5 Next: Worked example 1: a consulting firm finds a gap in the sources → 06 Chapter 6 · 1 min Worked example 1: a consulting firm finds a gap in the sources This is an illustration, not a client result. Imagine a 20-person firm that sells compliance consulting to clinics. It passes steps 1 to 5. Its pages are indexed, the text is in the HTML and the facts match. It then builds 12 prompts and runs each three times in three engines, which gives 108 answers. It is named in 17 of them, about 16%. Its closest competitor is named in 41, about 38%. In the source map, the answers keep citing two directories and one trade site. The firm is not listed on any of them. The plan has three parts. The firm completes its profile on both directories in week one. It asks three clients to leave honest reviews in week two. It pitches the trade site a short article using its own data in week four. It repeats the same 108 runs 60 days later. The numbers will not be a promise, but the same prompts and the same method make the change readable. End of chapter 6 Next: Worked example 2: a site blocks the bot it wanted → 07 Chapter 7 · 1 min Worked example 2: a site blocks the bot it wanted Again, this is an illustration. Imagine a software company whose robots.txt allows OAI-SearchBot. Yet its pages never appear as sources in ChatGPT search. In step 2 the team checks its CDN and finds a bot-protection rule that returns a 403 error to unknown crawlers. The rule blocks OAI-SearchBot even though robots.txt allows it. The team adds an allow rule for the IP ranges OpenAI publishes and checks its server logs for the bot. OpenAI says a robots.txt change can take about 24 hours to apply, so the team waits a few days and runs its prompts again. This is the kind of silent failure that steps 1 to 3 exist to catch. A crawler visit in the logs does not prove a page will be cited. It only shows the page can be read. End of chapter 7 Next: Which tools can run an AI search audit? → 08 Chapter 8 · 1 min Which tools can run an AI search audit? You can do the whole audit by hand. The tools save time when you have many prompts, many markets or a need to repeat it each month. There are three groups. Free and manual. A spreadsheet, the AI tools themselves, Search Console’s Generative AI report, Bing Webmaster Tools, your server logs and a validator for your markup. SEO suites. Ahrefs Brand Radar and the Semrush AI Visibility Toolkit track mentions, citations and share of voice across several engines. Both companies publish their own audit method, so read it as a vendor’s view. Stand-alone trackers. Tools built for AI visibility. We compare what they track and what they cost in our guide to AI brand visibility tools . Test by hand first. A hand baseline lets you judge whether a tool’s numbers are right. And because answers vary, treat any tool that reports a precise rank inside AI answers with caution. End of chapter 8 Next: How often should you repeat the audit? → 09 Chapter 9 · 1 min How often should you repeat the audit? Repeat it every quarter, and after any change that can flip a pass to a fail: a new robots.txt, a CDN or firewall change, a site rebuild, a rebrand or a new template. Keep each run’s sheet instead of overwriting it, so you can see if a gap is closing or if the change is noise. Quarterly is our recommendation. Competing guides suggest monthly for active programs and quarterly for slower ones. End of chapter 9 Next: What else do people ask? → 10 Chapter 10 · 1 min What else do people ask? Does structured data matter for AI search? Not as a requirement for Google’s AI features. Google lists no extra technical requirement beyond being indexed and eligible to show with a snippet. Structured data still helps with clear facts and rich results, so check that it is valid and matches the page. Do not expect it to guarantee a citation. Should you block GPTBot? It is a separate choice from being in ChatGPT search. OpenAI says each setting is independent. A site can allow OAI-SearchBot to appear in search results and disallow GPTBot to signal that its content should not be used for training. Decide based on your policy, not on fear of losing visibility. Can an AI tool audit itself? Be careful. An AI tool can describe how a site ought to be set up. It cannot see your server logs, your firewall or what other users are shown. Use it to draft prompts and sort notes, and use real tests for the findings. What if everything passes and you are still not cited? Then the gap is probably outside your site. Look at the source map from step 9. If the engines lean on directories, reviews and community threads where you are absent, more pages on your own site will not close the gap. End of chapter 10 Next: When should you hire an agency for an AI search audit? → 11 Chapter 11 · 1 min When should you hire an agency for an AI search audit? Hire help when you lack the time to run the prompts, when the technical steps need a developer, or when the audit shows gaps in outside sources that need a plan. Ask any agency what it will deliver. A useful audit gives you the prompt list, the raw answers, the source map, a ranked list of fixes and a date to repeat the test. Be wary of a report that is only a score, or that promises to get you into AI answers. The AI companies do not publish how they pick sources, so nobody can guarantee a result. End of chapter 11 Next: What are the common mistakes? → 12 Chapter 12 · 1 min What are the common mistakes? Auditing only your own site. The answers often come from other sites. Running each prompt once. One answer is a clue, not a result. Testing only brand questions. You will look better than you are. Add category and comparison questions. Changing the prompts between audits. You can no longer compare. Marking llms.txt or extra markup as a failure for Google. Google lists no such requirement. Treating a crawler visit as proof of citation. A visit shows access. It does not show use. Stopping at the report. An audit has value only when someone fixes the findings. End of chapter 12 Next: Our interest in this topic → 13 Chapter 13 · 1 min Our interest in this topic Reinforce Lab sells search and AI search services, including an audit. Nothing here is paid placement. Jamil Ahmed, who wrote this guide, is a Semrush Ambassador, and Reinforce Lab uses affiliate links for some tools. Read our FTC and affiliate disclosure . Our free diagnostic follows the steps above with a larger prompt set, repeated runs and a written plan. You can read about our SEO and AI search audit or get your free diagnostic . For the wider picture, see our guides on AI brand visibility and generative engine optimization . End of chapter 13 Next: Final thoughts → 14 Chapter 14 · 1 min Final thoughts Start with access, because a blocked or empty page cannot be cited. Then fix your facts. Then test with a fixed prompt list, run each prompt more than once, and map the sources behind the answers. Save a dated sheet, fix the biggest gaps and run it again in a quarter. The audit does not promise a result. It shows you where you stand, what to fix first and whether the fixes worked. Back matter Glossary A to Z A AI search audit A check of whether AI tools can reach your pages and whether they name or cite your brand. C Citation A link to one of your pages shown as a source in an AI answer. C Crawler A program that fetches web pages for a search index or an AI tool. G Grounding query A phrase an AI system used to find pages to base its answer on. M Mention Your brand named in the text of an AI answer, with or without a link. P Prompt set A fixed list of buyer questions you run through each AI tool. S Source map A count of the sites that AI answers cite for your prompts. Questions FAQs What is an AI search audit? A structured check of whether AI answer tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Perplexity and Google's AI Overviews can reach your pages, read them, and name or cite your brand for the questions buyers ask. It has a technical part (access, rendering, clear facts) and an observation part (a fixed prompt list run through each tool). How do you run an AI search audit for your website? Follow ten steps: check eligibility, bot access, HTML content, your facts and your pages, then build a fixed prompt list, run each prompt several times in each engine, check accuracy, map the cited sources, and record a dated baseline. Fix the access and facts problems first. How do you audit AI search visibility for a brand? Write 10 to 15 buyer questions, run each three times in each engine you care about, and record whether your brand is mentioned, whether a page of yours is cited, how you are described and which competitors appear. Keep mentions and citations in separate columns. How long does an AI search audit take? A basic audit takes about a day. That is our estimate: 10 prompts run three times in three engines is 90 answers to save and score, plus the technical checks. A larger prompt list, several markets or a full source map takes longer. How many prompts should an AI search audit include? Use 10 to 15 for a first audit. That is our recommendation, and published guides range from 5 to 30. Keep the list fixed so you can compare later audits, and use mostly questions that do not contain your brand name. Why run each prompt more than once? Answers vary. SparkToro asked 600 volunteers to run 12 prompts through ChatGPT, Claude and Google's AI features, 2,961 times in total. It found less than a 1 in 100 chance of getting the same list of brands twice and about a 1 in 1,000 chance of the same list in the same order. Is an AI search audit the same as an SEO audit? No, but they overlap. An SEO audit asks whether pages can rank. An AI search audit asks whether pages can be used as sources and whether your brand is described correctly in the answer. A blocked or empty page fails both. Which tools can run an AI search audit? You can do it by hand with a spreadsheet, the AI tools, Search Console's Generative AI performance report and Bing Webmaster Tools' AI Performance report. SEO suites such as Ahrefs Brand Radar and the Semrush AI Visibility Toolkit and stand-alone trackers can repeat it at scale. Test by hand first so you can judge their numbers. How often should you repeat an AI search audit? Every quarter, and after any robots.txt, CDN, firewall, template or rebrand change. That is our recommendation. Keep every run's sheet so you can tell a real change from noise. What does an agency AI search audit include? It should give you the prompt list, the raw answers, a map of the sources behind them, a ranked list of fixes and a date to repeat the test. Be wary of a report that is only a score or that promises placement in AI answers, because the AI companies do not publish how they choose sources. copy_text: Home Blog AI Growth Systems AI Lead Generation: How It Works, Tools and… Guide AI Growth Systems AI Lead Generation: How It Works, Tools and How to Build a System AI lead generation explained: what AI can and cannot do, the five layers of a system, tools by layer, a nine-step build, speed to first response, email law and a worked example. Jamil Ahmed Published 1 Nov 2026 Updated 15 Nov 2026 15 Chapters 12 Min read A to Z Glossary 01 What is AI lead generation? 1 min 02 What can AI do in lead generation, and what can it not do? 1 min 03 The five layers of an AI lead generation system 1 min 04 Which AI lead generation tools exist? 1 min 05 How do you build an AI lead generation system? 2 min 06 Why does speed to first response matter? 1 min 07 Do AI-generated leads convert better than organic search leads? 1 min 08 How do buyers find you through AI tools? 1 min 09 How should AI score leads and personalize messages? 1 min 10 What does the law say about AI outreach? 2 min 11 Worked example: a 12-person B2B firm 1 min 12 How do you measure AI lead generation? 1 min 13 What are the common mistakes? 1 min 14 Our interest in this topic 1 min 15 Final thoughts 1 min Chapter 01 of 15 0% read Chapters 0% 01 What is AI lead generation? 02 What can AI do in lead generation, and what can it not do? 03 The five layers of an AI lead generation system 04 Which AI lead generation tools exist? 05 How do you build an AI lead generation system? 06 Why does speed to first response matter? 07 Do AI-generated leads convert better than organic search leads? 08 How do buyers find you through AI tools? 09 How should AI score leads and personalize messages? 10 What does the law say about AI outreach? 11 Worked example: a 12-person B2B firm 12 How do you measure AI lead generation? 13 What are the common mistakes? 14 Our interest in this topic 15 Final thoughts About 12 min in total Short answer AI lead generation uses AI to find, qualify, reach and follow up with prospects: building lists, adding data, scoring fit and intent, drafting first messages, routing leads and nurturing the rest. It works best as a system with five layers and a person reviewing output, and it must follow email and privacy law. Measure qualified leads and customers, not volume. 01 Build a system with five layers: capture, enrichment, qualification, routing and first response, and nurture. All write to one CRM record. 02 There is no single AI lead tool. Vendors describe a stack, with one tool per layer. Names in vendor guides are examples, not endorsements. 03 A 2011 HBR study of 1.25 million leads found contact within an hour made qualification nearly seven times likelier. It is old, but speed still matters. 04 The FTC says CAN-SPAM makes no exception for business email, and each violating email can carry penalties of up to $53,088. 05 We found no study showing AI-generated leads convert better than organic search leads. Compare your own results by source. 06 Review the first 50 to 100 AI drafts. One builder reports errors in roughly 10 to 20% of first-batch drafts. 07 G2 and Semrush surveys show buyers use AI to shortlist vendors, so being named correctly in AI answers is part of inbound lead generation. AI lead generation means using AI to find, qualify, reach and follow up with prospects: building lists, adding data, scoring fit and intent, drafting first messages, routing leads to the right person and nurturing the rest. It works best as a system with clear stages and a human checking the output, not as one tool that “does leads”. It also carries real risks: wrong facts in messages, damaged sender reputation and breaches of email and privacy law. This guide explains how AI lead generation works, which tools fit each stage, how to build a system step by step, and how to stay within the law. It includes a worked example, a note on speed to first response and an honest look at claims that AI leads convert better. We cite only sources we could read at the publisher, and we say when a figure is old, a vendor’s own data or a survey. 01 Chapter 1 · 1 min What is AI lead generation? Lead generation is the work of getting interested people or companies into your sales process. AI adds software that can read text, research companies, classify intent and write drafts. So an AI lead generation process can read a free-text inquiry and judge how urgent it is, research a company website and summarize what it does, score a lead against your ideal customer profile, and draft a first reply that refers to the prospect’s real situation. Sales teams still talk to people. The software handles the repeat work before and after. There are two directions. Inbound means people find you and ask, through your site, search, AI tools, ads or referrals. Outbound means you choose prospects and contact them, usually by email, phone or social messages. AI can help with both, and the rules and risks differ. End of chapter 1 Next: What can AI do in lead generation, and what can it not do? → 02 Chapter 2 · 1 min What can AI do in lead generation, and what can it not do? Job Where AI helps Where a person must decide Find prospects Builds lists from your ideal customer description and public data Who you may lawfully contact, and the ideal customer itself Add data Fills in role, size, tools and recent news Whether the data is accurate and was gathered lawfully Score leads Weighs fit and intent signals, and reads free-text inquiries The scoring rules, and what counts as qualified Write messages Drafts a first email or reply that uses real context Tone, accuracy and approval before sending Route and follow up Assigns leads and sends reminders Who owns the relationship Nurture Tailors email content by role and interest Offers, promises and timing Hold conversations Answers simple questions in chat and books meetings Complex questions, pricing, and anything sensitive One practitioner who builds these systems says that, in the first batch of AI-drafted emails, the model gets the tone wrong, the trigger wrong or invents a fact in roughly 10 to 20% of cases, and recommends human review of the first 50 to 100 drafts. That is one builder’s experience and not a study, but it matches a simple rule: do not let a model send unreviewed messages to real prospects until you have tested it. End of chapter 2 Next: The five layers of an AI lead generation system → Reinforce Lab service · Lead Generation Systems Want a lead system built around qualified leads? Reinforce Lab starts with a free diagnostic of your Google and AI search visibility and a 90-day plan. See lead generation systems → Or get a free diagnostic first 03 Chapter 3 · 1 min The five layers of an AI lead generation system A working system has five connected layers that all write to one customer record. Capture. Website forms, chat, landing pages, ad lead forms, events and outbound lists. Tag every lead with its source. Enrichment. Add company size, industry, location and role, from your CRM or a data provider, so you are not relying on what the person typed. Qualification. Score each lead against your ideal customer profile. Combine fit, from the data, with intent, from behavior such as pricing page visits or a demo request. Routing and first response. Assign the lead to an owner or a sequence, and send a fast first reply, drafted by AI and reviewed by a person. Nurture. Keep lower-priority leads warm with useful email until they are ready. Missing any layer creates a leak, where good prospects slip away. Our lead generation systems service builds this structure, and our AI workflow automation page covers the links between the tools. End of chapter 3 Next: Which AI lead generation tools exist? → 04 Chapter 4 · 1 min Which AI lead generation tools exist? There is no single platform that does everything. Vendors describe a stack of tools, one for each layer. The table shows the categories with example names that vendors’ own guides list. They are examples, not recommendations, and prices and features change, so check each vendor’s current page. Layer What the tool does Example tools named in vendor guides Data and enrichment Finds companies and contacts, adds firmographic detail Apollo, ZoomInfo, Clay, Hunter Email verification Checks that addresses are real before sending ZeroBounce, NeverBounce, Hunter Intent and signals Shows which accounts are worth contacting now 6sense, Leadfeeder Orchestration Moves data between tools and applies rules Zapier, Make, n8n, Clay Sending and deliverability Sends campaigns and protects sender reputation Instantly, Smartlead, lemlist CRM and nurture Tracks every contact, runs sequences HubSpot, Pipedrive, Salesforce, ActiveCampaign Chat and capture Answers questions and collects details on your site Intercom, Tidio, HubSpot chat Many tools have a free tier or a trial, and you can run a small system with one CRM and one automation tool. We found no independent data on typical tool costs, so test with a small plan first. Large language models such as ChatGPT or Claude can also research a company and draft text, but they need a real data source for facts. A model without data will guess. End of chapter 4 Next: How do you build an AI lead generation system? → 05 Chapter 5 · 2 min How do you build an AI lead generation system? Step 1: Write your ideal customer profile Review your closed-won deals. Write down the company type, size, roles, problems, triggers and the reasons you lost. Everything that follows depends on this. Step 2: Pick one system of record Every lead from every source should land in one CRM. Without this, reports and duplicate checks break. Step 3: Connect your capture points Link forms, chat, ad lead forms and event lists to the CRM, and tag each lead with its source. Step 4: Add enrichment Use your CRM’s enrichment or a data tool to fill in company and role data. Keep the source of each field, and check a sample for accuracy. Step 5: Build simple scoring first Start with a few clear fit and intent signals. Each month, compare scores with which leads became customers, and adjust. Scoring that nobody reviews drifts away from reality. Step 6: Set routing rules Assign high-priority leads to a named owner at once, with a message in Slack or email. Send mid-priority leads to a sequence, and log low-priority leads without contacting them. Step 7: Draft first replies with AI, and review them Have the model draft a reply that uses the lead’s own words and context. A person approves each draft at first. Widen the freedom only for message types with a low error rate. Step 8: Build nurture paths Enroll lower-priority leads in short email sequences based on their role and interest, with a clear way to opt out. Step 9: Measure and improve Track response time, conversion by source and score, and pipeline created. Review the results each month and change one thing at a time. End of chapter 5 Next: Why does speed to first response matter? → 06 Chapter 6 · 1 min Why does speed to first response matter? A widely cited study in Harvard Business Review, from 2011, looked at 1.25 million sales leads received by 29 B2C and 13 B2B companies in the US. It found that firms that contacted a lead within an hour were nearly seven times as likely to qualify it, meaning to have a meaningful conversation with a key decision maker, as firms that waited even an hour longer, and more than 60 times as likely as firms that waited 24 hours or more. In a separate audit of 2,241 US companies, only 37% responded to a web-generated test lead within an hour, and 23% never responded. This data is old and comes from before generative AI. Even so, it shows why a fast, accurate first reply is the part of the system where AI can help most. Draft the reply with AI, route it to a person and keep a human in the loop for anything that is not routine. End of chapter 6 Next: Do AI-generated leads convert better than organic search leads? → 07 Chapter 7 · 1 min Do AI-generated leads convert better than organic search leads? We found no study that shows this. The question assumes AI-generated leads are one kind of lead, and they are not: a lead is a lead whichever source it comes from. What we can say, from sources we read, is that the channel and the quality of the process matter. First Page Sage, an SEO agency, published funnel benchmarks from more than 50 B2B SaaS clients. In that data, SEO visitors became leads at 2.1% and paid search at 0.7%, and 51% of marketing-qualified leads from SEO became sales-qualified leads against 26% from paid search. That is one agency’s client data and not a test of AI. It is a reminder that organic channels can produce strong leads, and that your own numbers by source are the only fair test. End of chapter 7 Next: How do buyers find you through AI tools? → 08 Chapter 8 · 1 min How do buyers find you through AI tools? AI also changes inbound lead generation, because buyers now use AI to build shortlists. G2 surveyed 1,169 B2B decision-makers in April 2025: 79% said AI search had changed how they research, and generative AI chatbots were the top source influencing vendor shortlists at 17.1%. Semrush surveyed 643 US B2B professionals in 2026, and of the 519 who use AI at work, 66% regularly use it to research vendors. Both are vendor surveys with their own limits. So part of a lead generation plan is to be named and described correctly when buyers ask AI tools. Our guides to generative engine optimization and checking if AI tools mention your brand explain how. End of chapter 8 Next: How should AI score leads and personalize messages? → 09 Chapter 9 · 1 min How should AI score leads and personalize messages? Keep scoring simple and visible. One practitioner who builds these systems scores each account on four separate dimensions, such as how well its tools fit, hiring signals, a recent trigger event and match to the ideal customer profile, and routes by total score: high scores go to a person, middle scores to a nurture sequence and low scores are logged and not contacted. That is one builder’s design, not a standard, but the pattern is sound because the rules are inspectable and the routing is not another model call. For personalization, the goal is a short message that refers to something real, such as a hire, a product launch or a question the person asked, and ties it to one concrete benefit. A generic “I noticed your impressive growth” line is worse than none. Check that every personal detail is true before sending. Be careful with social platforms, too. Some ban scraping and automated collection in their terms, so read the terms of any network before you gather data from it, and prefer contact data that people gave you or that came from a lawful source. End of chapter 9 Next: What does the law say about AI outreach? → 10 Chapter 10 · 2 min What does the law say about AI outreach? This is general information, not legal advice. Take advice for your markets, because rules differ by country and by channel. In the US, the FTC’s CAN-SPAM guide says the law covers all commercial messages, meaning email whose primary purpose is the commercial advertisement or promotion of a product or service. It says the law makes no exception for business-to-business email, and that each separate email in violation can be subject to penalties of up to $53,088. The main requirements are: Do not use false or misleading header information. The From, To, Reply-To and routing details must be accurate and identify the sender. Do not use deceptive subject lines. Identify the message as an ad, clearly and conspicuously. Include your valid physical postal address. Tell recipients clearly how to opt out, and make sure your spam filter does not block opt-out requests. Honor opt-out requests within 10 business days. The opt-out method must work for at least 30 days after you send. Monitor what others do for you. If you hire a company to send email, both you and the sender may be held responsible. Rules in the EU and UK are often stricter about consent and about how personal data is collected and used, and a tool does not make you compliant by itself. Public data is not automatically free to scrape or use for marketing, and some platforms ban scraping in their terms. Check where each contact came from, keep the source on the record, keep one suppression list that every tool checks, and use a person to review messages. If you are unsure, ask a lawyer who knows your markets. Also treat deliverability as a risk. Sending many messages from new domains can damage sender reputation, so start small and use authenticated domains you own. End of chapter 10 Next: Worked example: a 12-person B2B firm → 11 Chapter 11 · 1 min Worked example: a 12-person B2B firm This is an illustration, not a client result. Imagine a firm that sells compliance training to mid-sized clinics. It has a website form that gets about 40 inquiries a month and a small outbound list. Replies take about two days. The team writes its ideal customer profile from 30 closed deals. It connects the form, a chat widget and its email to one CRM. It uses AI to read each free-text inquiry, tag the topic and urgency, and draft a reply that answers the person’s question and offers two meeting times. A salesperson reviews and sends each draft, with a target of under one hour in working hours. High-fit leads go to a named owner, and others enter a three-email sequence with an opt-out. For outbound, the team builds a list of 150 clinics from public sources, checks each against its rules, and sends a few reviewed, plain messages with its address and an opt-out. It tracks reply rate and meetings, and pauses at the first sign of spam complaints. After 90 days it compares response time, meetings and closed deals by source. The result may be small or large. The system makes it measurable. End of chapter 11 Next: How do you measure AI lead generation? → 12 Chapter 12 · 1 min How do you measure AI lead generation? Time to first response for inbound leads. Conversion from lead to qualified lead to customer , by source and by score. Cost per qualified lead , including tool costs and staff time. Reply rate, bounce rate and complaint rate for outbound email. Pipeline and revenue by source , in your CRM. Error rate of AI drafts , counted from the review step. Compare results with your own past numbers first. Public benchmarks vary, and most come from a single vendor’s clients. End of chapter 12 Next: What are the common mistakes? → 13 Chapter 13 · 1 min What are the common mistakes? Buying a tool before defining the customer. The tool will scale a vague target. Sending unreviewed AI messages. Wrong facts and odd tone cost trust. Scraping contacts without checking the rules. Public does not mean free to use. Ignoring deliverability. Spam complaints can block your whole domain. Complex scoring too early. Start simple and learn from outcomes. Splitting leads across tools. Keep one system of record. Measuring volume, not quality. Count qualified leads and customers. End of chapter 13 Next: Our interest in this topic → 14 Chapter 14 · 1 min Our interest in this topic Reinforce Lab sells lead generation, automation and AI search services. Nothing here is paid placement, and we do not endorse the example tools named above. Jamil Ahmed, who wrote this guide, is a Semrush Ambassador, and Reinforce Lab uses affiliate links for some tools. Read our FTC and affiliate disclosure . You can read about our lead generation systems and get your free diagnostic . End of chapter 14 Next: Final thoughts → 15 Chapter 15 · 1 min Final thoughts AI lead generation works when it is a system: a clear customer profile, one record of every lead, simple scoring, fast and reviewed first replies, honest nurture and the right legal checks. Start small, measure by qualified leads and customers, and widen only where the data shows it works. Back matter Glossary A to Z C CRM Customer relationship management software that stores every lead and contact. E Enrichment Adding data, such as company size and role, to a lead record. I ICP Ideal customer profile: a written description of the customers you want most. L Lead A person or company that has shown interest or fits your target and may become a customer. M MQL and SQL A marketing-qualified lead fits your market, and a sales-qualified lead has shown real buying interest. S Suppression list A list of people you must not contact, such as those who opted out. Questions FAQs What is AI lead generation? Using AI to find, qualify, reach and follow up with prospects: building lists, adding company data, scoring fit and intent, drafting first messages, routing leads and nurturing the rest. People still review messages and talk to buyers. How does AI lead generation work? A system captures leads from forms, chat and lists, enriches them with company and role data, scores them against your ideal customer, routes them to an owner or sequence, drafts a first reply for review and nurtures lower-priority leads. How do I use AI for lead generation? Write your ideal customer profile, pick one CRM, connect capture points, add enrichment, build simple scoring, set routing rules, use AI to draft reviewed first replies, build nurture paths and measure qualified leads and customers. What are the best AI tools for lead generation? There is no single best tool. Vendors describe a stack with tools for data, verification, orchestration, sending and a CRM. Examples they name include Apollo, Clay, Hunter, Zapier, n8n, HubSpot and Instantly. Test a small plan and check current terms. Are there free AI tools for lead generation? Many tools offer a free tier or a trial, and you can run a small system with one CRM and one automation tool. Check each vendor's current terms, since features and limits change. Are AI lead generation tools GDPR compliant? A tool does not make you compliant by itself. You are responsible for where contact data came from, your legal basis, consent rules for email and keeping a suppression list. Rules in the EU and UK differ from the US, so take legal advice for your markets. Is cold email legal for B2B in the US? The FTC says CAN-SPAM covers all commercial email and makes no exception for business email. You need accurate headers, honest subject lines, an ad disclosure, a postal address and a working opt-out honored within 10 business days. Penalties can reach $53,088 per email. Do AI-generated leads convert better than organic search leads? We found no study that shows it. A lead is a lead whatever its source. One SEO agency's B2B SaaS client data shows SEO leads reaching sales at 51% against 26% for paid search, but it is not a test of AI. Compare your own results by source. How fast should you respond to a new lead? As fast as you can. A 2011 HBR study of 1.25 million leads found that contact within an hour made a lead nearly seven times likelier to qualify than contact an hour later. The data is old, but it supports fast, reviewed first replies. What are the risks of AI lead generation? Wrong facts in messages, damaged sender reputation, breaches of email and privacy law, poor data and brand damage. Reduce them with human review, small sends, authenticated domains, source records and a shared suppression list.
