An AI visibility score is a single number, usually from 0 to 100, that a tool builds from how often AI answers name your brand, link to your site and place you ahead of competitors. There is no standard formula. Each tool picks its own inputs and weights, so a score of 40 from one tool is not the same as a 40 from another. The useful way to read a score is as a trend from one tool, with the parts shown separately and an honest margin for noise. This guide explains what the score measures, shows the formulas that several tools publish, and applies two of them to the same sample data so you can see how the numbers differ. It also covers how to calculate your own, what a “good” score means, and how to report it. We cite only pages we could read at the publisher, and we state when a source is a vendor’s own documentation. 01 Chapter 1 · 1 min What is an AI visibility score? An AI visibility score is a composite metric. It condenses several counts from a fixed set of AI answers into one figure. The counts come from running a list of buyer questions through tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Google’s AI Overviews, then recording what each answer says. The goal is to show, in one number, whether AI tools include your brand when buyers ask about your category. You may also see the phrases “AI brand visibility score” and “AI visibility”. They mean the same idea. Our guide to checking if AI tools mention your brand shows how to run the underlying test by hand. End of chapter 1 Next: What goes into an AI visibility score? → 02 Chapter 2 · 1 min What goes into an AI visibility score? Most tools use some mix of the following parts. The names differ, but the ideas are alike. Part What it measures Simple formula Mention rate How often an answer names your brand Answers that name you divided by all answers Citation rate How often an answer links to your site as a source Answers that cite your domain divided by all answers Prompt coverage How many different questions name you at least once Prompts where you appear divided by prompts asked Position How early you are named in an answer that lists brands Often 1 for first, 1/2 for second, 1/3 for third Share of voice Your mentions compared with all brand mentions in your set Your mentions divided by mentions of you and your competitors Sentiment How the answer describes you A positive, neutral or negative label A mention and a citation are different. An answer can name you without a link, or link to your page without naming you. Keep them in separate columns. They need different fixes. End of chapter 2 Next: How do different tools calculate it? → Reinforce Lab service · SEO & AI Search Audit Want the parts of your score, with denominators? Reinforce Lab starts with a free diagnostic of your Google and AI search visibility and a 90-day plan. See the AI search audit → Or get a free diagnostic first 03 Chapter 3 · 1 min How do different tools calculate it? Several vendors publish their formulas. Reading them shows that “AI visibility score” is a label, not a shared standard. The table uses each vendor’s own documentation. Tool Formula, as published Notes RankRaft 100 × (0.45 × mention rate + 0.35 × citation rate + 0.20 × prompt coverage) Leaves position out on purpose. Shows a 95% margin. AnswerixAI 100 × (0.6 × mention rate + 0.25 × citation rate + 0.15 × position factor) Scales the position factor down when few answers name you. cloro 100 × (0.6 × mention rate + 0.25 × citation rate + 0.15 × position factor) Same weights as AnswerixAI. Position is the mean of 1 divided by position. BugViso 0.35 × visibility + 0.20 × share of voice + 0.20 × position + 0.15 × citations + 0.10 × sentiment Counts unbranded prompts only, and averages engines equally. MentionOwl Not published Its guide says you cannot recompute the headline number. Am I Cited’s guide describes a “typical” weighting of about 25% for mention frequency, 25% for citation rate, 20% for position, 15% for query coverage and 15% for share of voice, and says there is no industry-standard formula. Verticality makes the same point: a score means something only once you know its questions, engines, time window and denominator. End of chapter 3 Next: Worked example: one set of answers, different scores → 04 Chapter 4 · 1 min Worked example: one set of answers, different scores This example uses the sample data in RankRaft’s documentation. It shows 10 prompts run across 3 engines in a week, which gives 210 answers. You are named in 63 answers, cited in 21 answers, and named at least once for 6 of the 10 prompts. The arithmetic below is ours. Mention rate: 63 divided by 210 is 30%. Citation rate: 21 divided by 210 is 10%. Prompt coverage: 6 divided by 10 is 60%. Now apply two published formulas. RankRaft: 100 × (0.45 × 0.30 + 0.35 × 0.10 + 0.20 × 0.60) = 100 × (0.135 + 0.035 + 0.12) = 29 . AnswerixAI: this formula needs a position factor, which the sample does not give. We assume that on average you are named at position 2, so the raw factor is 0.5. AnswerixAI scales it by mentions divided by mentions plus 20, which is 63 divided by 83, or 0.76, so the factor becomes about 0.38. The score is 100 × (0.6 × 0.30 + 0.25 × 0.10 + 0.15 × 0.38) = 100 × (0.18 + 0.025 + 0.057), which is about 26 . The same 210 answers give a mention rate of 30%, a score of 29 from one tool and about 26 from another. Neither is wrong. They weight the parts differently, and the second uses a position input we assumed. This is why you should never compare a score from one tool with a score from another. End of chapter 4 Next: How noisy is the score? → 05 Chapter 5 · 1 min How noisy is the score? Answers vary from run to run. SparkToro had 600 volunteers run 12 prompts through ChatGPT, Claude and Google’s AI features 2,961 times, and found less than a 1 in 100 chance of getting the same list of brands twice for the same prompt. So a score from one run is a snapshot. RankRaft shows the effect in its own formula. It gives a 95% margin of 100 × 1.96 × the square root of p(1 − p) divided by n, where p is the mention rate and n is the number of answers. With a 30% mention rate and 210 answers, that is about plus or minus 6 points, by our arithmetic. The formula treats every answer as independent, so the true uncertainty may be larger, since answers to the same prompt are related. The lesson is that small changes in a score may be noise. Use more prompts, repeat runs and read trends over weeks. End of chapter 5 Next: Why do two honest tools show different scores? → 06 Chapter 6 · 1 min Why do two honest tools show different scores? Different weights. One tool may weight mentions at 60% and another at 45%. Different prompts. A prompt set built from your sales calls gives a different result from a generic set. Branded prompts. A question that names you is answered with your name almost every time. BugViso reports that all 120 branded answers in its data named the brand, and so it counts unbranded prompts only. Different engines. A tool that tracks two engines gives a different number from one that tracks five. Different counting rules. Some tools leave out failed or empty answers. RankRaft leaves out runs where Google shows no AI Overview, instead of counting them as misses. Different timing. Weekly, daily and one-off checks smooth noise in different ways. End of chapter 6 Next: Does the score include Google AI Overviews? → 07 Chapter 7 · 1 min Does the score include Google AI Overviews? Check the tool’s documentation, because tools differ. Google shows an AI Overview for only some searches, so a score that counts every run as a miss when no overview appears will look lower than one that leaves those runs out. RankRaft, for example, says it counts only answers that were actually shown, and leaves out a run where Google shows no AI Overview, instead of scoring it as “not mentioned”. Some tools do not track Google’s AI features at all, and some also blend ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Claude with equal or unequal weights. When you compare periods, make sure the engine list, the prompt list and these counting rules did not change. For Google’s own data, use the Generative AI performance report in Search Console, which shows impressions in AI Overviews and AI Mode for your site. End of chapter 7 Next: How do you calculate your own AI visibility score? → 08 Chapter 8 · 1 min How do you calculate your own AI visibility score? Write 10 to 15 buyer questions in your customers’ words, mostly without your brand name. Pick your engines and run each prompt three times in each, in a fresh session. Save the full answers. Record, for each answer, whether you are named, whether your site is cited, who else is named and in what order. Count the parts. Mention rate, citation rate and prompt coverage are easy to compute in a spreadsheet. Add share of voice against three to five named competitors. Report the parts first. Show each number with its denominator, for example “named in 63 of 210 answers”. Only then combine them, if you must have one number. Publish the weights, keep them fixed and note the date and the prompt set. A simple sheet is enough. Our guide to AI brand visibility tools compares software that does this at scale. End of chapter 8 Next: What is a good AI visibility score? → 09 Chapter 9 · 1 min What is a good AI visibility score? We found no reliable public benchmark. A score depends on the prompts, engines and formula, so a “good” number for one tool says nothing about another. Share of voice also depends on how many brands the tools name in your market. If the tools name three brands per answer, a share near 33% is average. If they name 15, a share near 7% is average. So judge yourself in three ways. Compare with the competitors in your own test, with the same tool and prompts. Compare with your own baseline over time. And look at the parts, because a rising mention rate with a flat citation rate tells a different story from the reverse. Be wary of any vendor that offers a grade such as “good” or “excellent” without showing its method. End of chapter 9 Next: What is AI brand monitoring? → 10 Chapter 10 · 1 min What is AI brand monitoring? AI brand monitoring is the ongoing version of this test. Software runs your prompts on a schedule, stores each answer and shows the trend, often with alerts when something changes, such as a new competitor or a wrong fact. It is useful when your prompt list or your markets outgrow a spreadsheet. A tool still needs a person to act on what it finds. Test any tool against a hand baseline before you rely on it. End of chapter 10 Next: How do you improve a low score? → 11 Chapter 11 · 1 min How do you improve a low score? Read the parts and fix the weakest one. If this is low It may mean Start with Mention rate AI tools do not know you, or rarely pick you Clear facts, answer-first pages and honest mentions on other sites Citation rate Your pages are not used as sources Crawler access, readable HTML, sourced answers. See how to rank in AI Overviews . Prompt coverage You appear for few questions Pages for the questions you miss, built from sales calls Share of voice Competitors are named far more often Study the sources the answers cite, and earn a place on them Sentiment The description is old or negative Fix the pages and profiles the answers use Our guide to generative engine optimization explains the method in more detail. One more rule helps. Decide in advance what counts as a mention, and write it down. A brand name inside a longer word should not count, a repeated mention inside one answer should count once, and a cited link that is not named in the text is a citation, not a mention. Tools that publish their counting rules, such as AnswerixAI and cloro, say that matching is by whole word and that links are removed before the text count. A clear rule keeps the numbers the same from one month to the next, even when different people run the test. End of chapter 11 Next: How should you report it to leadership? → 12 Chapter 12 · 1 min How should you report it to leadership? Keep the report short and honest. Show the three or four parts with their denominators, the trend over at least three periods, the margin or the number of runs, and the list of actions taken. Say which tool and prompt set you used. Avoid a single headline number without the parts behind it, and never compare it with a score from another tool. Add the link to business results, such as demo requests from pages you updated, when you can measure them. End of chapter 12 Next: What does a simple scoring sheet look like? → 13 Chapter 13 · 1 min What does a simple scoring sheet look like? You do not need software to start. This layout gives you every part of the score. The three rows are made up to show the format. Prompt ID Engine Run Named Cited Order named Competitors named P-03 ChatGPT 1 Yes No 3 of 5 A, B, C, D P-03 ChatGPT 2 No No none A, B, E P-03 Perplexity 1 Yes Yes 1 of 4 A, C, F From this sheet you can count mention rate, citation rate, prompt coverage and share of voice with simple formulas. Add a date and the exact prompt text in another tab. Keep the sheet after every test. In six months, the history is more useful than any single score. End of chapter 13 Next: How does the score differ for different businesses? → 14 Chapter 14 · 1 min How does the score differ for different businesses? B2B software: Comparison and “best for” questions drive shortlists, so include them. Citations from review sites and your own comparison pages matter. Local and service firms: Include questions with a city name. Answers often depend on listings and reviews, so check those sources. Online stores: Include product and “is it worth it” questions. Product data and reviews on other sites matter. Publishers and educators: Citation rate may matter more than mention rate, since the aim is to be the source. In every case, build the prompt set from real buyer questions. A score based on questions your buyers never ask tells you nothing. End of chapter 14 Next: What questions will leaders ask about the score? → 15 Chapter 15 · 1 min What questions will leaders ask about the score? Be ready for these three. “Is it going up?” Show the trend, the number of runs and the margin. “Why is a competitor higher?” Show the source map: which sites the answers cite for them and not for you. “What did we do about it?” Show the list of fixes, with dates and the pages changed. If you cannot answer the third question, the score is a dashboard and not a program. End of chapter 15 Next: What are the common mistakes? → 16 Chapter 16 · 1 min What are the common mistakes? Trusting one number. Keep mentions, citations and share of voice separate. Comparing tools. Scores from different formulas are not the same measure. Counting branded prompts. They inflate the result. Running each prompt once. The same prompt gives different answers. Ignoring the margin. A move of a few points can be noise. Changing prompts between periods. You can no longer compare. Chasing the score. The goal is accurate, useful presence, not a number. End of chapter 16 Next: Our interest in this topic → 17 Chapter 17 · 1 min Our interest in this topic Reinforce Lab sells search and AI search services. We do not sell an AI visibility score or a tracking tool, and nothing here is paid placement. Jamil Ahmed, who wrote this guide, is a Semrush Ambassador, and Reinforce Lab uses affiliate links for some tools. Read our FTC and affiliate disclosure . Our free diagnostic reports the parts with their denominators. You can get your free diagnostic or read about our SEO and AI search audit . End of chapter 17 Next: Final thoughts → 18 Chapter 18 · 1 min Final thoughts An AI visibility score is a summary, not a measurement of the truth. Read the parts, know the formula, repeat the runs and watch the trend. Use the score to decide what to fix next, and judge the work by accurate answers and by the leads that follow. Back matter Glossary A to Z A AI visibility score A number, usually 0 to 100, that summarizes how often AI answers name or cite your brand. C Citation rate The share of answers that link to your site as a source. M Margin The range within which a measured rate may move because of chance. M Mention rate The share of answers that name your brand. P Prompt coverage The share of prompts where your brand appears at least once. S Share of voice Your mentions divided by all brand mentions in your set. Questions FAQs What is an AI visibility score? A single number, usually 0 to 100, that a tool builds from how often AI answers name your brand, link to your site and place you ahead of competitors, across a fixed set of questions. Each tool uses its own formula. What is the AI brand visibility score? It is another name for the AI visibility score. It summarizes mentions, citations and sometimes share of voice, position and sentiment for your brand across AI answers to a fixed prompt list. How is an AI visibility score calculated? Tools count the answers that name you, the answers that cite your domain and the prompts where you appear, then weight them. RankRaft publishes 0.45 mention rate, 0.35 citation rate and 0.20 prompt coverage. AnswerixAI publishes 0.6, 0.25 and 0.15 for position. Is there a standard formula for an AI visibility score? No. Vendors choose their own inputs and weights, and some do not publish them. A 40 from one tool is not the same measurement as a 40 from another, so only compare scores from the same tool and prompt set. What is a good visibility score on AI platforms? We found no reliable public benchmark. A good score depends on the prompts, engines, formula and competitors. Compare yourself with competitors in your own test and with your own baseline over time. What is AI visibility? How often and how accurately AI tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Google's AI Overviews name your brand, link to your site and describe you when people ask questions about your field. How accurate is an AI visibility score? It is directional. SparkToro found under a 1 in 100 chance of the same brand list twice for one prompt. RankRaft's formula gives about a 6 point margin at a 30% mention rate and 210 answers, and real uncertainty may be larger. Should branded prompts count in an AI visibility score? Usually not. A question that names you is answered with your name almost every time. BugViso reports that all 120 branded answers in its data named the brand, so it counts unbranded prompts only. How do I calculate my own AI visibility score? Write 10 to 15 unbranded buyer questions, run each three times in each engine, record mentions, citations and competitors, then count the parts with denominators. Combine them only if you publish fixed weights. What is AI brand monitoring? Software that runs your prompts on a schedule, stores the answers and shows trends and alerts. It helps when a spreadsheet is no longer enough, and still needs a person to act on the findings. Avoid any firm that guarantees citations or rankings, because no one controls AI answers. 01 Judge the method, not the label. GEO, AEO, LLM SEO and AI SEO are used for similar work. 02 Ask for a baseline, a prompt list you approve and raw answers, not a single visibility score. 03 OpenServed reviewed 142 agency GEO case studies: 27% reported no AI metric, 13% tied results to leads or revenue and none stated a budget. 04 No one can guarantee a number one ranking, says Google. A generative engine optimization agency helps your brand get found, understood and cited by AI tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Google’s AI Overviews. To choose a good one, look for a method you can inspect: a prompt list you approve, a baseline measured before work starts, named changes, honest limits and clear ownership of your data. Walk away from any firm that guarantees citations or rankings, because no one controls AI answers. This guide explains what these agencies do, whether you need one, twelve questions to ask with good and poor answers, red flags, how to compare proposals and what the cost depends on. We cite only sources we could read at the publisher. Reinforce Lab is one of the agencies you may compare, so we say at the end how to test us the same way. 01 Chapter 1 · 1 min What does a generative engine optimization agency do? Generative engine optimization, or GEO, is work that improves how often and how accurately AI tools name your brand and cite your pages. Our guide to generative engine optimization explains the method. An agency usually sells some mix of these services: A baseline audit. A fixed list of buyer questions run through several AI tools, with mentions, citations, descriptions and competitors recorded. Our AI search audit guide covers the method. Technical fixes. Crawler access, indexing, rendering, structured data and site facts. Content work. Answer-first pages, comparison pages, updates and sourced evidence. Off-site work. Profiles, reviews, digital PR and presence on the sites the AI answers cite. Measurement. Repeated prompt tests, Search Console and Bing reports, and AI referral traffic in analytics. The names vary. Some firms say GEO, others AEO, LLM SEO or AI SEO. Google says that from its point of view, optimizing for generative AI search is still SEO, and it advises care with third-party “AEO” or “GEO” advice. So judge the work, not the label. End of chapter 1 Next: Do you need an agency at all? → 02 Chapter 2 · 1 min Do you need an agency at all? Not always. The options are in-house, an agency or a tool. The table shows when each tends to fit. Option Fits when Watch for In-house You have an SEO lead, a writer and developer time Nobody owns off-site work or measurement Agency You lack time or skills, need a plan, or need outreach and technical fixes Overlap with your SEO provider, vague scope Tool only You want monitoring and have people to act on it A dashboard that nobody acts on. See our guide to AI brand visibility tools . Google’s own advice on hiring an SEO applies here too. It says some sites do not need a hire, and it warns that no one can guarantee a number one ranking on Google, and to beware of firms that claim a special relationship with Google or a “priority submit”. End of chapter 2 Next: What does the evidence say about GEO agencies? → Reinforce Lab service · Generative Engine Optimization Want a baseline you can judge us by? Reinforce Lab starts with a free diagnostic of your Google and AI search visibility and a 90-day plan. See generative engine optimization → Or get a free diagnostic first 03 Chapter 3 · 1 min What does the evidence say about GEO agencies? Independent evidence is thin, and we found none on average fees. Four sources help you set expectations. Agency case studies are often weak. OpenServed analyzed 142 GEO case studies published by 68 agencies. It found that 27% reported no AI metric, only 13% tied AI search to leads or revenue, and only 5 of 142 mentioned the prompts they tracked. None of the 142 stated a budget. The median result was measured over six months, and only 15% within three months. This is one directory’s review of agency-published material, classified by its own method, so treat the figures as a rough picture. No one can promise a result. Google says no one can guarantee a number one ranking, and Google says that no third-party tool has access to its internal ranking or AI systems. Answers change. SparkToro had 600 volunteers run 12 prompts through ChatGPT, Claude and Google’s AI features 2,961 times. There was less than a 1 in 100 chance of the same list of brands twice. A good agency reports a rate across many runs, not a rank. Some measurement is free. Google’s Search Console has a Generative AI performance report for AI Overviews and AI Mode impressions, and Bing Webmaster Tools has an AI Performance report for citations in Copilot. A good agency uses both in its baseline. End of chapter 3 Next: Twelve questions to ask a GEO agency → 04 Chapter 4 · 2 min Twelve questions to ask a GEO agency Ask every candidate the same questions and compare the answers in writing. The table shows what a good answer and a poor answer sound like. Question A good answer A poor answer 1. How do you choose the prompts? From your sales calls, tickets and search data, agreed with you, then frozen “We use our standard set”, or most prompts contain your brand name 2. What is our baseline today, by engine? A citation map built before the proposal, per question and per engine One visibility score with no questions behind it 3. How do you measure, and how often? Repeated runs, mentions and citations reported separately, with the numerator and denominator One screenshot, or “we monitor continuously” with no method 4. What will you change on our site? A written list by item, with an approval path “We will optimize your content for AI” 5. How do you handle AI crawlers? Names each bot and separates search from training “Block or allow all AI bots” 6. Which sources outside our site will you work on? A named list of sites the answers already cite for your questions “We will publish more blog posts” 7. Who writes and who checks? Named people, human review, your approval before publishing Volume promises, unnamed writers, AI-only drafts 8. How do you connect citations to leads? Tagged AI referrals, analytics and CRM records “Citations are the KPI” 9. What can you not promise? Placement in any AI answer Guaranteed citations or “position 1 in ChatGPT” 10. Show one case: what changed and when? Dated changes, a before and after per question, caveats about other changes A percentage with no baseline or dates 11. What do we own if we stop? The prompt list, reports, content and tracking data, in usable formats Everything lives in their tool 12. When would you tell us not to buy? A real list, such as no buyer use of AI for your category or basic site problems They can never say no End of chapter 4 Next: What are the red flags? → 05 Chapter 5 · 1 min What are the red flags? A guarantee of citations, rankings or traffic. No baseline before the proposal. Prompts that the agency chose and will not show, or that contain your brand name. One AI tool only, or one screenshot as proof. Reports that stop at mentions or a single score. A price with no deliverables. A claim of a special relationship with Google or any AI company. Work only on your own site, with nothing on the sources the answers use. A contract that locks your data and content in their platform. Unreviewed AI-written content, especially in health, finance and legal fields. Google adds a point worth remembering: you are responsible for what companies you hire do on your site. A deceptive tactic is your problem as well as theirs. End of chapter 5 Next: How much does a generative engine optimization agency cost? → 06 Chapter 6 · 1 min How much does a generative engine optimization agency cost? We found no independent data on typical fees. Published ranges come from agencies’ own pages and guides, and they disagree. OpenServed notes that price ranges in other guides are unsourced and conflict, and that none of the 142 case studies it reviewed states a budget. Instead of comparing monthly numbers, compare what you receive. These things move a price: How many AI tools and markets are tracked. How many prompts are tested, and how often. How much content is written, and by whom. How much technical work your site needs. Whether outreach and digital PR are included. Whether tracking tool fees and CRM reporting are in scope. How much of your team’s time the work needs, for approvals and input. GEO is usually sold in three ways: a one-time audit, a project such as a rebuild of key pages, or a monthly retainer. A fixed audit first is often the safest start. It gives you a baseline and a plan at a known cost, and you can use it to judge a longer program. End of chapter 6 Next: What should the first 90 days look like? → 07 Chapter 7 · 1 min What should the first 90 days look like? A sensible first quarter has a clear order. This is our recommendation, not a standard. Ask any agency to show its own version in writing. Period Work What you should receive Weeks 1 to 2 Agree the prompt list, competitors and success numbers. Run the baseline. Check crawler access and rendering. The prompt list, raw answers, a source map and a technical check Weeks 3 to 6 Fix access, facts and the few pages closest to buying questions. Claim and correct key profiles. A change log with dates and reasons Weeks 7 to 10 Publish or refresh answer-first pages with sourced evidence. Start outreach to the sources the answers cite. The pages, a list of sites approached and the status of each Weeks 11 to 13 Repeat the same prompt test and compare with the baseline. Review Search Console and Bing reports. A report that separates mentions from citations and says what else changed If an agency cannot describe its first 90 days in this much detail, it probably does not have a repeatable method. End of chapter 7 Next: Should one firm run both your SEO and your GEO? → 08 Chapter 8 · 1 min Should one firm run both your SEO and your GEO? It often helps, because the two share a base. Access, indexing, content quality and links serve both, and a plan that treats them separately can send two teams to edit the same pages. If another agency runs your SEO, ask each firm to state who owns which pages and who approves changes. Be careful with any firm that sells GEO as a separate product and ignores SEO, or that asks you to drop a provider that is doing sound work. Google’s own view is that its AI features rely on its core Search systems, so weak SEO tends to limit GEO. End of chapter 8 Next: How do you compare proposals? → 09 Chapter 9 · 1 min How do you compare proposals? Send every candidate the same request: a sample report, a case study with dates, a first-month plan, a list of owners and a proposed scope. Then score each on the same table. Criterion Ask for What to check Method Sample prompts, raw answers, citations Can you inspect the scoring? Fit Your priority questions and competitors Do the prompts reflect real buying decisions? Delivery Owners, approvals, access, change log Can changes ship and be checked? Proof A dated case with a baseline Are limits and other changes stated? Terms Scope, exclusions, notice period, handover Does the fee match the work, and do you own the output? Add the hours your own team will spend. A cheaper retainer that needs several hours a week from your marketing lead can cost more than a dearer one that runs on a short weekly review. End of chapter 9 Next: Worked example: a software company compares three proposals → 10 Chapter 10 · 1 min Worked example: a software company compares three proposals This is an illustration, not a client case. Imagine a 40-person software company that sells to logistics teams. It asks three agencies for the same packet. Agency A sends a visibility score and a promise of top citations in 90 days. Agency B sends a baseline of 15 prompts it chose, several containing the company’s name. Agency C asks for the company’s sales call notes, builds 14 prompts from them with the company, and sends a baseline of 126 answers across three tools, with a map of the sites the answers cite and a list of eight site changes. The company drops Agency A for guaranteeing a result and sending no method. It drops B because the prompts flatter the brand. It starts a fixed-price audit with C, owns the prompt list and the data, and decides on a retainer after reading the results. The choice did not depend on price. It depended on what could be inspected. End of chapter 10 Next: Generative engine optimization agencies for SaaS and B2B → 11 Chapter 11 · 1 min Generative engine optimization agencies for SaaS and B2B If you sell software or B2B services, ask for experience with long buying cycles and comparison pages, since AI tools often answer “X vs Y” and “best tools for Z” questions. Ask which review sites and community threads the answers cite in your category, and how the agency will help you appear on them honestly. Our SaaS SEO guide covers the search side of this work, and our page on B2B SaaS explains how we work with software firms. End of chapter 11 Next: GEO consultant or agency? → 12 Chapter 12 · 1 min GEO consultant or agency? A consultant is a good fit when you need a plan and an expert’s review, and you have people to do the work. An agency fits when you also need the work done. In either case, ask the same twelve questions, and check who does the hands-on work. End of chapter 12 Next: How long does it take to see results? → 13 Chapter 13 · 1 min How long does it take to see results? Access and fact fixes can change retrieval-based answers within weeks. OpenAI says a robots.txt change can take about 24 hours to apply for ChatGPT search. Content and off-site work take longer. OpenServed found a median measurement period of six months in published case studies, but those are agency-chosen examples. Ask what the agency will count at day 30, day 90 and month six, and treat any promise of a date for citations as a red flag. End of chapter 13 Next: What should you own when the work ends? → 14 Chapter 14 · 1 min What should you own when the work ends? Get these in writing: the prompt list, the baseline, access to or exports from the tracking tool, AI referral traffic tagged in your own analytics, and the pages and content created for you. Ask about the notice period and what happens to your data if you leave. End of chapter 14 Next: Which free checks can you run to test an agency’s claims? → 15 Chapter 15 · 1 min Which free checks can you run to test an agency’s claims? You can check much of what an agency tells you without paying for a tool. Open your Search Console and read the Generative AI performance report, which shows impressions in AI Overviews and AI Mode. Open Bing Webmaster Tools and read its AI Performance report for citations in Copilot. Run the agency’s sample prompts yourself, three times in each tool, and compare your results with its screenshots. Check your robots.txt and your firewall for the bots it says it will manage. Ask for the prompt list behind any case study, and run those prompts today. If the agency says a page now ranks or is cited, check that it still does. An agency with a sound method will welcome these checks. End of chapter 15 Next: How do you test Reinforce Lab the same way? → 16 Chapter 16 · 1 min How do you test Reinforce Lab the same way? Reinforce Lab is an agency, so you should apply this guide to us. Our generative engine optimization service starts with a baseline, and our SEO and AI search audit works like the audit above. We will show you a sample report, the method and the limits. We do not guarantee citations. Jamil Ahmed, who wrote this guide, is a Semrush Ambassador, and Reinforce Lab uses affiliate links for some tools. Read our FTC and affiliate disclosure . You can get your free diagnostic and judge it by the questions above. End of chapter 16 Next: What are the common mistakes? → 17 Chapter 17 · 1 min What are the common mistakes? Choosing on price alone. A low fee for vague work can cost more than a clear scope. Letting the agency choose the prompts alone. You know your buyers. Accepting a score as proof. Ask for the answers behind it. Paying a large retainer before a baseline exists. Ignoring overlap with your SEO provider. Agree who does what. Forgetting approvals. The fee runs on while drafts wait. End of chapter 17 Next: Final thoughts → 18 Chapter 18 · 1 min Final thoughts The best generative engine optimization agency for you is the one whose method you can inspect. Ask for a baseline, a prompt list you approve, named changes, honest limits and clear ownership. Start with a fixed audit, compare proposals on deliverables and decide on a longer program after you have read the results. Back matter Glossary A to Z B Baseline A measurement of where you stand before any work starts. C Citation A link to your page shown as a source in an AI answer. G GEO Generative engine optimization: work that helps AI tools cite and recommend your content. P Prompt set A fixed list of buyer questions run through each AI tool. R Retainer A fixed monthly fee for ongoing work. S Source map A count of the sites AI answers cite for your prompts. Questions FAQs What does a generative engine optimization agency do? It helps AI tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Google's AI Overviews find, understand and cite your brand. Typical services are a baseline audit, technical fixes, content work, off-site work and repeated measurement. How do I choose a GEO agency? Ask every candidate the same questions and compare written answers: how prompts are chosen, what the baseline is, what will change on your site, which outside sources they will work on, what they cannot promise and what you own if you leave. What should I look for when hiring a GEO agency? Look for an inspectable method: a prompt list you approve, raw answers, mentions and citations reported separately, named changes, dated case studies with caveats, and clear ownership of your data and content. How much does a GEO agency cost? We found no independent data on typical fees, and published ranges from agencies disagree. OpenServed found that none of 142 GEO case studies stated a budget. Compare deliverables, scope, tool fees and your team's time, not the monthly number. How do I compare GEO services agencies? Send each the same request: a sample report, a dated case study, a first-month plan, an owner list and a proposed scope. Score method, fit, delivery, proof and terms in one table, and add the hours your own team will spend. What are the red flags when hiring a GEO agency? Guarantees of citations or rankings, no baseline, prompts you cannot see or that contain your brand name, one AI tool only, a score with no method, a price with no deliverables and a contract that locks your data in their tool. What does a GEO consultant do? A consultant reviews your baseline, advises on a plan and checks the work, while your team does the writing and fixes. An agency also does the work. Ask both the same questions. Can an agency guarantee citations in ChatGPT or Google AI Overviews? No. Google says no one can guarantee a number one ranking, and AI answers vary. SparkToro found under a 1 in 100 chance of the same brand list twice. Treat any guarantee as a red flag. How long does GEO take to show results? Access and fact fixes can change retrieval-based answers within weeks, and OpenAI says robots.txt changes can take about 24 hours to apply. Content and off-site work take longer. OpenServed found a six-month median in published agency case studies. Which GEO platform lets agencies manage multiple client accounts? Several AI visibility tools offer agency or multi-client plans. Check prompts, engines and exports before you buy, and test any tool against a hand baseline. Our guide to AI brand visibility tools compares what they track and what they cost. Connect only the data and tools it needs, add checks between steps, and put a named person at every gate that could reach a customer or cost money. Build a fixed workflow first and use autonomous agents only where the path cannot be known. Measure value and control quality, then widen scope. 01 Anthropic advises finding the simplest solution and adding complexity only when needed. Workflows follow predefined code paths. Agents direct their own process. 02 Use a six-layer architecture: data and identity, knowledge, tools, orchestration, controls and human approval, and observability. 03 Keep the CRM and warehouse as systems of record. Agents or rules propose changes, and the tool that owns the setting carries them out after approval. 04 Set review gates by what a mistake would cost. Always approve published content, launches, budget changes, email sends, claims and customer data use. 05 Put banned claims, disclosures, links and suppression lists in code checks, not in prompts. 06 Gartner predicts over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027, and 70% of CMOs say their marketing processes are not mature enough to scale AI. 07 Track value measures and control measures, such as reviewer changes and factual-error rate. To build an AI marketing agent system, start with one narrow task and a written list of its steps. Connect only the data and tools that task needs, add checks between the steps, and put a named person at every gate where a mistake would reach a customer or cost money. Build it as a fixed workflow first, and use a more autonomous agent only where the path cannot be known in advance. Measure the results and the quality of your controls, then widen the scope. This guide explains the parts of such a system, a six-layer architecture, how workflows and agents differ, how to design human review, and a nine-step build plan. It also covers readiness data, permissions, measurement and a worked example. We cite only sources we could read at the publisher, and we label practitioners’ frameworks as such, since there is no industry standard for this architecture. 01 Chapter 1 · 1 min What is an AI marketing agent system? An AI marketing system is a set of connected parts that do marketing work with the help of language models: research, briefs, drafts, lead scoring, routing, campaign checks and reports. The parts share data, follow written rules and report to people. It differs from a single AI tool because it joins steps across your CRM, content system, email platform, analytics and ad accounts. Some call this approach AI growth marketing: search, content and automation working as one engine, with people reviewing what matters. At Reinforce Lab we use the term AI Growth Systems for the same idea, and our guide to what an AI growth system is explains it. End of chapter 1 Next: What is agentic marketing, and what can AI agents do in marketing? → 02 Chapter 2 · 2 min What is agentic marketing, and what can AI agents do in marketing? Agentic marketing means marketing work that AI agents carry out in part: they pursue a goal, choose steps and use tools, inside limits that people set. The term has no official definition, so vendors use it in different ways. We use it for the system this guide describes. An AI marketing agent is software that uses a language model to work toward a marketing goal. For example, it can read a report, draft an email or update a field in your CRM. It is different from a chat assistant, because it takes actions in your tools and not only answers questions. Which jobs suit an AI agent for marketing? Preparing weekly reports and flagging odd changes in the numbers. Researching a topic or a competitor and writing a summary with sources. Scoring and routing new leads by rules you write down. Drafting briefs, outlines and first drafts for a person to edit. Checking campaign setup, tags and links before launch. Drafting personalized outreach for a person to review, using fields from your CRM. Summarizing campaign performance and suggesting what to test next. Start with bounded, repeatable, measurable tasks. Keep customer-facing content, budgets and claims behind a person’s approval. The nine-step plan below shows how. How do you use an AI agent for marketing? Pick one task. Write the steps as you do them today. Give the agent only the tools and data that task needs. Run it in read-only mode first, check every output, and widen its permissions only after it has been right for weeks. End of chapter 2 Next: Workflows or agents: what should you build? → Reinforce Lab service · AI Growth Systems Want one AI marketing workflow designed with review gates? Reinforce Lab starts with a free diagnostic of your Google and AI search visibility and a 90-day plan. See AI Growth Systems → Or get a free diagnostic first 03 Chapter 3 · 1 min Workflows or agents: what should you build? Anthropic, which publishes guidance on building agents, draws a clear line. Workflows are systems where language models and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths. Agents are systems where the model dynamically directs its own process and tool use. Its advice is to find the simplest solution possible and to increase complexity only when needed, which may mean not building an agentic system at all. Agentic systems often trade latency and cost for better task performance. Workflows offer predictability and consistency for well-defined tasks, and agents suit open-ended problems where you cannot predict the number of steps. Anthropic also warns that agents’ autonomy means higher costs and the potential for errors to build up from step to step, and recommends extensive testing in sandboxes with guardrails. For marketing, that means most tasks should be workflows: a fixed chain of steps, with checks and a gate. Use an agent where a task is open-ended, such as researching a market across many sources, and keep it inside tight limits. End of chapter 3 Next: Five patterns and where they fit marketing → 04 Chapter 4 · 1 min Five patterns and where they fit marketing Anthropic describes patterns that you can combine. The table maps them to marketing jobs. The marketing examples are ours, except where Anthropic names them. Pattern What it does Marketing example Prompt chaining Splits a task into fixed steps, each using the last output, with checks between them Outline, check the outline against rules, then write the draft. Anthropic also names writing marketing copy and then translating it. Routing Classifies an input and sends it to a specialized next step Sort inbound inquiries into sales, support and partnership paths Orchestrator and workers A central model breaks down a task, delegates and combines the results Research a topic across several sources and merge the findings Evaluator and optimizer One model generates and another critiques, in a loop Draft a brief, score it against a rubric, revise Autonomous agent The model plans and uses tools in a loop, pausing for human input An open-ended research task with stop conditions and approval points End of chapter 4 Next: A six-layer architecture → 05 Chapter 5 · 1 min A six-layer architecture Practitioners describe the layers in different ways. The version below combines the common parts. Skip a layer and the system becomes useless or risky. Layer Job Typical parts 1. Data and identity Holds the facts the system may read, and who each person or account is across channels CRM, warehouse, analytics, consent records 2. Knowledge Holds approved brand rules, offers, product facts and claims for retrieval A knowledge base, approved-claims library, style guide 3. Tools Lets the system read and act: create a draft, update a record, pause a campaign APIs, connectors, MCP servers for CMS, CRM, email, ads, analytics 4. Orchestration Runs the steps in order, handles retries and handoffs between steps and people Workflow code, automation platforms, step limits 5. Controls and human approval Enforces permissions, spend caps, privacy rules, checks and approvals Review queues, code checks, scoped access 6. Observability and measurement Records what happened and whether it worked Run logs, alerts, evaluation sets, dashboards One principle holds across the sources we read: your CRM and warehouse stay the systems of record. If identity is messy, every agent repeats the mess faster. Keep decisions and actions separate. An agent or rule proposes a change with a reason, and the tool that owns the setting carries it out after an approval that matches the risk, with a log of who approved it. End of chapter 5 Next: What technical stack do you need to build an AI marketing agent? → 06 Chapter 6 · 1 min What technical stack do you need to build an AI marketing agent? You do not need a big stack to start. An autonomous AI marketing agent usually has the same few parts, whether you build it or buy it: Part What it does Keep it simple by Model Reads the task and writes or decides. Starting with one model and one task. Orchestration Runs the steps in order, calls tools and handles retries. Using a workflow tool before writing your own code. Tools and connections Lets the agent read your CRM, ad account, analytics and CMS. Giving read access first and write access later. Knowledge store Holds brand rules, approved facts and past results. Starting with a short, approved document set. Review queue Sends drafts and actions to a person for approval. Requiring approval for anything that goes public or spends money. Logs and measures Records what the agent did and what happened next. Logging every action from day one. This matches the six layers above. The stack is the set of tools you choose for each layer. Pick the smallest set that does one job well, then add parts when a real need appears. End of chapter 6 Next: How should human review work? → 07 Chapter 7 · 1 min How should human review work? Design review before you build the agent. Set each gate by what a mistake would cost, not by how confident the model sounds, because models are often wrong in fluent prose. One practitioner framework sorts actions into three levels, which we find useful: Level Marketing actions Always approve Published content, paid campaign launches, budget changes, email sends, price or results claims, anything that uses customer data Spot-check a sample Internal drafts, keyword clusters, competitor summaries Usually safe to automate Formatting, tagging, scheduling approved drafts, routine report generation A related model uses four autonomy bands: human-only, AI-assisted drafting, approval-gated automation and bounded autonomous execution. Every workflow sits in exactly one band, and the band sets its permissions, approvals and monitoring. Keep most work at the draft-only band longer than feels necessary. Make the reviewer real. A reviewer needs to understand the output, to actually read it, and to have the authority to change or stop it. A person clicking “approve” on a queue of forty items they cannot judge is a logged rubber stamp, not oversight. Limit the queue size, show the evidence next to each item and track how often reviewers change or reject output. A rate near zero may mean the review is not working. End of chapter 7 Next: What goes in the knowledge layer? → 08 Chapter 8 · 1 min What goes in the knowledge layer? The knowledge layer is what stops the system from improvising. It holds the approved information that drafts must draw on, kept in one place and owned by a named person. A useful starting set has six parts: Product and service facts: what you sell, who it is for, prices or price ranges, limits and what is not included. An approved-claims library: statements you may make, each with its source and date, and a list of claims you may not make. Brand voice rules: tone, words to use and avoid, and two or three examples of writing you like. Required disclosures: legal notices, affiliate or sponsorship statements, and regulated wording. Customer and market facts: your ideal customer profile, segments and objections, without personal data. Past results: a few strong examples and the reasons they worked, so the system learns from your own record. Review this layer on a set schedule, and whenever a price, offer or rule changes. If the knowledge is old, every draft will be old as well. Keep it separate from the prompts, so a person can update a fact without editing code, and so the system can show which source each statement came from. End of chapter 8 Next: A nine-step build plan → 09 Chapter 9 · 1 min A nine-step build plan Pick one narrow task. Content briefs, lead scoring or report drafts work. “Run marketing” does not. Check first whether the task should be automated at all. List the steps in plain words. A fixed list is a chain. Branches mean routing. Connect only the tools the task needs. Read access comes first. Publishing, sending and budget changes come last. Load the grounding material. Brand rules, product facts, an approved-claims library, required disclosures and a few past examples. Put checks between steps. Length limits, banned claims, disclosures, broken links and suppression lists belong in code, where a check is cheap and certain. A prompt cannot guarantee them. Add an evaluator pass if you can write the rubric. If you cannot, skip it. Gate anything public or paid behind a person. Log every run. Inputs, sources with dates, tool calls, outputs, reviewer decisions, cost and time. Measure, then widen the scope. Test in a sandbox or a small pilot first, with normal and odd inputs, and add autonomy one level at a time. End of chapter 9 Next: How do you set permissions and protect data? → 10 Chapter 10 · 1 min How do you set permissions and protect data? Give each agent only the applications, fields and actions its task needs. Prefer read-only, draft-only or sandbox access, and remove tool functions the agent does not need, instead of trusting it to skip them. Run the agent under its own identity rather than someone’s personal login, so each action can be scoped, audited and revoked. Treat reading analytics, publishing, reading CRM records, updating a lead, sending email and moving budget as separate permissions. Agents that read web pages or files can be steered by instructions hidden in that content, a risk called prompt injection. Security practitioners recommend minimizing the tools an agent can call, granting the least permissions each tool needs, requiring human approval for high-impact actions and enforcing authorization in downstream systems instead of trusting the model. Keep personal data out of tools without a data-handling agreement, and check consent and local law before you use customer data in a new way. End of chapter 10 Next: How do agents handle context, memory and failure? → 11 Chapter 11 · 1 min How do agents handle context, memory and failure? A system that runs for many steps needs rules for what it knows, when it must stop and what happens when something breaks. Anthropic’s guidance gives a useful base. It says an agent should gain “ground truth” from its environment at each step, such as tool results, to judge its progress, and that agents can pause for human feedback at checkpoints or when they hit blockers. It also recommends stopping conditions, such as a maximum number of iterations, to maintain control, and says the design and documentation of an agent’s tools deserve as much care as its prompts. For marketing, translate that into five rules. Give each run only the context it needs, and keep long-term facts in the knowledge layer, not in a chat history. Check each tool result before the next step. Set a step limit and a spend limit. Stop and escalate when data is missing or sources conflict, and never guess. Log the failure with the inputs, so that a person can fix the cause and not only the symptom. End of chapter 11 Next: What does the readiness data say? → 12 Chapter 12 · 1 min What does the readiness data say? Surveys of large organizations suggest caution. They are not forecasts for a small team. Gartner predicted in June 2025 that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027, because of rising costs, unclear business value or inadequate risk controls. It also found “agent washing,” with only about 130 real agentic vendors among thousands. Gartner’s 2026 CMO Spend Survey of 401 marketing leaders found that 70% say their internal marketing processes are not mature enough to implement and scale AI, and only 30% report mature or fully developed AI readiness. Most were at companies with over $1 billion in revenue. Gartner’s 2025 marketing technology survey found average stack utilization of 49%, 29% of leaders with agents in production, and 45% of those with pilots or production agents reporting that vendor agents were not meeting expectations. The message is to define value first, start small and keep the controls simple. End of chapter 12 Next: How do you measure the system? → 13 Chapter 13 · 1 min How do you measure the system? Track two sets of measures. One shows whether the system creates value. The other shows whether the value is real and safe. Value measures Control measures Time saved per task, cycle time from request to live Share of outputs changed or rejected by reviewers Qualified leads, conversions, revenue per message Factual-error rate found at review Cost per asset or per qualified lead Policy violations and incidents Response time to new leads Exceptions and escalations Record a baseline for 4 to 8 weeks before you start, and compare after the pilot. Results move for many reasons, so treat a change as a sign to investigate. End of chapter 13 Next: Worked example: a content-to-lead system for a B2B firm → 14 Chapter 14 · 1 min Worked example: a content-to-lead system for a B2B firm This is an illustration, not a client result. Imagine a 15-person B2B services firm that wants more qualified leads from its guides and fewer delays in follow-up. It plans one system with three connected workflows, built in this order. First, a lead intake workflow. A form creates a CRM record, tags the source and routes the inquiry. A model reads the free-text message to label topic and urgency, and drafts a first reply from approved facts. A salesperson reviews and sends each draft. Second, a content workflow. A strategist approves a brief. The system attaches a dated source pack. A writer drafts from the brief and sources. An editor checks each claim. The system then runs checks for links, tags and consent, and creates tasks for email and sales. Third, a weekly report workflow. The system pulls Search Console, analytics and CRM numbers into a fixed template and drafts a short narrative. An analyst verifies the figures. The team starts each workflow in shadow mode, where the AI step runs next to a person doing the task today, and compares the outputs. It tracks response time, qualified leads from the guides, reviewer changes and factual errors. After 90 days it keeps the steps with low error rates and removes the rest. Only then does it consider letting the system act without approval, and only for formatting and scheduling. End of chapter 14 Next: Should you build or buy? → 15 Chapter 15 · 1 min Should you build or buy? We found no independent data on typical costs. The choice depends on your team and your data. Buying a platform suits standard jobs, such as email flows or lead routing, where the vendor has proven features. Building with an automation tool or code suits jobs that depend on your own data, rules and approvals. Many teams do both: buy the platforms and build the glue and the controls. Before you buy, audit what you own, since utilization of existing tools is often low, and ask each vendor what its agent can see, what it can change and what logs and approval controls it provides. Our AI workflow automation , marketing automation and lead generation systems pages describe how we approach these builds. End of chapter 15 Next: What are the common mistakes? → 16 Chapter 16 · 1 min What are the common mistakes? Starting with an agent. Most tasks need a workflow. Skipping the data layer. Messy identity and unchecked facts spread faster with automation. Giving write access too early. Start read-only and draft-only. Rubber-stamp review. Make reviewers real, and track their changes. Putting rules in prompts. Banned claims, disclosures and suppression lists belong in code. No logs. Without records you cannot learn or investigate. Many pilots, no system. One connected workflow beats five separate experiments. No owner. Each workflow needs one named person who is accountable. End of chapter 16 Next: Our interest in this topic → 17 Chapter 17 · 1 min Our interest in this topic Reinforce Lab builds AI Growth Systems and sells the services named above. We have an interest in this method, and nothing here is paid placement. Jamil Ahmed, who wrote this guide, is a Semrush Ambassador, and Reinforce Lab uses affiliate links for some tools. Read our FTC and affiliate disclosure . You can read about our AI Growth Systems or get your free diagnostic . End of chapter 17 Next: Final thoughts → 18 Chapter 18 · 1 min Final thoughts A good AI marketing system is more plumbing than magic: clean data, approved knowledge, narrow tools, fixed steps, checks in code, real human review and honest measurement. Build one workflow, prove it, and widen the scope only when the record shows it works. Back matter Glossary A to Z A Agent A system where a model directs its own process and tool use in a loop. H Human gate A point where a named person must approve before work moves on. P Prompt injection Instructions hidden in content that try to steer an AI tool that reads it. S Shadow mode Running an AI step alongside a person doing the same task, and comparing outputs. S System of record The main database for a type of data, such as the CRM for contacts. W Workflow A system where models and tools follow predefined code paths. Questions FAQs How do you build an AI marketing agent system? Start with one narrow task and its written steps, connect only the tools it needs, load approved brand facts, add code checks between steps, gate anything public or paid behind a person, log every run, and measure before widening scope. What is the architecture of an AI marketing system? A common design has six layers: data and identity, knowledge such as approved claims, tools and connectors, orchestration, controls with human approval, and observability with logs. There is no industry standard, so treat this as a practitioner framework. What is the difference between a workflow and an agent? Anthropic defines workflows as systems where models and tools follow predefined code paths, and agents as systems where the model directs its own process and tool use. It advises the simplest solution and adding complexity only when needed. How do you build a human-in-the-loop AI marketing system? Design review first. Always require approval for published content, launches, budget changes, email sends, price or results claims and use of customer data. Spot-check internal drafts, and automate formatting and scheduling. Make reviewers real and track their changes. Which marketing tasks should an AI agent do first? Bounded, repeatable, measurable ones such as report preparation, lead routing, tagging, data-quality checks, anomaly alerts and scheduling approved assets. Avoid starting with customer-facing content or budget control. How do you keep an AI marketing agent safe? Give it least-privilege access, start read-only, run it under its own identity, enforce rules in code, require approval for high-impact actions, log every action and guard against instructions hidden in web content. What is AI growth marketing? The phrase describes search, content and automation working together as one engine, with AI doing repetitive work and people reviewing what matters. Reinforce Lab calls this approach AI Growth Systems. Are marketing teams ready to scale AI agents? Surveys of large companies suggest not yet. Gartner's 2026 CMO survey found 70% say marketing processes are not mature enough to scale AI, and its 2025 martech survey found 45% of those with agents said vendor agents missed expectations. How do you measure an AI marketing system? Track value measures such as cycle time, qualified leads and cost per asset, and control measures such as reviewer change rate, factual-error rate, policy violations and incidents. Record a baseline of 4 to 8 weeks first. Should you build or buy an AI marketing system? Buy platforms for standard jobs and build the glue and controls for jobs that depend on your own data and approvals. We found no independent cost data. Audit tools you own and ask vendors what their agents can see, change and log. What is agentic marketing? Marketing work that AI agents carry out in part: they pursue a goal, choose steps and use tools inside limits that people set. The term has no official definition, so vendors use it in different ways. What are AI agents for marketing? Software that uses a language model to work toward a marketing goal, such as preparing a report, researching a topic, scoring leads or drafting content for review. They act in your tools, not only answer questions. How do you use an AI agent for marketing? Pick one bounded task, write down its steps, give the agent only the tools and data it needs, run it read-only first, check every output and widen permissions only after weeks of accurate results. What is an AI marketing agent? An AI marketing agent is software that uses a language model to pursue a marketing goal by choosing steps and using tools, within limits and human approval that you set. How do you build an AI marketing agent system architecture? Build it in layers: inputs and goals, a knowledge layer, the agent or workflow, tools with limited permissions, a human review step and a measurement layer. Start with one job, read-only access and approval for every action. What is the technical stack for an autonomous AI marketing agent? A model, an orchestration tool, connections to your marketing tools, a knowledge store, a review queue and logs. Start small and add parts only when a real need appears. What are AI marketing agents? AI marketing agents are software that can plan and carry out marketing tasks, such as researching topics, drafting content or routing leads, using tools you connect. A person should approve anything public or costly. Start by mapping one process, find where work waits or repeats, automate the frequent, rule-based, internal, low-risk steps, and keep a person at every gate that could reach a customer. 01 Start with the bottleneck, not the tool. Map one process and mark where work waits, repeats or is copied by hand. 02 Gartner's 2026 CMO survey of 401 leaders: 70% say their marketing processes are not mature enough to scale AI, and only 30% report mature readiness. Most respondents were at $1 billion plus companies. 03 Gartner's 2025 martech survey: stack utilization was 49%. Audit what you own before you buy more. 04 Gartner found 29% of marketing tech leaders have AI agents in production, and 45% of those with pilots or agents say vendor agents are not meeting expectations. 05 McKinsey's 2025 survey of 1,993 respondents: 88% report regular AI use in a function, but about one-third have begun to scale. 06 Let AI write the narrative, never the numbers. Pull figures from the source system. 07 Use an autonomy ladder: suggest, draft, act with approval, act and report. Most marketing tasks should stay at levels one to three. Marketing workflow automation is the use of software, and increasingly AI, to move marketing work from step to step without people carrying it by hand: from request to brief, draft, review, publish and report. To start, map one process, find where work waits or gets repeated, and automate the steps that are frequent, rule-based, internal and low risk. Keep a person at every gate where a mistake would reach a customer. This guide explains what marketing workflow automation is, how it differs from customer-facing automation, and what the evidence says about readiness. It then gives a way to choose where to start, eight workflows to automate first, an autonomy ladder, a build plan and a worked example. We cite only sources we could read at the publisher, and we say when a figure is a survey of large companies or a practitioner’s framework. 01 Chapter 1 · 1 min What is marketing workflow automation? A marketing workflow is the path that work takes inside a team: a campaign request arrives, someone writes a brief, assets are made, reviewers approve them, they go live, and results are reported. Marketing workflow automation connects those steps so that tasks are created, assigned, checked and passed on by rules. AI adds work that rules cannot do, such as drafting a brief from a call transcript, summarizing a long document, checking a draft against a style guide, or writing the first version of a report. It is different from the customer-facing flows that send emails when someone signs up or leaves a cart. Those are covered in our guide to marketing automation examples . Workflow automation is about how your own team works. Both can use AI, and a good plan treats them together, because a customer flow still needs a brief, an approval and a report. End of chapter 1 Next: What does the evidence say about readiness? → 02 Chapter 2 · 2 min What does the evidence say about readiness? Most surveys come from large organizations. They are useful as a warning, and less useful as a forecast for a small team. Four findings stand out. Use is wide, scale is not. McKinsey’s 2025 survey of 1,993 respondents in 105 countries found that 88% report regular AI use in at least one business function, up from 78% a year before. But most organizations are still experimenting or piloting, and about one-third say they have begun to scale. McKinsey says marketing and sales is among the functions that most often report AI use. Marketing teams are not ready. Gartner’s 2026 CMO Spend Survey, conducted from January to March 2026 among 401 marketing leaders, found that CMOs allocate an average of 15.3% of their marketing budgets to AI. It reports that 70% of CMOs say becoming an AI leader is a critical goal, yet 70% also say their internal marketing processes are not mature enough to implement and scale AI, and only 30% report mature or fully developed AI readiness. Most respondents were at companies with over $1 billion in revenue. Tools go unused. Gartner’s 2025 Marketing Technology Survey reports that average martech stack utilization is 49%, up from 33% in 2023, and that 77% of respondents were at companies with $1 billion or more in revenue. A tool you do not use is waste, so audit what you have before you buy more. Agents are early. The same Gartner survey found that 29% of marketing technology leaders have AI agents in production and 52% are piloting. Of those with pilots or agents in production, 45% report that vendor-offered agents are not meeting expectations for business performance. The lesson is to start small, with processes you understand, and to measure results before you scale. End of chapter 2 Next: Where should you start? → Reinforce Lab service · AI Workflow Automation Want one marketing workflow mapped and automated? Reinforce Lab starts with a free diagnostic of your Google and AI search visibility and a 90-day plan. See AI workflow automation → Or get a free diagnostic first 03 Chapter 3 · 1 min Where should you start? It is tempting to ask what AI can automate. A better question is where your work currently slows down. Draw the path from request to report, and mark the places where people wait, repeat work, search for information or copy data from one tool to another. Those are the candidates. Then score each one on five points. Question A good first candidate How often does it happen? Daily or weekly Does it follow clear rules? Yes, most of the steps are the same each time Is it internal? Yes, not sent straight to customers What if it goes wrong? A small, fixable error Can you measure it? You know the time or error rate today Process comes before tools. Pick one process that already hurts, define what success looks like, and build around that. End of chapter 3 Next: Eight workflows to automate first → 04 Chapter 4 · 2 min Eight workflows to automate first Workflow What gets automated Where AI helps Human gate 1. Campaign request intake A form creates a task, assigns an owner and a due date Drafts a brief from the request and past campaigns Owner approves the brief 2. Content production Brief, source pack, draft, edit and publish stages with owners Drafts from the brief and sources only Editor checks every claim 3. Review and approval Routes items to the right reviewer and logs decisions Checks drafts against written rules Named person approves 4. Lead routing Form to CRM, owner assignment, Slack or email alert Reads free-text messages to judge topic and urgency Owner decides the reply 5. Repurposing A published piece creates tasks for social, email and sales Drafts summaries and first versions per channel Channel owner edits and approves 6. Pre-launch QA Checks links, tracking tags, consent and suppression lists Spots missing or odd items Owner signs off the launch 7. Reporting Pulls numbers from source systems into a fixed template Drafts the narrative and flags unusual changes Analyst checks figures and claims 8. SEO operations Alerts for drops, refresh lists, brief templates from Search Console data Drafts briefs and summaries of what changed SEO lead decides what to do One practitioner rule is worth keeping for reporting: let AI write the narrative, never the numbers. Figures should come from an export or an API, and not from the model. Three things break accuracy fastest: asking the model to calculate, letting it claim a cause from a correlation, and feeding it screenshots in place of data. Another practitioner view is to begin content automation with support jobs, such as turning interview transcripts into briefs, repurposing a long piece or checking a draft against a style guide, and not with fully generated articles, since that is where brand and quality risk concentrate. End of chapter 4 Next: How much freedom should AI have? → 05 Chapter 5 · 1 min How much freedom should AI have? A practical way to set limits is an autonomy ladder. This is a practitioner framework, not a standard, but it is easy to use. Suggest. The AI researches and recommends, and a person acts. Draft. The AI prepares the output in the real tool, such as a CRM note or campaign draft, and a person edits and approves it. Act with approval. The AI does the task after a person approves each action. Act and report. The AI acts within strict limits and logs everything for review. Most marketing tasks should stay at levels one to three. Move up one level at a time, and only for a task where the record shows few errors. Before any AI step touches live work, run it in shadow mode: let it work in parallel with the person who does the task today, and compare the outputs. Put approval gates at positioning and messaging, factual claims about price or results, audience choices and any new use of personal data, all customer-facing content before first use, major budget changes and anything regulated or hard to undo. End of chapter 5 Next: How do you build one workflow? → 06 Chapter 6 · 1 min How do you build one workflow? Write the process as it runs today. List each step, who does it, how long it takes and where it waits. Pick one outcome that you can measure, such as the days from request to publish. Define the states. For example: requested, briefed, in production, in review, approved, live, reported. Each move needs a clear condition. Automate the plain parts first. Task creation, reminders, routing, status changes and notifications need no AI. Add AI where rules cannot work. Drafts, summaries, classification and checks. Give it a fixed brief and only approved sources. Add the human gates. Name the person at each, and write what they may approve. Run in shadow mode, then pilot with one team or one campaign. Measure and review after a month. Keep what works, remove what does not. End of chapter 6 Next: Which tools do you need? → 07 Chapter 7 · 1 min Which tools do you need? You usually need three kinds. A work management tool holds the tasks, owners and statuses; vendors such as Wrike and StoryChief publish guides on marketing workflows in their tools. An orchestration tool, such as Zapier, Make or n8n, moves data between systems. Your CRM and email platform are the system of record for contacts and customer messages. These are examples that vendors name, not recommendations, and features and prices change. Before you buy, audit the tools you have. Gartner found stack utilization of 49%, so you may already own what you need. Our AI workflow automation service covers this kind of design, and our marketing automation service covers customer-facing flows. End of chapter 7 Next: How is a workflow different from an AI agent? → 08 Chapter 8 · 1 min How is a workflow different from an AI agent? A workflow is the whole path that work takes. An agent is a piece of software that handles a repeatable step inside it, often by using a language model and tools. A MarTech article from November 2026 makes the same point: accelerating one isolated task can push bottlenecks downstream to other teams, and the hard part is connecting separate pilots into a system. So design the workflow first, then decide which steps an agent should handle. A workflow with clear states, owners and gates is easier to automate than a loose set of tasks, whether you use plain rules, an AI step or an agent. End of chapter 8 Next: What should a workflow card contain? → 09 Chapter 9 · 1 min What should a workflow card contain? Write one short card for each workflow, so everyone knows how it works and who owns it. Use the same fields every time. Field Example entry Name and owner Guide production, owned by the content lead Trigger An approved request in the intake form States Requested, briefed, in production, in review, approved, live, reported Inputs Brief, dated source pack, brand rules AI steps and limits Drafts from the brief and the pack only, never adds facts Human gates Strategist approves the brief, editor checks claims, owner approves launch Data used No personal data. Only approved tools. Measures Days to live, rework rate, errors found at review Review date Monthly for the first quarter, then quarterly The card is also your audit trail. If something goes wrong, you can see what the workflow was allowed to do and who approved each step. End of chapter 9 Next: Who should own marketing workflow automation? → 10 Chapter 10 · 1 min Who should own marketing workflow automation? Someone must own each workflow and its results. In a small team, that is often the marketing lead or a marketing operations person, with a developer or an outside partner for the technical links. In a larger team, marketing operations usually owns the design, and each channel owner approves the gates in their area. Marketing needs a good working relationship with IT. Gartner’s martech survey notes that half of martech funding comes from outside marketing, including 34% from IT, so IT should be part of the plan from the start. Agree early who handles access, security and vendor review. End of chapter 10 Next: What does an end-to-end campaign workflow look like? → 11 Chapter 11 · 1 min What does an end-to-end campaign workflow look like? Campaign work is where many workflows break, because it crosses teams, tools and channels. One practitioner guide describes a controlled sequence of define, build, launch, monitor and evaluate, with an observable acceptance condition for each move, not a vague status such as “nearly finished”. It advises defining one primary business outcome and an accountable owner, specifying the audience, exclusions, offer, channels and budget, and setting consistent campaign IDs and conversion events across ads, messages, landing pages and CRM records. It also says to gate launch on quality checks of creative, landing pages, consent, suppression lists and tracking, and to reconcile ad-platform conversions with CRM outcomes rather than accept each platform’s account of success. Use this as a template for your own states and gates. The hand-offs between teams, such as from creative to channel owners to analysts, are where an automated task list and a clear record of the approved version save the most time. End of chapter 11 Next: How do you measure it? → 12 Chapter 12 · 1 min How do you measure it? Cycle time from request to live, before and after.
